Its original right-hand semicircular tower (on quadrato foundations) is still to be seen, while its left-hand one incorporated a tomb, presumed to belong to Quintus Aterius, a famous orator at the court of Tiberius, and mentioned by him as the first to get up to refute Tiberius's feigned refusal of the imperial crown.

Marble from that tomb was used to cover the gate in restorations by Honorius in 403 AD, who at the same time blocked the two nearby posterns in the direction of Castra Praetoria and restored the porta Salaria. Unlike the nearby Via Salaria, the via Nomentana, which led to Nomentum, the modern Mentana), was of minor importance.

properties.name: Porta Ostiensis (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Aurelian Walls, Rome.

The original name of the gate was Porta Ostiensis, because it was located at the beginning of via Ostiense, the road that connected Rome and Ostia. Via Ostiense was an important arterial road, as evidenced by the fact that upon entering the gate of the same name, the road split, with one direction leading to the famous Emporium, the great market of Rome.

The gatehouse is flanked by two cylindrical towers, and has two entrances, which had been covered by a second, single-opening gate, built in front of the first by the Byzantine general Belisarius (530s–540s AD).

The structure is due to Maxentius, in the 4th century, but the two towers were heightened by Honorius. Its original — Latin — name was Porta Ostiensis, since it opened on the way to Ostia. Later, it was renamed to the Italian Porta San Paolo, because it was the exit of Rome that led to the Basilica of St. Paul Outside the Walls.

In 549 AD, Rome was under siege; the Ostrogoths of Totila entered through this gate, because of the treason of the Isaurian garrison. 

On 10 September 1943, two days after the armistice between the Allies and Italy had been agreed, Italian military and civil forces tried to block German seizure of the city, with 570 casualties.

properties.name: Porta Padana (Roma, Italia)
properties.description: Rome.

properties.name: Porta Portuensis (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Aurelan Walls, Rome.

It is an ancient city gate, located at the end of Via Portuense, where it meets Via Porta Portese, about a block from the banks of the Tiber in the southern edge of the Rione Trastevere of Rome.

The gate was rebuilt in 1644 as part of the Janiculum Walls which replaced the Porta Portuensis. The gate and walls were built by Vincenzo Maculani; commissioned by Pope Urban VIII. Just outside the gate, a large arsenal was erected by Clement XI starting from 1714.

Until the late 19th century, the Ripa Grande port (then the main river port of the city) was located nearby. The Via Portuense starts from it, which originally connected the city to Portus.

properties.name: Porta Praenestina (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Aurelian Walls, Rome.

The Porta Maggiore, as it came to be known later, is by far the best urban site to visit for an understanding and view of the ancient aqueducts. It is a monumental double archway built of white travertine. It was first known as the Porta Prenestina, perhaps a reference to the road over which is passes (the Via Praenestina). The "gate," built in 52 AD by the emperor Claudius, was originally intended to provide a decorative section of support for two aqueducts, the Aqua Claudia and the Anio Novus. At that time these aqueducts crossed the ancient Via Labicana and Praenestina roads thereby providing the opportunity to create at this location a sort of triumphal arch to the conquest of nature and its conqueror, the emperor Claudius. The two channels of these aqueducts, (the Aqua Claudia and Aqua Anio Novus), one lying on top of the other, can be seen when viewing the cross-section running through the travertine attic at the top of the gate.

The gate was incorporated in the Aurelian Wall in 271 by the emperor Aurelian thus truly turning it into an entrance (gate) to the city. Experts refer to this as an early example of “architectural recycling,” essentially adapting one existing structure, to another use. In this case using an aqueduct as a wall.

properties.name: Porta Querquetulana (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Servian Walls. Rome.

The Porta Querquetulana was one of two known gates in the Servian Wall on the Caelian. It stood between the Porta Caelimontana and Porta Esquilina. The name ‘Porta Querquetulana’ is derived from a grove or wood of oaks that stood just inside the gate. 

In this grove was a shrine, the Larum Querquetulanum sacellum, which stood on the Esquiline. Some place the gate in the valley between the Caelian and the Oppian, but there is no evidence of a Republican street here. The gate must have stood on the crest of the Caelian on the “Via Tusculana”, the road which led SE from the Colosseum valley to the “Via Caelimontana”. As for its lateral E–W position, most scholars place it near the Church of SS. Quattro Coronati. Some place it on the site of the mediaeval Arco di Basile, a monumental aqueduct arch which served as the entrance to the Lateran precinct until demolished in 1604. However, the discovery of an extra-mural Republican cemetery zone just to the W of the Arco di Basile makes it almost certain that the wall and the gate are both to be found in the area of SS. Quattro Coronati.

properties.name: Porta Quirinalis (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Servian Walls. Rome.

Gate in the Servian Wall along the steep N slope of the Quirinal, located near the present-day Via della Quattro Fontane. No architectural remains survive and the position of the gate is estimated based upon the hypothetical path of the Servian Wall and several preserved sections of road.

 The name derives from the nearby sacellum Quirini. Lanciani reports that remains of stairs were seen during excavations in 1892; these cappellaccio steps in opus quadratum may have been associated with the gate.

properties.name: Porta Rauduscula (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Servian Walls. Rome.

Gate in the Servian Wall on the Aventine without identified remains but known from textual sources, especially Varro’s catalogue of gates; in various ways, these sources derive the gate’s name from raudus, ‘copper or bronze’. Since the Capitoline base situates the neighborhood of the vicus portae R(a)udusculanae in Regio XII and, in addition, Varro’s catalogue lists the gate between the Porta Naevia and the Porta Lavernalis, there is general agreement that the Porta Rauduscula marked the intersection of the Servian Wall with a Republican street likely to have followed the central depression of the Aventine. While the existence of a gate is plausible, its identification remains entirely hypothetical.

properties.name: Porta Ratumenta (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Servian Walls, Rome.

Gate in the Servian Wall on the Capitol. The Porta Ratumenna is mentioned only in an anecdote from the early history of Rome, in which the victorious charioteer from Veii, Ratumenna, lost control of his horses, and was taken all the way from Veii to Rome at full speed, only to be thrown from his chariot at the gate which then took its name from him.

 In Plutarch, Ratumenna is thrown from his chariot as soon as his horses reached the Capitol; this suggests that the gate stood at the foot of this hill. Other versions of this story draw a strong connection with the Temple of Iuppiter Optimus Maximus; the horses proceeded to the Area Capitolina (without Ratumenna) to admire the terracotta chariots on the roof of the Temple of Iuppiter Optimus Maximus, or else the horses processed around the temple three times in a lustration. 

There is general scholarly consensus that this gate stood on or around the Capitol. Coarelli hypothesizes that ‘Porta Ratumenna’ was the original, Etruscan name of the Porta Carmentalis. Richardson is especially persuasive. He observes that a team of horses could only have accessed the Area Capitolina via the Clivus Capitolinus, or by the road which led up the saddle between the two summits of the Capitol from the Campus Martius. The latter is the more sensible choice, since the direct route from Veii brought Ratumenna to Rome along the Via Flaminia. Richardson thus identifies the Porta Ratumenna as a gate in the Servian Wall which stood at the top of Michelangelo’s Cordonnata.

properties.name: Porta Salaria (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Aurelian Walls, Rome.

Porta Salaria was part of the Aurelian Walls built by emperor Aurelian in the 3rd century, including pre-existing constructions in order to hasten the works. Under it passed the Via Salaria nova, which joined the Via Salaria vetus ("Old Via Salaria") outside the city. The gate had a single passage and was flanked by two semi-circular towers. The Horti Sallustiani were located in the city just inside the gate.

During the restoration by emperor Honorius in the early 5th century, the arch was strengthened in opus mixtum, and over it three large windows were opened.

The Goth king Alaric I entered Rome from this gate to begin the famous Sack of Rome. In 537 AD the area between Porta Salaria and Castro Pretorio was the location of the siege by the Goth king Witigis against the troops of Belisarius.

During the Middle Ages, unlike other gates of the city, Porta Salaria did not receive a Christian name.

On September 20, 1870 the part of the Aurelian Walls between Porta Salaria and Porta Pia witnessed the end of the Papal States. The gate was damaged by the artillery fire of the Italian troops, and the following year it was demolished. In 1873, it was rebuilt under the design of the architect Virginio Vespignani.

However, in 1921, it was again decided to demolish the gate to open the area to road traffic. The area is now occupied by Piazza Fiume.

properties.name: Porta Salutaris (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Servian Walls. Rome.

Gate in the Servian Wall located along the W edge of the Quirinal, at the top of a natural depression near Via della Dataria; no remains are extant. 

The name of this gate derives from the Temple of Salus, and the likelihood of this site is reinforced by the nearby Compitum: Vicus Salutis. The road passing through the gate, alternatively called the Vicus Salutaris or considered an extension of the Alta Semita, linked the Campus Martius and the Quirinal.

properties.name: Porta Sanqualis (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Servian Walls. Rome.

Gate in the Servian Wall, located on the Quirinal near the Temple of Didius Fidius. The limited remains of the gate which survive in the vicinity of Largo Magnanapoli indicate that it had an elongated rectangular plan with an enclosed inner court.

properties.name: Porta Settimiana (Rome, Italia)
properties.description:
Aurelian Walls, Rome.

Porta Settimiana is one of the gates of the Aurelian walls in Rome. It rises at the northern vertex of the rough triangle traced by the town walls - built by Emperor Aurelian in the 3rd century - in the area of Trastevere an up through the Janiculum.

properties.name: Porta Tiburtina (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Aurelian Walls. Rome.

The gate originally was an arch, built under Augustus, in the point in which three aqueducts (Aqua Marcia, Aqua Julia and Aqua Tepula) passed over the Via Tiburtina. The arch was restored by Emperors Titus and Caracalla.

The arch of Augustus was incorporated in the Aurelian Walls by Emperor Aurelian. At the time of Honorius' restoration, in the 5th century, a second, external opening was built, with five small openings that enlightened the room where the gate was operated.

With time, the gate changed its name into Porta San Lorenzo, because of the presence of the close by basilica of San Lorenzo fuori le Mura. Common people, however, called it Capo de' Bove or Porta Taurina, since the arch of Augustus was decorated with bull skulls.

properties.name: Porta Trigemina (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Servian Walls. Rome.

Important ‘Triple Gate’ in the Republican defenses along the Tiber bank, located somewhere between the S Forum Bovarium and the N tip of the Aventine, at the lower end of the Clivus Publicius.

 A gate of longstanding significance, the Porta Trigemina is mentioned both in connection with work commissioned for the Emporium in 174 BC, and as an area by the late-antique Regionary Catalogues. While this gate apparently functioned as the primary S gate in the section of the Servian Wall along the river, its location remains hypothetical. The remnants of a wall and an arch blocked with reticulate masonry are likely to have been in its vicinity. Lyngby’s suggested identification with the remains of a Grotta Oscura pylon further S along the Tiber bank has, for good reasons, not been accepted by subsequent scholarship.

Most agree that the “Arcus Lentuli et Crispini” is an Augustan renewal of the Porta Trigemina in the form of a monumental arch. Erected in 2 AD under the consuls P. Lentulus Scipio and T. Quinctius Crispinus Valerianus on a site between the S Forum Bovarium and the N tip of the Aventine, potentially on the same spot as the Porta Trigemina, it was destroyed in the 15th c. Since the wording of the dedicatory inscription coincides exactly with that of the “Arcus Dolabellae et Silani” on the Caelian, and since there is a parallel case of Augustan rebuilding, the “Fornix Augusti”, by the bridgehead of the *Pons Aemilius, Coarelli has plausibly discerned a large-scale Augustan program of converting the old city gates into monumental arches. The Porta Trigemina renewed as the Arch of Lentulus and Crispinus may be depicted in a lost relief recorded in the Codex Coburgensis.

Materially, the Arch of Lentulus and Crispinus seems to have replaced the earlier gate, yet since ‘Porta Trigemina’ is attested as a late-antique toponym, our map offers a single index number to represent both. The number is placed at the hypothetical site of the juncture between the Republican circuit wall and the street artery parallel to the river, which led from the S Forum Bovarium to the Emporium.

properties.name: Porta Triumphalis (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Servian Walls. Rome.

The ‘Triumphal Gate’ of Rome, reserved for the spectacular ceremony of a victorious general and his troops entering the Urbs ‘in triumph’. In 14 AD, as an unprecedented honor, the gate was proposed for the passage of Augustus’ funeral procession to the Campus Martius. 

Since Cicero is quite explicit that the prestige this gate bestowed upon entry into the city was far beyond that offered by any other gate in the Servian Wall, it seems safe to conclude, with Coarelli, that the Porta Triumphalis was situated along the course of the city walls. After a long history of scholarly dispute, the Porta Triumphalis is now placed NW of the twin temples of Fortuna and Mater Matuta and identified with one of the double gates of the Porta Carmentalis.

properties.name: Porta Viminalis (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Servian Walls. Rome.

Gate in the Servian Wall on the Viminal, between the Porta Collina and Porta Esquilina. It connects the Vicus Collis Viminalis with the “Via Tiburtina Vetus”. 

 Part of this gate has been discovered in front of the Termini train station in the shape of two converging walls in opus quadratum of peperino (from Gabii). These were part of the side walls of the gate, not just retaining walls for a trapezoidal opening in the Agger. The ground-plan may be reconstructed following Säflund. A line of aqueducts (Aqua Iulia, Aqua Tepula, Aqua Marcia) passed on the N side of the gate into the city.

properties.name: Porticus (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Portico, Rome.

Remains of a Republican portico found near S. Alessio on the NW Aventine, close to the ancient street under Via di S. Sabina; two walls of “yellow tufa” blocks, perpendicular to each other (one L. c. 19 m), were uncovered by Lanciani in the garden just NE of the church. At the intersection of these two walls stood a marble column atop a travertine slab. These remains have been plausibly addressed as a portico, and attributed to the late-Republican period. Recently, Vendittelli proposed that this portico be identified with the colonnades in the precinct of the Temple of Diana Aventina; this, however, is based on the inconclusive placement of Diana’s temple near S. Alessio.

properties.name: Porticus Agrippae (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Portico of Agrippa, Rome

The building was located in the Saepta Julia, a large square in the Campus Martius used for public comitia (assemblies). The square, a large free space surrounded by porticoes, was finished by Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa, admiral and friend of emperor Augustus, in 27 BC. The portico was added in 25 BC, to commemorate Agrippa's naval victories in 31 BC: it took its name from its decorations, which depicted the mythological expedition of Jason.

Studies of the Forma Urbis have located the portico in what is now Via della Minerva, near the basilica of Santa Maria sopra Minerva.

A brickwork wall preserved along the eastern side of the Pantheon has been assigned to the Porticus.

properties.name: Porticus Apollinis (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Portico of Apollo, Rome.

Portico, or porticoes, on the Palatine built by Augustus in close connection with his Temple of Apollo. Erected, perhaps, by 23 BC, these colonnades are known primarily through literary evidence.

 Propertius refers to ‘the golden portico of Phoebus [Apollo]’, due to the overall effect created by its giallo antico columns. The portico was adorned with statues of the 50 daughters of Danaus, which were probably rendered as female herms in a variety of colored marbles; three of these sculptures, datable to the Augustan period and rendered in black ‘nero antico’ marble, were discovered in 1869 by Rosa directly N of the Temple of Apollo. Fragments of similar female herms in red ‘rosso antico’ marble have also been reported. There may also have been statues of the sons of Aegyptus, but this is debated. With or without the additional figures, the use of polychrome marble imported from remote regions of the empire must have created a powerful visual effect. The accounts of Propertius and Ovid are generally thought to suggest that the statues of the Danaids were placed in the intercolumniations of the portico. However, study of the herms leads Balensiefen to propose a two-storeyed porticus with the Danaids placed along the upper storey, though such use of free-standing herms as caryatids would be unique in contemporary architecture.

Modern scholarship often equates the porticus of the Danaids described by Propertius and Ovid with the porticus connected to the Temple of Apollo and the Greek and Latin Library. However, literary sources addressing the Augustan Palatine use the noun ‘porticus’ mostly in the plural, thus the porticus of the Danaids may be just one of the several porticoes in the area. The close physical relation between the Portico of the Danaids and the Temple of Apollo has been placed within the late Republican tradition of building temples on terraces enclosed by porticoes.

properties.name: Porticus Fori Holitorium (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Portico of the Forum Holitorium, Rome.

Late-Republican “gateway” portico at the S end of the Forum Holitorium, just outside the Servian Wall, where it covered the street issuing from a 4th-c. BC gate. 

With parallel arcades, 5 m distant from each other, and exterior semi-columns on both sides, the portico is only partially preserved, without its ends, and consists of two sections which differ slightly in construction and date. The portion closer to the gate, extant to its entablature, is constructed of peperino on travertine footings; its orientation respects that of the other, pre-existing section — a more monumental construction entirely in travertine, though now reduced to mere remnants. Their successive phases or renewals notwithstanding, both sections can be attributed to the 1st c. BC based on materials and style. In its entirety, the portico formed a monumental entranceway to the city — paralleled perhaps only by the Porticus Aemilia (Campus Martius) outside the Porta Fontinalis. Further, the portico articulated the connection between the Circus Flaminius and the Forum Bovarium, both major stations on the triumphal route.

properties.name: Porticus Gaii et Lucii (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Portico of Gaius and Lucius, Rome.

A series of 15 shops (tabernae) and a two-storey arcaded portico ran in front of the Basilica Aemilia and shielded it from the Forum. It is commonly identified as the Porticus of Gaius and Lucius, but sometimes as the porticus Iulia.

properties.name: Porticus Iseum (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Portico of Isis, Rome.

Imposing triportico with central water basin found on a large terrace on the S slopes of the Oppian, in the probable position of the Iseum Metellinum and the sanctuary of Isis et Serapis of Regio III. This identification finds confirmation in the large number of Isiac statuary finds spread throughout this area. Two inscriptions found in the Via Labicana mention Isis. 

Numerous sculptures of Isis and other Egyptian deities have come to light near the Church of SS. Pietro e Marcellino, in Via Merulana–Via Buonarroti and Via dello Statuto to the N, and at scattered points on the Esquiline. Yet none of these finds was discovered in situ. The largest concentration of Isiac statuary was found in a wall 100 m W of SS. Pietro e Marcellino. In 1897 Lanciani argued that the statuary had been scattered from an original location in the area S of Via Curva on high ground above Via Labicana, where most of the Isiac finds were concentrated. On this terraced area on the S slopes of the Oppian, significant architectural remains also came to light.

properties.name: Porticus Liviae (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Portico of Livia, Rome.

A large public recreational complex surrounded by a quadriportico, dedicated in 7 BC, and built on the site of the house of Vedius Pollio, bequeathed to Augustus in 15 BC. 

On the Severan Marble Plan it is called PORTICVS LIVIAE and shown as an enclosed quadriportico within an open courtyard, in which stood a central rectangular feature. As noted by Panella, the latter may be identified either as a fountain, or as Ovid’s altar or temple to Concordia. The location of the portico has been fixed by placing the Marble Plan fragments on the modern network of streets; it lay on the steep N slopes of the Oppian, with steps leading down to the shops of the Clivus Suburanus. The Marble Plan further indicates that it was surrounded by small streets, shops and houses.

 Recent studies have shown that its orientation perpendicular to Via in Selci is still preserved in the ground-plan of modern houses; no trace of the central feature shown on the Marble Plan has been found, but traces of a pavement, possibly part of the Porticus Liviae or Vedius Pollio’s house, were discovered.

properties.name: Porticus Minucia (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Portico of Minucius, Rome.

Celebrated portico in the S Campus Martius, built in the last decade of the 2nd c. BC by M. Minucius Rufus; its colonnade encircled the earlier Temple of the Lares Permarini. The 4th-c. AD Regionary Catalogues list it in Regio IX: Circus Flaminius between the Porticus Philippi and the Crypta Balbi. The portico is shown in just that location on the Severan Marble Plan, where it is labeled MINI[CIA].

properties.name: Porticus Octavia (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Portico of Octavius, Rome.

Portico built by Cn. Octavius near the Theater of Pompey between 167 and 163 BC, the remains of which are yet to be discovered. Augustus restored the structure, keeping the original name of the founder, and placed there the insignia regained from the Dalmatians in 33 BC.

properties.name: Porticus Octaviae (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Portico of Octavia, Rome.

Name for the Augustan renovation of the Republican porticus Metelli, which was located in the area of the Circus Flaminius. The quadriportico followed the NE-SW orientation of the circus and enclosed the Temples of Iuno Regina and Iuppiter Stator. Between 27 and 23 BC a member of the imperial family restored the portico and added a library to the complex; at that time it was renamed ‘Porticus Octaviae’.

Scholarly consensus holds that the porticus Metelli was built by Q. Caecilius Metellus Macedonicus in 146 BC around the temples of Iuno Regina and Iuppiter Stator. Remains of the porticus Metelli are preserved. The pseudo-peripteral hexastyle Temple of Iuno Regina was built by M. Aemilius Lepidus during his censorship in 179 BC with a December 23rd dies natalis shared by the Temple of Diana. It was damaged by the fire of 156 BC. The Temple of Iuppiter Stator was built ex manubiis either in 146 or 131 BC by Q. Caecilius Metellus Macedonicus; its dies natalis was September 5th. Rome’s first marble temple, it was planned by Hermodorus of Salamis.

properties.name: Porticus Philippi (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Portico of Philippus, Rome.

This quadriportico, located along the NE side of the Circus Flaminius between the Porticus Octaviae and the Petronia Amnis, enclosed the Temple of Hercules Musarum. M. Fulvius Nobilior may have built it between 187 and 179 BC, yet according to Ovid and Suetonius, L. Marcius Philippus, who triumphed in 34 or 33 BC, restored the Temple of Hercules Musarum and built the portico around it. Near the temple was the formal gathering place of the collegium poetarum, which may have been established in Rome during the period in which the temple was built.

A fragment of the Severan Marble Plan depicts part of the enclosure; its S façade is a direct continuation of the S wall of the Porticus Octaviae. The outer perimeter of the porticus may have consisted of a wall with only one row of columns. It seems also that, unlike in the Porticus Octaviae, the temple was completely enclosed by the colonnade and lacked a monumental entrance.

properties.name: Porticus Pompeianae (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Porticoes of Pompey, Rome.

The porticoes of Pompey were directly behind the stage building of the Theatrum Pompeium, which was dedicated in 55 BC.

 The Severan Marble Plan provides the general ground-plan: on the N and S were roofed porticoes, behind which stood the Hecatostylum on the N, and shops on the S; on the E stood a roofed portico, with the Curia Pompei in the center and a slightly smaller square structure to its S, also protruding into the “Area Sacra” of Largo Argentina; on the W stood the stage-building (scaenae frons) of Pompey’s Theatre.

properties.name: Porticus Vici Aesculatorum (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Portico of the Vicus Aesculati, Rome.

Remnants of a monumental, double-sided Republican portico were found in the late 19th-c. between the Circus Flaminius and the Tiber in the vicinity of the Navalia, some 7 m beneath Via Arenula. 

The portico has a central longitudinal wall (at least 15 m long, 1 m thick) of opus incertum faced by tufa blocks and topped with profiled travertine blocks; the building techniques suggest a 2nd-c. BC date. On either side of this wall stood a row of columns, six of which are preserved up to a height of c. 3 m. The portico’s total depth, c.18 m, rivals that of Rome’s most notable colonnades, such as those in the Forum Iulium or Forum Augusti. While the total length of this monumental portico remains unknown, it clearly extended for a considerable distance in an E–W direction parallel to an ancient thoroughfare, which has plausibly been addressed as the main avenue of the Vicus Aesc(u)leti; across the street from the portico was the Augustan-era compital shrine of the vicus (Compitum: Vicus Aesc(u)leti).

The portico has been tentatively connected with the Navalia, though a commercial function for this street-side portico in the Vicus Aesc(u)leti seems more likely.

properties.name: Porticus Vispania (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Portico of Vipsania, Rome.

A famous portico built by Agrippa’s sister Vipsania Polla in the Campus Agrippae. It contained Agrippa’s annotated map of the world, which was erected there after his death by Augustus.

properties.name: Regia (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
House of the Pontifex Maximus, Rome.

The Republican headquarters of the Pontifex Maximus at the E end of the Forum, which Roman tradition credited Numa with building. 

The earliest remains date to the late 7th c. BC, and already by the end of the 6th c. BC the Regia assumed its permanent shape as a trapezoidal courtyard with a connected group of three smaller rooms facing the Atrium Vestae, the center room providing access from the street.

 The Regia burned once during the Triumviral period, in 36 BC, but was restored by Cn. Domitius Calvinus. The completed Temple of the Deified Julius Caesar seems to have provided the NE wall of the Regia with an arcuated porch which linked the two buildings.

properties.name: Rostra Augusta (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Speaker's Platform, Rome.

The speakers’ platform completed by Augustus at the W end of the Forum, referred to in the Imperial period as rostra Vetera. 

The Augustan rostra, heavily restored but still visible, incorporated the earlier rostra that Julius Caesar had built in this area of the Forum. Caesar’s rostra consisted of a curving façade which faced the Forum and a narrow platform approached from behind by a stair of 7 steps. Augustus seems to have retained the semicircular stair to the Caesarian rostra, but extended the platform a full 10 m toward the Forum square, widening the entire structure to form a frontal façade c. 24 m in width. The Augustan rostra, which faced the rostra aedis Divi Iulii on the opposite side of the Forum, marked the Forum’s W boundary.

properties.name: Rupes Tarpeia (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Tarpeian Rock, Rome.

The Tarpeian Rock, also known as rupes Tarpeia, was a steep cliff on the Arx from which convicted criminals were thrown to their deaths.

properties.name: Saepta Julia (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Voting Hall, Rome

An open rectangular piazza of extraordinary dimensions (c. 310 x 120 m), enclosed by porticoes in the Campus Martius and intended for the casting of votes by the comitia tributa (assembly of tribes). 

Planned by Julius Caesar in 54 BC, the Saepta was continued by M. Aemilius Lepidus after Caesar’s death and dedicated as the Saepta Iulia in 26 BC by Agrippa to honour Augustus.

 Located E of the Pantheum, Thermae of Agrippa, Stagnum and Hecatostylum, N of the Diribitorium to which it was joined, W of the Isis Campensis temple, and S of the Aqua Virgo, the piazza was framed by two porticoes: the Porticus Meleagri on the , and Portico of Agrippa on the W.

In the Imperial period, the function of the Saepta evolved by necessity to become a center for popular entertainment and relaxation. Agrippa decorated the Saepta lavishly with marble and paintings; two celebrated sculpture groups, one of Olympus and Pan and another depicting Achilles with Chiron, were displayed there in a public picture and sculpture gallery. When not serving the idle crowds of early-Imperial Rome, the immense enclosure could house gladiatorial combats, including those of Agrippa’s funerary games. After the Saepta burned in the conflagration of 80 AD, it was rebuilt, presumably without a change in plan, by Domitian and frequently served as a market for luxury goods.

properties.name: Septizodium (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Monumental facade, Rome.

The Septizodium was built in 203 AD by Emperor Septimius Severus. The origin of the name "Septizodium" is from Septisolium, from the Latin for temple of seven suns, and was probably named for the seven planetary deities (Saturn, Sun, Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus) or for the fact that it was originally divided into seven parts. The building had no known practical purpose and was probably meant to be a decorative façade, known as a Nymphaeum. Ancient and medieval sources describe its purpose as being intended to impress Severus' fellow Africans as they entered the city, as it was located at the place where the Via Appia passes the Palatine and leads east towards the Forum Romanum. Other examples of septizodia are known, all from Africa.

Ammianus Marcellinus refers to the building in an ambiguous passage: "The plebs...had come together at the Septemzodium, a popular place, where Marcus Aurelius built a Nymphaeum in a rather ostentatious style."

properties.name: Stagnum Agrippae (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Lake of Agrippa, Rome.

A large artificial basin filled with still water created by M. Agrippa in a natural, marshy depression (the palus Caprae) just W of his Thermae in the central Campus Martius.

Most believe the Stagnum received its water from the Aqua Virgo and drained into the Euripus. If fed by the Virgo, the water would have been quite clear and cool, so perhaps the Stagnum functioned as a natatio (swimming pool) for the Thermae of Agrippa. The lake was also broad and deep enough to be navigable; Tacitus describes a lavish banquet held aboard a pleasure barge which was steered about the Stagnum by tugs. Apparently, there was also sufficient room on the Stagnum quays (crepidines) for brothels and parading harlots. Further, as darkness fell, the adjacent Nemus of Agrippa was filled with song and twinkling lights; by the mid-1st c. AD the surrounding area had become a residential neighborhood.

properties.name: Tabularium (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Public Records Office, Rome. 

The large, polygonal structure of the late Republic, located on the saddle between the two summits of the Capitoline, overlooking the W end of the Forum Romanum, is conventionally known as the ‘Tabularium’ (public records office, depository of the tabulae publicae). 

The imposing remains of this structure were incorporated into Michelangelo’s Palazzo Senatorio, and its high colonnaded galleries still dominate the Forum. The masonry is dated either to the Sullan period or to the 2nd c. BC, but excavations under Palazzo Senatorio indicate that the Tabularium was built, in part, over ruins damaged in the Capitoline fire of 83 BC; its current footprint, therefore, was laid down after 83. This date is confirmed by the epigraphic evidence.

properties.name: Thermae Agrippae (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Baths of Agrippa, Rome.

In 25 BC Rome’s first public baths were built by Agrippa in the Campus Martius, just S of the Pantheum, W of the Saepta Iulia and the Porticus Agrippae and directly E of the Stagnum Agrippae.

 The baths included a gymnasium and a sweat-bath which Agrippa called the Laconian Pyriaterion. Perhaps when first initiated the complex was a Greek-style gymnasium with a palaestra, sporting grounds and gardens. The baths were only fully realized in 19 BC with the completion of Agrippa’s Aqua Virgo which supplied the Campus Martius and Trans Tiberim with water. 

The baths had elaborate decorations: Lysippus’ Apoxyomenos stood before the entrance, paintings were hung throughout, stuccoes adorned the walls and vaults, and encaustic decoration was applied to the terracotta surfaces. During Agrippa’s lifetime the baths may have been private, since Pliny notes the seeming contradiction between Agrippa’s call to make all paintings public property and the existence of paintings in the hottest rooms of his thermae. At his death in 12 BC, Agrippa bequeathed his Baths to the people of Rome and made provisions so that they might bathe free of charge.

The plan of the bath complex survives only in part. The Severan Marble Plan depicts a large circular chamber surrounded by blocks of rooms to the W and S; due to the circumstances of the fragment’s preservation, the areas N and E of the rotunda do not survive. A large section of this circular, domed space is preserved along Via dell’Arco della Ciambella. 

The structure was restored on numerous occasions and substantially rebuilt after the fire of 80 AD; as a result, only a small portion of the original opus quadratum and reticulatum masonry survives. Preserved throughout these restorations were asymmetries of the bath’s original layout and its N–S orientation, an axis derived from the pre-existing buildings and street pattern. For these reasons, the 3rd c. AD and later plans are thought to reflect the Agrippan layout of the baths, if not their specific details.

properties.name: Thermae Caracallae (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Baths of Caracalla, Rome.

Construction of the baths was probably initiated by emperor Septimius Severus and completed during the reign of his son, Caracalla. They were inaugurated in 216 AD. The baths were located in the southern area of the city, Regio XII, where members of the Severan family commissioned other construction works: the via nova leading to the baths and the Septizodium on nearby Palatine Hill.

 The site chosen for the baths formerly belonged to a vast garden estate known as the horti Asiniani, developed by Gaius Asinius Pollio during the reign of Augustus. The Farnese Bull sculptural group which was later moved into the Baths of Caracalla was already present at the site in the time of Pollio, who imported it to display in his gardens.

The estate of Pollio was appropriated by Caracalla to build his baths and the existing structures were demolished down to their ground floors, filled in with earth and incorporated into the foundations of the new bath complex. The remains of one of these structures, a noble domus (house), were excavated by Francesco Ficoroni in the mid 18th century, and again in 1860-67 by G.B. Guidi.

For work to have been mostly completed in the time of Caracalla, workers would have had to install over 2,000 metric tons (2,200 short tons) of material every day for six years in order to complete it between 211 (when Severus died) and 216 AD.

Work on additional decorations continued under Caracalla's successors Elagabalus and Severus Alexander. The baths were likely mostly finished by 235 AD. Later renovations were conducted under Aurelian (after a fire) and by Diocletian. Under Constantine the Great the caldarium was modified.

The building was heated by a hypocaust, a system of burning coal and wood underneath the ground to heat water provided by a dedicated aqueduct. The baths were free and open to the public.

properties.name: Thermae Constantini (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Baths of Constantine, Rome.

The last of Rome's bath complexes, they were constructed in the irregular space between the vicus Longus, the Alta Semita, the clivus Salutis and the vicus laci Fundani, and as this was on a side-hill, it was necessary to demolish 4th-century houses then on the site (beneath which are ruins of second- and third-century houses) and make an artificial level over their ruins.

 Because of these peculiar conditions these thermae differed in plan from all others in the city - no anterooms were provided on either side of the caldarium, for instance, since the building was too narrow. The building was oriented north-south so as to heat it using the sun, with principal entrances on the west side, with a flight of steps down from the hill's summit to the campus Martius, and on the middle of the north side.

As the main structure occupied all the space between the streets on the east and west, the ordinary peribolus was replaced by an enclosure across the front which was bounded on the north by a curved line, an area now occupied by the Palazzo della Consulta. The frigidarium seems to have its longer axis north and south instead of east and west, and behind it were tepidarium and caldarium both circular in shape.

The only reference to these baths in ancient literature is in Ammianus Marcellinus.

properties.name: Thermae Diocletiani (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Baths of Diocletian, Rome.

The baths were commissioned by Maximian in honor of co-emperor Diocletian in 298 AD, the same year he returned from Africa. Evidence of this can be found in bricks from the main area of the baths, which distinctly show stamps of the Diocletianic period. These, according to the ancient guidebook Mirabilia Urbis Romae, were known as "Palatium Diocletiani". This evidence shows the effect of the massive project on the brick industry in that all work by them was redirected and under control of the emperor. Building took place between the year it was first commissioned and was finished sometime between the abdication of Diocletian in 305 AD and the death of Constantius in July 306 AD.

In the early 5th century, the baths were restored. The baths remained in use until the siege of Rome in 537 AD when the Ostrogothic king Vitiges cut off the aqueducts.

properties.name: Thermae Neronis (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Baths of Nero, Rome.

The Baths of Nero were a series of complex baths on the Campus Martius in ancient Rome, built by Nero in 62 AD and rebuilt by Alexander Severus in 227 or 229 AD. They covered an area of about 190 by 120 metres. Their extent is shown by the modern-day piazza della Rotonda, via del Pozzo delle Cornacchie and via della Dogana Vecchia, all now on their site.

It was initially supplied by the Aqua Virgo, which already supplying the neighbouring Baths of Agrippa, then (on its restoration in the 3rd century) by the Aqua Alexandrina. According to Sidonius Apollinaris, it was still in use in the 5th century. It was probably the first "imperial-type" complex of baths

properties.name: Thermae Septimii Severi (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Baths of Septimius Severus, Rome.

They were part of the Domus Severiana extention to the Imperial palaces on the Palatine hill built by Septimius Severus. They were fed by a branch of the Aqua Claudia, which spanned the valley between the Palatine Hill and the Caelian Hill and whose arches are still visible.

properties.name: Thermae Titi (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Baths of Titus, Rome.

The Baths of Titus or Thermae Titi were public baths (Thermae) built in 81 AD in Rome, by Emperor Titus. 

The baths sat at the base of the Esquiline Hill, an area of parkland and luxury estates which had been taken over by Nero for his Domus Aurea. Titus' baths were built in haste, possibly by converting an existing or partly built bathing complex belonging to the reviled Domus Aurea. They were not particularly extensive, and the much larger Baths of Trajan were built immediately adjacent to them at the start of the next century.

The Baths of Titus were restored during the reign of Hadrian as well as in  238 AD but no further repairs are known. It is thus likely that the entire complex underwent a process of early abandonment. Large parts of the building were still standing in the 16th century when Andrea Palladio described the floor plan. The ruins were demolished shortly afterwards, their marble and building materials being reused for the building of palaces and churches such as the side chapels of the Church of the Gesù or the fountain of the Cortile del Belvedere in the Vatican.

properties.name: Thermae Traiani (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Baths of Trajan, Rome.

The Baths of Trajan were a massive thermae, started in 104 AD and dedicated during the Kalends of July in 109 AD.

 Commissioned by Emperor Trajan, the complex of baths occupied space on the southern side of the Oppian Hill on the outskirts of what was then the main developed area of the city, although still inside the boundary of the Servian Wall. The architect of the complex is said to be Apollodorus of Damascus. The baths were being utilized mainly as a recreational and social centre by Roman citizens, both men and women, as late as the early 5th century.

 The complex seems to have been deserted soon afterwards as a cemetery dated to the 5th century (which remained in use until the 7th century) has been found in front of the northeastern exedra. The baths were thus no longer in use at the time of the siege of Rome by the Ostrogoths in 537 AD; with the destruction of the Roman aqueducts, all thermae were abandoned, as was the whole of the now-waterless Mons Oppius. Early Christian writers misnamed the remains the 'Baths of Domitian'.

properties.name: Tigillum Sororium (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Rome.

One of Rome’s most ancient monuments, the Tigillum Sororium was a beam supported by two vertical posts that spanned a road, probably the Sacra Via.

 Dionysius of Halicarnassus relates that the beam served in the expiation of Horatius and that located nearby were two altars, one to Iuno Sororia and the other to Ianus Curiatus. The Arval calendar reports that the Tigillum Sororium was located AD COMPITVM ACILI; thus its location is fairly secure, despite the absence of archaeological remains.

properties.name: Turris Murorum Aureliani (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Aurelian Wall Tower, Rome.

The Aurelian Walls were constructed between 270 and 275 AD at the behest of the Emperor Aurelian, as a defence for the city from the threatened invasion of barbarians from the North of Europe. The new enclosing wall had a perimeter of about 19 km and was constructed of sections of wall about 6.5m in hieght, with a parapet walkway along the top, punctuated every thirty metres by higher towers, covered by terraces.

properties.name: Turris Murorum Aureliani (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Aurelian Wall Tower, Rome.

The Aurelian Walls were constructed between 270 and 275 AD at the behest of the Emperor Aurelian, as a defence for the city from the threatened invasion of barbarians from the North of Europe. The new enclosing wall had a perimeter of about 19 km and was constructed of sections of wall about 6.5m in hieght, with a parapet walkway along the top, punctuated every thirty metres by higher towers, covered by terraces.

properties.name: Turris Murorum Aureliani (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:

The new enclosing wall had a perimeter of about 19 km and was constructed of sections of wall about 6.5m in hieght, with a parapet walkway along the top, punctuated every thirty metres by higher towers, covered by terraces.

properties.name: Villa Publica (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Rome.

One of the oldest and most important Republican buildings in the Campus Martius, established in 435 BC by the censors C. Furius Paculus and M. Geganius Macerinus. It was not a functioning villa for farming, but instead a place where Rome’s armies were levied and regulated and where the census was administered.

 The term ‘Villa Publica’ seems to have been applied not only to the specific structure but also to the surrounding open space, in which most of the business of the Villa Publica took place.

The structure of the villa itself has not been located, but is known to have stood somewhere near the Republican Saepta. This also served, from time to time, as the place where embassies from Rome’s enemies were housed. The building was probably destroyed at some time after 55 BC, when it was depicted on a denarius by P. Fonteius Capito, but before the reign of Tiberius, when Valerius Maximus refers to the Villa Publica in the past tense.

properties.name: Amphitheatrum Castrense (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Amphitheatre, Rome.

The amphitheatre is dated to the first decades of the 3rd c. AD by the style of the bricks and the absence of brick stamps. It was part of an Imperial villa complex which was built by emperors of the Severan dynasty. The open arches of the outer walls were walled up when the building was incorporated into the Aurelian Walls (271-275 AD), at which point it stopped being used for spectacles and began to be used as fortification, and the ground level around the building was lowered. 

In the middle of the 16th century the remains of the second story were demolished for defensive needs. 

In the 18th century, a Hypogeum was found beneath the arena, filled with the bones of large animals. This leads researchers to believe that the spectacles here included Venationes, the hunting and killing of wild animals. Palladio and Étienne Dupérac made drawings about the ruins.

properties.name: Amphitheatrum Flavium (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Colosseum, Rome.

The Flavian Amphitheatre is an oval amphitheatre in the centre of Rome. Built of travertine, tuff, and brick-faced concrete, it is the largest amphitheatre ever built. The Colosseum is situated just east of the Roman Forum. 

Construction began under the emperor Vespasian in 72 AD, and was completed in 80 AD under his successor and heir Titus. Further modifications were made during the reign of Domitian. These three emperors are known as the Flavian dynasty, and the amphitheatre was named in Latin for its association with their family name (Flavius).

The Colosseum could hold, it is estimated, between 50,000 and 80,000 spectators, having an average audience of some 65,000; it was used for gladiatorial contests and public spectacles such as mock sea battles (for only a short time as the hypogeum was soon filled in with mechanisms to support the other activities), animal hunts, executions, re-enactments of famous battles, and dramas based on Classical mythology. The building ceased to be used for entertainment in the early medieval era. 

It was later reused for such purposes as housing, workshops, quarters for a religious order, a fortress, a quarry, and a Christian shrine.

properties.name: Amphitheatrum Statilii Tauri (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Amphitheatre of Statilius Taurus, Rome.

T. Statilius Taurus built the first stone amphitheatre in Rome, which he dedicated in 29 BC. 

This private amphitheater may not have been very large, as it was often passed over for important imperial spectacles. In 64 AD fire destroyed the theatre, which was probably built in large part of wood; consequently its location within the Campus Martius remains a matter of speculation.

properties.name: Athenaeum Hadriani (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Intellectual school of Hadrian, Rome.

The Athenaeum was a school (ludus) founded by the Emperor Hadrian in Rome, for the promotion of literary and scientific studies (ingenuarum artium) and called Athenaeum from the city of Athens, which was still regarded as the seat of intellectual refinement. The Athenaeum was situated near the Capitoline Hill: its site was discovered in 2009 during excavation for the construction of the Rome Metro C Line, in the middle of what is now Piazza Venezia.

properties.name: Athenaeum Maecenatis (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Auditorium of Maecenas, Rome.

“Auditorium of Maecenas” is the modern name for the sunken apsidal room accessed by a ramp built into the Servian Wall S of the Porta Esquilina within a large residential complex in the Gardens of Maecenas. 

It was a subterranean room which extended back into the Agger. It is identified with the Horti Maecenatis on the basis of water pipes inscribed with the name of C. Fronto, a subsequent owner. The location confirms the long-established identification with Maecenas, for his Esquiline horti are known to have straddled the Agger. On the basis of walls in opus reticulatum and red-white mosaics from the first phase of the building, it is dated to the late Republic, perhaps c. 40 BC. Horace mentions the horti of Maecenas in the first book of his Satires, which appeared c. 35 BC. In a second building phase, the floor was paved with marble in opus sectile and the walls decorated with Third-Style wall-painting; similarities with the villa of Agrippa Postumus near Pompeii, presumably dating from before his exile to Planasia in 8 AD, provide a date in the first decade of the 1st c. AD. This work was perhaps undertaken by Tiberius who took up residence here in 2 AD. 

On the basis of a Callimachus grafitto, it was first thought that the 7 rising concentric steps in the apse were part of an auditorium, a roofed theatre for literary performances. Alternatively, the steps may have been used to display flower pots (viridarium), or perhaps they were part of a water feature (nymphaeum); the general ground-plan suggests a dining room (triclinium). It was probably a multi-functional space. For convenience, the traditional name is used here. There is no surviving trace of a roof, or of a drainage system in the floor which would have been required if the structure were exposed to the elements; we may perhaps assume a wooden roof.

properties.name: Circus Flaminius (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Race track, Rome.

Large open space — not a formal circus — in the SW Campus Martius, between the Theatrum Marcelli and the Temple of Mars, and oriented along the NW axis of the road which led to the Tiber and beyond that, to Veii. 

The area was topographically significant since it gave its name, sometime after the Augustan era, to Regio IX: Circus Flaminius. The Circus Flaminius occupied the prata Flaminia, property donated to the people of Rome in 221 BC by C. Flaminius; however, the original property may not have corresponded exactly to the later extension of the circus. 

The strong triumphal character of the Circus Flaminius is stressed by the high density of sacred structures (most of them victory monuments) — either identified through archaeological remains or mentioned in ancient accounts — that cluster around it and define its boundaries. While it is generally assumed that the long sides of the Circus were monumentalized by temples, there is no evidence that any sacral buildings other than the Temple of the Dioscuri delimited the SW side. In fact, the Marble Plan from the Via Anicia shows commercial horrea (warehouses) flanking the temple.

properties.name: Circus Maxentii (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Race track of Maxentius, Rome.

The Circus of Maxentius is part of a complex of buildings erected by emperor Maxentius on the Via Appia between 306 and 312 AD. It is situated between the second and third miles of the Via Appia between the basilica and catacombs of San Sebastiano and the imposing late republican tomb of Caecilia Metella, which dominates the hill that rises immediately to the east of the complex. It is part of the Parco Regionale Appia Antica (Appian Way Regional Park).

The Circus itself is the best preserved in the area of Rome, and is second only in size to the Circus Maximus in Rome. The only games recorded at the circus were its inaugural ones and these are generally thought to have been funerary in character. They would have been held in honour of Maxentius' son Valerius Romulus, who died in 309 AD at a very young age and who was probably interred in the adjacent cylindrical tomb (tomb of Romulus). The imperial box (pulvinar) of the circus is connected, via a covered portico, to the villa of Maxentius, whose scant remains are today obscured by dense foliage, except for the apse of the basilical audience hall, which pokes out from the tree tops. The complex was probably never used after the death of Maxentius in 312 AD (archaeological excavations indicate the tracks were covered in sand already in antiquity).

properties.name: Circus Maximus (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Race track, Rome.

Rome’s oldest and largest circus, a hairpin-track designed for chariot racing, situated in the valley between the Palatine and Aventine near the Forum Bovarium.  

The Circus Maximus was an important venue for public entertainments, which included wild-beast hunts (venationes), mock battles, and athletic contests (i.e., running, boxing, wrestling) in addition to equestrian events. 

Roman tradition credits the Tarquins with founding the Circus, but the structure, which had been modestly built up in the 2nd c. BC, only achieved its definitive form under Julius Caesar and Augustus. Though little archaeological evidence remains from the Augustan Circus, detailed literary accounts, especially that of Dionysius of Halicarnassus, allow a relatively reliable reconstruction of the monument.

Caesar inherited a circus with an already well-defined race course: 12 starting gates (carceres) stood at the Forum Bovarium end, two turning posts (metae) were fixed within the track and their axis was adorned with statues set on columns; in the Republican period, there was no continuous central barrier wall. At an early point, the “Cloaca Circi Maximi” had been installed to drain the valley floor and thus provide an area suitable for racing. The starting gates themselves were unroofed, wooden stalls with an arcaded, tufa façade facing the track. Each gate had a pair of wooden doors, which were simultaneously opened ‘by a single rope’ at the start of the race. A set of ova (eggs) used to count laps stood in the track near the carceres where they were readily visible to the charioteers. Before Caesar’s modifications, most spectators sat in wooden stands erected along portions of the long sides of the Circus; limited stone seating was reserved for the élite. An arch erected by L. Stertinius in 196 BC is often placed at the SE end of the Circus on the spot that would later mark the center of the semicircular stands; however, this monument is known only to have stood ‘in the vicinity of the Circus’, in Maximo circo ; given the vagueness of Livy’s description, the arch cannot be indicated on our rendering.

Several ancient cults native to the valley were honoured within the circus. Near the first turning post (primae metae, at the SE end of the track) was an underground altar belonging to the archaic deity Consus. The shrine of Murcia stood within the track near the primae metae on the Aventine side. The Temple of Sol rose within the seating area on the Aventine side of the Circus, just opposite the finish line; it was to Sol that the Circus as a whole was consecrated.

properties.name: Circus Varianus (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Race track, Rome.

The Circus Varianus was a circus, possibly started around the time of Caracalla, residing in the palatial villa complex known as the Sessorium, beside the Amphitheatrum Castrense. This circus has been identified as the space in which Elagabalus raced horses under the family name of Varius, lending the site the name of "Circus Varianus." The remnants of the circus survive to the south of Porta Maggiore, next to the Aurelian Wall, near the church of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme. The dimensions of the circus measure 565 x 125 meters, just slightly smaller than the Circus Maximus (600 x 150 m).

properties.name: Ludus Magnus (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Gladiatorial Training School, Rome.

The Ludus Magnus was the largest of the gladiatorial schools in Rome. It was built by the emperor Domitian, alongside other building projects undertaken by him such as three other gladiatorial schools across the Roman Empire. 

The training school is situated directly east of the Colosseum in the valley between the Esquiline and the Caelian hills, an area already occupied by Republican and Augustan structures. While there are remains that are visible today, they belong to a reconstruction that took place under the emperor Trajan where the Ludus plane was raised by about 1.5 metres (4 ft 11 in). The Ludus Magnus was essentially a gladiatorial arena where gladiators from across the Roman Empire would live, eat, and practice while undergoing gladiatorial training in preparation for fighting at the gladiatorial games held at the Colosseum.

properties.name: Naumachia (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Naval battle amphitheatre, Rome.

Extensive water basin built by Augustus in Trans Tiberim and dedicated in 2 BC to stage mock naval battles and aquatic displays for the Roman people.

 In the Res Gestae, Augustus gives the dimensions of this large basin as 1800 by 1200 Roman feet (533 x 355 m), with a possible average depth of 1.5 m. There was ‘an island in the middle’ of the basin, probably for distinguished spectators, and the island was connected to the bank by a bridge of notable span. The useful life of the basin reached into the time of Titus; literary sources (including Augustus himself) imply that it was soon surrounded by the nemus Caesarum, the Grove of the Caesars.

According to Frontinus, the main reason for the construction of the Aqua Alsietina was to supply water for the Naumachia and the adjacent gardens in Trans Tiberim; its conduit ended behind the Naumachia.

properties.name: Stabula Factionem (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Stables of the Chariot Factions, Rome.

Stables for the horses belonging to the racing teams (factiones) in Rome, located in the W Campus Martius near the Trigarium. In the Augustan period there were four factiones: Albata, Prasina, Russea, and Veneta.

The factio Prasina was located near the Church of S. Lorenzo in Damaso, which retained the topographical attribute in its alternate mediaeval name: S. Laurentii in Prasino; an inscription mentioning the statio Prasina was found in situ nearby. About 50 m to the E, the possible remains of the factio Veneta were unearthed beneath Palazzo Regis and Palazzo Farnese. Although the locations of the other two factiones are unknown, several inscriptions found within a restricted area suggest that the two stables were located next to each other. Moreover, corroborating evidence for this location is offered by the existence of the V[ICVS STA]BLARIVS in this area.

properties.name: Stadium Domitiani (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Athletic stadium of Domitian, Rome.

The Stadium was used almost entirely for athletic contests. For "a few years", following fire-damage to the Colosseum in 217 AD, it was used for gladiator shows.

The Stadium of Domitian was dedicated in 86 AD, as part of an Imperial building programme at the Field of Mars, following the damage or destruction of most of its buildings by fire in 79 AD. It was Rome's first permanent venue for competitive athletics. It was patterned after the Greek model and seated approximately 15,000 - 20,000 – a smaller, more appropriate venue for foot-races than the Circus Maximus. The substructures and support frames were made of brick and concrete – a robust, fire-retardant and relatively cheap material – clad in marble. 

Stylistically, the Stadium facades would have resembled those of the Colosseum; its floor plan followed the same elongated, U-shape as the Circus Maximus, though on a much smaller scale. Various modern estimates judge the arena length at approximately 200 – 250 metres, the height of its outer perimeter benches at 30 m (100 ft) above ground level and its inner perimeter benches at 4.5 m (15 ft) above the arena floor. This arrangement offered a clear view from most seats. The typically Greek layout gave the Stadium its Latinised Greek name, in agones (the place or site of the competitions). The flattened end was sealed by two vertically staggered entrance galleries and the perimeter was arcaded beneath the seating levels, with travertine pilasters between its cavea (enclosures). The formation of a continuous arena trackway by a raised "spina" or strip has been conjectured.

The Stadium of Domitian was the northernmost of an impressive series of public buildings on the Campus Martius. To its south stood the smaller and more intimate Odeon of Domitian, used for recitals, song and orations. The southernmost end of the Campus was dominated by the Theater of Pompey, restored by Domitian during the same rebuilding program.

properties.name: Theatrum Balbi (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Theatre of Balbus, Rome.

The smallest of the three stone theatres in Rome, built in the S Campus Martius by L. Cornelius Balbus (minor), probably after his triumph in 19 BC, as a part of the Augustan program of ‘adorning the city’.

 It was dedicated in 13 BC during a flood of the Tiber, and stood S of the Porticus Minucia. Like the Theatrum Pompeium, the cavea of the Theatre of Balbus was oriented to face E. A number of its support walls in opus reticulatum have been preserved beneath Palazzo Mattei di Paganica. To the E of the stage building stood a large three-sided portico, which came to be known as the ‘crypta Balbi’. In the center of this portico stood a large rectangular structure of uncertain interpretation, which also seems to have been built by Balbus. The E portion of the complex is shown on the Severan Marble Plan and its remains are preserved near Via delle Botteghe Oscure. Excavations have shown that earlier residential buildings were destroyed to make room for the portico, and the region immediately to the E of the theatre contained a number of private structures by the time Augustan intervention began in this area.

properties.name: Theatum Marcelli (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Theatre of Marcellus, Rome.

The Augustan successor of the theatrum ad aedem Apollinis and the second stone theatr built in Rome, located at the E end of the Circus Flaminius in front of the Temple of Apollo Medicus.

 Dedicated in either 13 or 11 BC by Augustus, the theatre was named after his nephew M. Claudius Marcellus. 

When Julius Caesar initiated the building project in 44 BC, he had to remove temples and houses from the area, including the Temple of Pietas on the NW end of Forum Holitorium, to prepare the site for the theatre. The construction took place under Augustus, who bought more land near the Temple of Apollo to extend the site. Even though the construction was not complete, part of the celebrations of the ludi Saeculares in 17 BC. took place in the theatre. Possibly a larger theatre was intended at the time of Caesar; while the 4th c. AD Regionary Catalogues list its capacity at 20,500 loca, others estimate it held c. 13,500 spectators.

Space for only a narrow thoroughfare remained between the rear of the theatre and the terrace walls of the Apollo and Bellona temples. If the widespread scholarly opinion that this passage served as part of the triumphal procession route is correct, Augustus’ architects must have had difficulty fitting the large theatre building on the site. However, the triumphal parade, which originated in the Circus Flaminius, may not have followed this paved street, but rather have passed through the orchestra of the theater itself, with the cavea conveniently open to seat spectators. Since two circular monuments, the Perirrhanterion and the columna Bellica, may have obstructed the passage behind the theatre, a route through the orchestra seems likely.

Most of the theater’s plan is preserved on the Severan Marble Plan. The foundations of the cavea survive to our day, having served as the infrastructure for Palazzo Savelli-Orsini. The lower vaulted arcades of travertine, located beneath the cavea and facing the Temple of Apollo Medicus, were uncovered when more than 4 m of débris was removed during the Italian government’s ‘liberation’ of the monument between 1926 and 1932. Two symmetrically-placed halls of basilical plan were located on either side of the stage building. The function of the semicircular walled space behind the stage building that appears on the Marble Plan (on a now-lost fragment) with a pair of centrally-placed, small square features is a matter of debate.

properties.name: Theatrum Pompeium (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Theatre of Pompey, Rome.

Pompey’s Theatre, dedicated in September 55 BC, was the first permanent stone theatre in Rome, and it remained the largest, and arguably the most important, of the three permanent theaters in the Campus Martius that existed by the end of the Augustan period.

 It was known specifically as Pompeium theatrum or Pompeianum theatrum, and also under the more general terms theatrum Marmoreum, theatrum Magnum, or simply Theatrum. 

Adjoining the theater on the E was a quadriportico enclosing a sculpture garden, the Porticus Pompeianae. Pompey’s Theatere was perhaps restored by Agrippa as aedile in 33 BC along with all other public buildings. It was also restored by Augustus but it is not known when. Subsequent restorations are attested in abundance, and this makes it difficult to reconstruct the appearance of Pompey’s Theater under Augustus with absolute certainty.

The curved seating area, or cavea, of Pompey’s Theatre has a continuing presence in the urban fabric of the modern city: it is visible in the distinct curvature of certain streets (Via di Grottapinta for the internal curve, Via del Biscione and Piazza Pollarola for the external curve), and in the ground-plan of houses built on the theatre’s radial foundations, partly extant in cellars. Modern maps thus allow an accurate reconstruction of the cavea; this reconstructed cavea belonged to the original construction phase of Pompey’s Theatre. The orchestra, the open area at ground level within the cavea, was a perfect semicircle. The outline of the cavea is also known from drawings of a lost fragment of the Severan Marble Plan, one in the Codex Ursinianus. The cavea faced E onto the stage building, or scaenae frons. Comparative evidence from other theatres of the 1st c. BC lets us reconstruct a stone, rectilinear scaenae frons for Pompey’s Theatre in the Augustan period. The scaenae frons shown on the Marble Plan with its central rectangular exedra and two lateral curved exedrae dates only to its Domitianic rebuilding after the fire of 80 AD. The Marble Plan shows two widely-spaced, parallel rows of 5 squares, adjoining the scaenae frons to the N and S, and extending beyond the outer limits of the cavea. The absence of an outer wall on the N and S suggests that this may have been a thoroughfare that passed between the theater and portico.

properties.name: Trigarium (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Race track, Rome

Horseracing track located in the W Campus Martius. The term ‘trigarium’ is generally interpreted as the racing track for chariots drawn by three horses (trigae), an event held only in Archaic times.

 Nonetheless, there could have been a revival of these races in the Imperial period. The Trigarium served as the temporary racetrack (circus temporalis) of the ludi Saeculares to host horse races; it not only shared a topographical contiguity with the Tarentum but also a typological association. Perhaps other ceremonies of archaic character and involving horse races, such as the Equirria and the October equus, were held in the Trigarium.

properties.name: Ara Iovis Vinimi (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Altar of Jupiter Viminus, Rome.

Ancient altar to Iuppiter Viminus, the titular deity of the collis Viminalis, located on the Viminal.

 An ancient drawing found in the excavations of Monte delle Giustizia, in the vicinity of the Porta Viminalis, depicts a cylindrical altar inscribed VIM resting on a rectangular plinth. A statue of Jupiter found near the point where Via Cavour joins Piazza dei Cinquecento may have been linked to the cult; yet it is of late-Imperial date and was not recovered in situ, so its value as evidence for the Augustan shrine is limited. Though the exact locale of the altar remains elusive, these two pieces of evidence suggest a location near the Porta Viminalis.

properties.name: Ara Martis (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Altar of Mars, Rome.

This altar, the primary cult site of Mars in Rome, was one of the most important and ancient religious monuments in the Campus Martius. 

Though the dedication of the plain itself to Mars was linked with the expulsion of the Tarquinii, the altar was thought to date from the time of king Numa. During the Republic, the altar was closely associated with the activities of the censors, and thus was linked with the Villa Publica, in which it probably stood.

properties.name: Ara Maxima Herculis (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Great Altar of Hercules, Rome.

A monumental altar to Hercules at the Forum Boarium, the oldest and most revered centre of Hercules’ cult in Rome and also the alleged starting point for Romulus’ delimitation of the pomerium.

 The altar’s approximate location and grand size can be deduced from Servius, who mentions it as ‘behind the gates of the Circus Maximus’ and explains the epithet Maxima by citing ‘the magnitude of the structure’. Dionysius of Halicarnassus describes it as ‘near’ the Forum Boarium and, while judging the construction inferior, stresses the altar’s extremely high reputation; it was the place where ‘oaths are taken and agreements made for sealing business transactions’.

 The remains of a large, solidly built podium, exceeding 20 x 30 m, of Anio tufa blocks with travertine facing under the E part of S. Maria in Cosmedin have convincingly been attributed to the altar. The objection by Richardson that this place is “poorly located to be a turning point in the pomerium of Romulus” hardly forms a valid argument, but his conclusion that the platform “is clearly not temple foundations but a solid mass” 

The altar must have formed the focal point of an agglomeration of sanctuaries to Hercules in this area. Its connection with the Invictus epithet of Hercules is not explicitly attested and rests on the attested cult of Hercules Invictus ad circum Maximum as well as a postulated temple of Hercules E of the altar, combined with a series of mid- to late-Imperial Hercules Invictus inscriptions some 50 m N of it.

properties.name: Ara Pacis Augustae (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Altar of Pax Augusta, Rome.

The Altar of Augustan Peace in the Campus Martius was voted by the senate in 13 BC to celebrate Augustus’ return from Gaul and Spain and dedicated on 30 January 9 BC.

 It stood in the N campus about 30 m W of the Via Flaminia, near the intersection of Via in Lucina and Via dell’Impresa. Fragments of its decorative friezes were first unearthed in 1568, and sporadic excavations continued to bring forth pieces of the altar for the next three and a half centuries. The remaining portions were finally excavated in 1938. The reconstructed altar now stands beside Via di Ripetta across from the remains of the Mausoleum of Augustus.

The dimensions of the Ara Pacis Augustae are rather modest. It was constructed entirely of Luna marble, and consists of a rectangular screen wall (11 x 10 m) with doorways on the E and W, inside which the U-shaped altar stood beneath the open sky on a stepped platform. It was originally situated at the edge of a terrace, so that a staircase of 9 steps was necessary to communicate between the plaza of the “Horologium Augusti” and the W entrance, while the E entrance was even with the level of the Via Flaminia. The altar and its screen wall were almost entirely covered with decorative friezes; the most famous depict a religious procession in which Augustus and members of his family figure prominently. The altar’s decoration also included allegorical scenes from Roman mythology, elaborate floral panels, and depictions of garlands and bucrania. It is possible that the ara of Fortuna Redux, which was built to celebrate another adventus of Augustus, may have had a similar design.

properties.name: Ara Saturni (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Altar of Saturn, Rome.

The ancient altar of Saturn in the Forum, variously attributed to Ianus, the Pelasgians, Hercules, and Servius Tullius.

 Sources locate the altar ‘at the bottom of the Clivus Capitolinus’ and ‘in front of the Senaculum’. The Senaculum was an open area in front of the Temple of Concord and Basilica Opimia in the late Republic, an area later occupied by Tiberius’ Temple of Augustan Concord. On the basis of these and other references, Coarelli has identified the cappellacio blocks behind the Rostra of Augustus, which Lanciani had associated with the Volcanal, as the remains of the altar of Saturn.

properties.name: Atrium Vestae (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
House of Vesta, Rome.

The precinct of Vesta just E of the Forum, which contained living quarters for the 6 Vestal Virgins, a paved court and, after 12 BC, the Domus Publica which Augustus donated to the Vestals.

 The complex was renovated in the 1st c. BC, probably under Julius Caesar. Recent excavations suggest that the form of this 1st c. BC building complex was maintained through the 1st c. AD.

The limits of the complex are relatively well-defined. The Atrium was bordered on the W by the ramp to the Palatine, the Scalae Graecae; on the N by a precinct wall which separated the complex from the Sacra Via; and to the E by a party wall shared with the Domus Publica. The S border during the Augustan period is less distinct, though the Via Nova and rising slope of the Palatine form probable limits. 

The structures within these bounds during the Augustan period remain elusive, due to later Imperial construction on the site which substantially altered the 1st c. BC complex. The grove of Vesta (lucus Vestae) mentioned by Cicero once stood in this region, though its continued existence in the Augustan era is doubtful.

properties.name: Auguraculum (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Augury, Rome.

The Auguraculum was a spot located on the Arx, in arce from which the augurs observed the flight of birds.

properties.name: Auguraculum (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Augury, Rome.

Site for augurs’ observations on the Quirinal.

It stood on the collis Latiaris, the lowest and most southerly lobe of the Quirinal (near SS. Domenico e Sisto), but its exact location within this region is unknown. On analogy to the auguraculum in Cosa, it was probably a relatively small (5 x 5 m) open space demarcated with cippi (Castagnoli 13). While there may have been a thatched hut at the Auguraculum on the Arx, there was no building at this site.

properties.name: Capitolium Vetus (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Shrine to Jupiter, Juno and Minerva, Rome.

The most ancient shrine in Rome dedicated to Jupiter, Juno and Minerva, the Capitolium Vetus was located on the Quirinal at the top of a steep street leading from the Temple of Flora.

 Varro explicitly notes that the Capitolium Vetus was older than the Temple of Iuppiter Optimus Maximus Capitolinus. No archaeological remains of the structure survive, but Varro’s use of ‘sacellum’ implies that the Capitolium Vetus was of modest dimensions, perhaps no more than an open area with altars.

properties.name: Domus Romuli (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
House of Romulus, Rome.

An archaic hut built of ‘sticks and reeds’ was located on the S Palatine slope near the Domus: Augustus and the Scalae Caci by literary sources.

 In antiquity, unusual care was taken to preserve the exact appearance of the archaic dwelling, which was maintained as a sacred site.

properties.name: Iseum (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Isis, Rome.

The most important temple of Isis in Rome (and eventually, the Mediterranean) stood in the central Campus Martius, immediately E of the Porticus Meleagri, where it shared a sanctuary with an equally significant but separate Temple of Serapis. 

The construction of this great Iseum is often, though without good reason, attributed to Caligula. It is more likely, however, that the temple was vowed by the Second Triumvirate in 43 BC.

This temple was completely destroyed by fire in 80 AD and subsequently rebuilt by Domitian.

properties.name: Iseum (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Isis, Rome.

Imposing triportico with central water basin (piscina) found on a large terrace on the S slopes of the Oppian, in the probable position of the Iseum Metellinum and the sanctuary of Isis et Serapis of Regio III.
