This identification finds confirmation in the large number of Isiac statuary finds spread throughout this area. Two inscriptions found in the Via Labicana mention Isis. Numerous sculptures of Isis and other Egyptian deities have come to light near the Church of SS. Pietro e Marcellino, in Via Merulana–Via Buonarroti and Via dello Statuto to the N, and at scattered points on the Esquiline.

properties.name: Lacus Curtius (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Lake of Curtius, Rome,

An irregular polygonal monument in the Forum square for which the Romans had a number of explanatory traditions. Excavations have revealed three layers of pavement, the lowest of cappellacio, the middle of tufa (2nd c. BC), and the uppermost of travertine (1st c. BC). 

Within the area of the Lacus Curtius, enclosed in antiquity by a marble parapet, there sits a circular plinth, probably used to support a puteal (well-head). Suetonius notes that the people threw coins into the Lacus Curtius annually as an offering to Augustus’ health, but there does not seem to have been any water here in the Augustan period.

properties.name: Lacus Iuturnae (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Spring of Juturna, Rome.

A natural spring in the SE corner of the Forum, where excavations in 1900 revealed a marble-lined basin c. 2 m deep and c. 10 x 10 m at the top, aligned with the Temple of Castor. 

It is not known when the spring, noted for its excellent water, was first associated with Iuturna. The pre-Augustan phases are normally ascribed to L. Aemilius Paullus (after the battle of Pydna in 168 BC) and to L. Caecilius Metellus in conjunction with his restoration of the Temple of Castor in 117 BC, when the basin was reduced to c. 7.5 x 7.5 m. In a third phase of development, the basin was further reduced to c. 5 x 5 m and lined with marble, a reworking normally associated with Tiberius’ rebuilding of the Temple of Castor in 6 AD. The Lacus Iuturnae is represented on the Severan Marble Plan.

properties.name: Lupercal (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Cave of the she-wolf, Rome.

A grotto at the base of the SW Palatine, near the Circus Maximus, believed to be the site where Faustulus discovered Romulus and Remus with the she-wolf.

 The site featured a spring, and was once surrounded by a grove; the original ficus Ruminalis grew here, but by the Augustan period, only vestigia of the fig-tree remained near the Lupercal.

Following literary sources, the Lupercal can be located on the lower SW Palatine. Dionysius of Halicarnassus places it at the foot of the Germalus between the Velabrum and Circus Maximus, and also associates the grotto with the Temple of Victory, which stood atop the SW Palatine. Further, the Lupercal is described as in Circo, and used as a landmark for a Palatine theatre proposed but never realized by C. Cassius Longinus (c. 154 BC).

Augustus takes credit for building the Lupercal; although what this meant architecturally is unclear, an imperial intervention would have entailed significant alterations. Concurrently, the festival of the Lupercalia was reorganized by Augustus. Within the Lupercal were several statues, including a bronze depiction of the she-wolf suckling the twins and an equestrian statue of Drusus. The presence of an equestrian monument suggests the change in atmosphere the Augustan rebuilding may have brought to a once idyllic, watery grove.

properties.name: Mithraeum (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Mithras, Rome.

One of the largest Mithraic temples in Rome is hidden next to the Circus Maximus. Discovered in 1931 as part of Rome’s fascist-era building projects, the small subterranean space was once dedicated to the mystery cult of the god Mithras.

properties.name: Mithraeum (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Mithras, Rome.

Found in the cellars of the rear part of the Palazzo Barberini, dating to the 2nd c. AD.

The excavated room consists of a central room, on either side of which there is a smaller, narrower room; they are of the same size (probably 1st c. AD). One of these rooms was changed into a Mithraeum later on. The sanctuary is rectangular (H. 4.42 L. 11.83 Br. 6.25) and is divided into a central aisle (Br. 1.95) and two side-benches, sloping towards the walls. Along the front of the r. bench (H. 0.83 Br. 1.40) as well as of the l. bench (Br. 2.45) runs a broad ledge, covered with marble.

The two benches show moreover, approximately in the middle and on floor-level, hollows for the basins. The basin of the l. bench is half-round and covered by a lid. This bench can be ascended via three steps, and it supports four brick columns, which help to support the arched roof. Behind the r. bench, which can be ascended via two steps, runs a small canal.

On the level with the side-benches against the back wall, the arched cult-niche (H. 2.15 D. 1.03) has been constructed. The arch joins the last column of the bench. On its right two fishes are painted, a remnant of the signs of the zodiac. The inside of the niche is covered with sea-shells and pumice to give it a cave-like appearance. At the foot of the niche two projecting elevations have been made (H. 0.82 Br. 0.50-0.70 D. 0.90), which are plastered on the inside and painted with undefiniable motives in blue, green and red.

properties.name: Mithraeum (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Mithras, Rome.

It was built in the courtyard of the insula, c. 200 AD. The main cult room (the speleum, "cave"), which is about 9.6m long and 6m wide, was discovered in 1867 but could not be investigated until 1914 due to lack of drainage. The exedra, the shallow apse at the far end of the low vaulted space, was trimmed with pumice to render it more cave-like.

Central to the main room of the sanctuary was found an altar, in the shape of a sarcophagus, and with the main cult relief of the tauroctony (the image of Mithras slaying a bull) on its front face. The torchbearers Cautes and Cautopates appear on respectively the left and right faces of the same monument. A dedicatory inscription identifies the donor as one pater Cnaeus Arrius Claudianus, perhaps of the same clan as Titus Arrius Antoninus' mother. Other monuments discovered in the sanctuary include a bust of Sol kept in the sanctuary in a niche near the entrance, and a figure of Mithras petra generix, i.e. Mithras born of the rock. Fragments of statuary of the two torch bearers were also found . One of the rooms adjoining the main chamber has two oblong brickwork enclosures, one of which was used as a ritual refuse pit for remnants of the cult meal. All three monuments mentioned above are still on display in the mithraeum.

properties.name: Mithraeum (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Mithras, Rome.

Discovered in 1912 by Ettore Ghislanzoni, the mithraeum at the baths is considered the largest documented gathering space for the worshippers of Mithras, in the 2nd-3rd c. AD. 

The mithraeum was approximately 23 m (75 ft) long and 10 m (33 ft) wide with a cross-vaulted ceiling.

The floor of the main room was covered with a black and white mosaic. Benches lined the walls. A fresco portraying Mithra (or a torch bearer) is on the western wall. The only other ornamentation was a marble block, roughly carved into the shape of a snake. In the floor near the entrance a circular pit was found covered with a marble slab, with a terracotta bowl containing the remains of staves of wheat. A rectangular hole in the floor gives access to a small tunnel that runs under the center of the main hall into an adjoining room, where there is an entrance/exit with staircase. This, a unique feature in a mithraeum, has been controversial. Most scholars view this as a fossa sanguinis, a ritual pit over which the bull at the center of the Mithraic mythology was slaughtered, bathing one or more initiates in its blood. Others think it was used as a sort of stage trap door allowing a person to stage a surprising entry into the room.

properties.name: Mithraeum (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Mithras, Rome.

Under the church there is a 2nd c. AD, mithraeum, related to the presence of the barracks of Roman soldiers in the neighbourhood. 

The cult of Mithras was especially popular among soldiers. The remains of Castra Peregrinorum, the barracks of the peregrini, officials detached from provincial armies for special service to the capital, were found right under Santo Stefano Rotondo. The mithraeum belonged to Castra Peregrinorum but it was probably also attended by the soldiers of Cohors V Vigilum, whose barracks stood nearby on the other side of Via della Navicella.

properties.name: Mithraeum (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Mithras, Rome.

The original Mithrauem had a central aisle, a niche and side benches. Fine frescoes were found on the walls of the ancient Mithraeum as well as a stucco sculpture of Mithras the Bull Slayer, one of the main images of the Mithras cult. During the Dutch excavations in the 1950s, pieces of mosaic were found within the newly discovered rooms underneath Santa Prisca. Renovations in 220 AD yielded a larger central cult room and the addition of new ones while the frescoes were covered with new, more elaborate paintings.

properties.name: Pantheon (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple to all the gods, Rome.

Famed temple erected by Agrippa in the Campus Martius, c. 27 BC, with his other building projects there: the Saepta Iulia, Diribitorium, Thermae of Agrippa, Nemus: Agrippa, and Stagnum Agrippae.

 Evidence suggests that Agrippa’s Pantheon had a rectangular pronaos entered from the N by way of two flights of stairs, which was linked, perhaps via a S projection, to a marble-paved, enclosed circular component, which was almost certainly hypaethral.

Under the façade of the Hadrianic Pantheon, 19th-c. Italian excavations uncovered a rectangular foundation c. 44 x 20 m; its N wall, composed of 10 travertine piers and rubble infill, lies beneath the 8 front columns of the Hadrianic pronaos, while centered on its S wall is a projection 21.25 m wide (the depth cannot be determined due to the massive foundations for the Hadrianic rotunda). Traces of two levels of marble paving slabs were located below the rotunda’s floor, one plausibly attributed to the Agrippan monument, the other to its Domitianic restoration. Further, fragments of a circular wall (L. 10 m, H. 1.65 m, W. 0.61 m) were revealed along the SE edge of the Hadrianic rotunda’s foundations; it has the same degree of curvature as the Hadrianic Pantheon.

The Augustan Pantheon was destroyed along with other buildings in a huge fire in the year 80 AD. Domitian rebuilt the Pantheon, which was burnt again in 110 AD.

The degree to which the decorative scheme should be credited to Hadrian's architects is uncertain. Finished by Hadrian but not claimed as one of his works, it used the text of the original inscription on the new façade (a common practice in Hadrian's rebuilding projects all over Rome; the only building on which Hadrian put his own name was the Temple to the Deified Trajan).

properties.name: Sacellum Acilium (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Shrine to the Acilii, Rome.

An Augustan compital shrine marking the intersection of the Sacra Via with a street running N–S on the S slope of the Carinae. 

Its well-preserved remains were excavated by Colini in 1932 during the opening of Via dell’Impero. The compitum consisted of a small distyle shrine atop a square podium (c. 2.75 x 3 m) reached by a short flight of 4 steps. Inscriptions date the monument to 5 BC, identify it definitively, as well as indicate that the surrounding neighborhood was known as the Vicus Compiti Acili. This shrine was a notable landmark in the Augustan era; the calendar of the Arvals describes the Tigillum Sororium as ad compitum Acili.

properties.name: Sacellum Concordiae Augustae (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Shrine to Concordia Augusta, Rome.

A travertine altar inscribed CONC]ORD[IAE] AVG SACR and a massive travertine base (1.58 x 1.62 m), most likely for a statue, were found in situ at the Forum Boarium in 1939; the findspot is close by the Cloaca Maxima and just E of the major N–S traffic artery along the Forum Bovarium. 

The altar and base have been convincingly interpreted as the remains of a compital shrine and attributed to the Augustan period. As a compitum, the shrine is an important testimony for the existence of residential quarters in this area, which must have demarcated the W border of the forum.

properties.name: Sacellum Fontis (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Shrine to Fons, Rome.

A shrine to Fons built from Corsican spoils was dedicated by Papirius Maso, probably in 221 BC.

 There are no known remains, but on the basis of a fragment of the fasti viae Ardeatinae it is agreed to have stood outside the Porta Fontinalis, probably on the saddle between the Arx and the Quirinal next to the Via Flaminia.

properties.name: Sacellum Fortunae (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Shrine of Fortuna, Rome.

Shrine of Fortuna, on the Vicus Longus, believed to be founded by Servius Tullius. Plutarch describes the cult site both as an altar and as a shrine; it probably comprised an altar surrounded by an enclosure wall. The exact site of the shrine along the Vicus Longus is unknown, as is the Latin translation of the Greek epithet ‘Εὔελπις’ (bonae spei, bene sperans, bona, felix, and tutela have all been proposed).

properties.name: Sacellum Iani Quirini (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Shrine to Janus Quirinus, Rome.

The shrine of Ianus Quirinus, was one of the oldest monuments in the Forum; perhaps it served originally as a bridge (ianus) carrying the Sacra Via over the Cloaca Maxima. 

Its precise location in the Forum in the Augustan period is unclear. Ancient sources locate the Ianus sanctuary ‘at/near the bottom of the Argiletum’ and ‘in front of the doors’ of the Curia Iulia. It is probably to be identified with the small structure in brick and travertine still visible at the corner of the Basilica Paulli facing the Curia, an identification reinforced by Cozza’s location of fragment 212c of the Severan Marble Plan. 

According to tradition, the doors of the Ianus Quirinus shrine were closed when Rome was at peace. Augustus boasts in his Res Gestae that these doors had been closed only twice before his time, but three times while he was princeps. The shrine is depicted on coins of Nero as a small rectangular building in ashlar masonry with double doors and no visible roof.

properties.name: Sacellum Murciae (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Shrine to Murcia, Rome.

The shrine of the archaic divinity Murcia stood within the track of the Circus Maximus near the first turning post (the SE meta) on the Aventine side.

 Varro relates that the small shrine was once surrounded by a grove, but this had been reduced to a single myrtle tree, a vestigium, by the Augustan era. In late antiquity the valley was called the vallis Murcia after the goddess, but perhaps only after her shrine had been substantially enlarged.

properties.name: Sacellum Pudicitiae Plebeiae (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Shrine to Pudicitia Plebeia, Rome.

Shrine to Pudicitia Plebeia, founded in 296 BC by the patrician matron Verginia in part of her residence on the Vicus Longus along the SE slope of the Quirinal. 

While Livy records that the cult fell into oblivion after worship was taken up by women of questionable character, Festus writes as though the cult was still active in his day; thus it may well have had a presence in Augustan Rome.

properties.name: Sacellum Veneris Cloacinae (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Shrine to Venus Cloacina, Rome.

A small, circular shrine in the Forum dedicated to Cloacina, the divinity of the Cloaca Maxima, later identified with Venus. 

It is first mentioned near the beginning of the 2nd c. BC by Plautus. The shrine, depicted on coins of c. 42 BC, was located in front of the Republican tabernae novae, probably at the spot where the Cloaca entered the Forum, and can be securely identified with the circular marble base discovered in front of the Porticus Gaii et Lucii.

properties.name: Sacellum Victoriae Virginis (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Shrine to Victoria Virgo, Rome.

Small shrine to Victoria Virgo which stood on the SW Palatine between the temples of Magna Mater and Victoria. Dedicated on August 1, 193 BC by M. Porcius Cato, the shrine shares its dies natalis with the adjacent aedes of Victoria.

The brick ruins visible today date from the Hadrianic period; below these are incomplete late-Republican foundations for a rectangular room which has been identified as the aedicula of Victoria Virgo based upon their date and literary sources that place Cato’s shrine in close proximity to the Palatine Temple of Victory. While the Republican shrine was certainly much smaller than the Hadrianic building, its full dimensions are not preserved.

properties.name: Sacellum Vici (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Shrine to the Vicus, Rome.

Compital shrine of an unnamed Esquiline neighborhood near the Clivus Suburanus, discovered in 1888 in situ near S. Martino ai Monti.

 An isolated structure surrounded by street pavement, the compitum was refurbished in 10 BC with an inscribed marble statue base for Mercury behind a marble-revetted podium (c. 4 x 5 m), perhaps for an aedicular shrine; an older, altar-like structure of travertine behind the statue base was carefully preserved in the course of these building measures.

 According to its inscription, Augustus dedicated the statue in 10 BC from the collected monies submitted to him in his absence by the Roman people on New Year’s day; this closely follows Suetonius’ report of Augustus’ practice in the case of neighborhoods ‘such as Apollo Sandalarius, Iuppiter Tragoedus, and others’. Due to its archaeological context, the reported modalities of its realization, and its secure date several years before the introduction of the Regiones Quattuordecim in 7 BC, the monument is of singular importance for the incipient Augustan transformation of Rome’s vicus-neighborhoods and their compital cults.

 Unfortunately, the name of this vicus is not mentioned in the inscription and remains unknown.

properties.name: Sacellum Vici Aesculatorum (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Shrine to the Vicus Aesculati, Rome.

The Augustan-era compital shrine of the Vicus Aesc(u)leti, whose marble altar and travertine pavement were found in situ during late-19th c. construction work in Via Arenula, SW of the Circus Flaminius near the Tiber, where the shrine faced an ancient NW-SE thoroughfare.

 Both the altar and its pavement carry dedicatory inscriptions of the vicomagistri ‘of the 9th year’; thus they probably date from c. 2 AD. The compital aedicula, remains of which are also preserved, seems to have been restored under Domitian. The findspot of the compital sanctuary firmly anchors the location of the Vicus Aesc(u)leti neighborhood, and suggests that the thoroughfare in front of it be identified as the neighborhood’s eponymous street.

properties.name: Sacellum Vici Cornicularii (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Shrine to the Vicus Cornicularius, Rome.

Inscriptions belonging to the marble compital aedicula (shrine) of the vicus Cornicularius were found in the course of foundation work for the Nuova Esattoria at the foot of the Oppian’s S slope. 

The oldest inscription dates from 22 AD and lists the magistri of the vicus ‘in the 27th year’, which means that this vicus was established in 6/5 BC; a second inscription, which dates between A.D. 53 and 55, records the location of the vicus in Regio III. While the precise findspot within the lot of the Esattoria has not been documented, the inscriptions were “evidently found in situ”, thus the area of the vicus-neighborhood can be approximated with some certainty.

properties.name: Sacellum Vici Salutis (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Shrine to the Vicus Salutis, Rome.

Compital shrine marking the intersection of the Alta Semita and Vicus Salutis, restored by Agrippa while aedile in 33 BC. 

The findspot of this fragmentary inscription within S. Maria Maddalena suggests the location of the crossroads and indicates that this portion of the Quirinal had a residential function in the Augustan era. This shrine is of especial importance as it establishes a firm association between its location and the toponym ‘Salutis’ which allows the collis Salutaris, the Temple of Salus and the Porta Salutis to be placed nearby.

properties.name: Tarentum (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Dis and Proserpina, Rome

Sacred precinct enclosing the subterranean altar of Dis and Proserpina, located at the extreme NW periphery of the Campus Martius.

 Stressing its vicinity to the Tiber is Servius, who identifies the Tarentum with a part of the river itself. Ovid mentions the Vada Tarenti, which was probably the original ford where the Via Tecta crossed the river in the NW Campus Martius to continue N as the Via Triumphalis. The sharp turn that the Euripus takes in the NW Campus Martius before entering the Tiber has been interpreted as an attempt to preserve the topographic integrity of the pre-existing sanctuary of the Tarentum.

Since no ancient evidence mentions a temple dedicated to Dis and Proserpina in Rome, it seems that only the altar of Dis and Proserpina was located inside the Tarentum; like other subterranean altars, it was a sacred location in itself and did not need a temple. Most probably the Tarentum consisted of an open paved area.

properties.name: Templum (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple, Rome.

One of the earliest of the four known temples in the sacral area near Largo Argentina, Temple A was built on virgin soil c. 250-225 BC.

 First erected as a small prostyle, tetrastyle shrine in Grotta Oscura tufa (9.5 x 16 m on a podium H. 4 m.), the temple was expanded and elaborated in the 2nd c. BC probably to bring it in line with the style of Temple C. At this point, the building was faced with Monteverde tufa, expanded to a hexastyle prostyle temple, and received a fine peperino altar (12 x 14.5 m) built over the old staircase. In its final modification, during the third quarter of the 1st c. BC, the building acquired a new tufa podium (15 x 27.5 m) and a ring of 30 Anio tufa columns with Attic bases and Corinthian capitals. The column shafts were coated with white stucco to appear as marble. 

In the 12th c., this temple was incorporated into the Church of S. Nicola dei Caesarini or Calcarari (‘lime-burners’), hence its fine state of preservation. This temple has been identified as the Temple of Iuturna, built by Q. Lutatius Catulus (cos. 241) after his sea-victory over Carthage, and as the Temple of Feronia vowed by L. Aemilius Papus at the battle of Telamon in 225 BC; neither hypothesis is entirely satisfactory.

properties.name: Templum (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple, Rome.

One of the four known temples in the sacral area near Largo Argentina, Temple D is the least well-known, and lies, largely unexcavated, below Via Florida. 

From its earliest phase, c.200-150 BC, only a cement podium remains; during a second phase, dated to the late 2nd-early 1st c. BC, a larger cement podium (23.5 x 37 m) was built, engulfing the earlier shrine; this phase is dated by remains of the tufa pavement which unified the surrounding area at that time. The superstructure was rectangular in plan, with a colonnaded façade; fluted plaster pilasters were set into the brick-faced cella, which had a marble-covered cement floor and an unusually large marble threshold block. The superstructure, probably a Domitianic restoration, gives few clues to the building’s appearance in the Augustan era.

Temple D has been identified as the Temple of the Lares Permarini, vowed by L. Aemilius Regillus in 190 BC during a naval battle against Antiochus III, and dedicated by M. Aemilius Lepidus in 179 BC. This identification is not accepted, since the Temple of the Lares Permarini is known from the fasti Praenestini to have stood ‘within the Porticus Minucia’. Thus, Temple D remains without a solid identification.

properties.name: Templum Aesculapii (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Aesculapius, Rome.

The Temple to Aesculapius (Greek Asclepius), built on the Tiber island in 293 BC after a serious plague occasioned the introduction of the cult to Rome.

 From this time on, the Insula Tiberina acted as a place of refuge and of healing in the Republican city. Both literary and epigraphic evidence suggests that the temple, along with the entire island, underwent a major reconstruction and monumentalization around the mid-1st c. BC.

The Temple of Aesculapius is believed to have stood on the SE end of the island, probably under the Church of S. Bartolomeo. Although the temple is archaeologically unknown, the mid-1st c. BC travertine and tufa revetment at the S tip of the island imitating a trireme prow and its reliefs (head of Aesculapius and a staff entwined with a serpent), as well as the terracotta votive offerings from the head of the Pons Fabricius, strongly support this location. It seems likely that a small-scale temple stood at the very S end, directly above the prow. 

The Severan Marble Plan suggests that the small precinct was composed of a courtyard enclosed with a series of rooms.

properties.name: Templum Antonini et Faustinae (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Antoninus and Faustina, Rome.

The temple was constructed by the Emperor Antoninus Pius, beginning in 141 AD. It was initially dedicated to his deceased and deified wife, Faustina the Elder. Because of this, Faustina was the first Roman empress with a permanent presence in the Forum Romanum.

 When Antoninus Pius was deified after his death in 161 AD, the temple was re-dedicated to both Antoninus and Faustina by his successor, Marcus Aurelius.

The building stands on a high platform of large grey peperino tufa blocks. The later of two dedicatory inscriptions says, "Divo Antonino et Divae Faustinae Ex S.C." meaning, “For the divine Antoninus and for the divine Faustina, by decree of the Senate.”

The eight monolithic Corinthian columns of its pronaos are 17 metres (56 ft) in height. The rich bas-reliefs of the frieze under the cornice, featuring griffins, acanthus scrolls, and candelabra, were often copied from the sixteenth through the nineteenth centuries.

Based on numismatic evidence, the temple was originally fenced off from the Via Sacra and a large, seated statue of Faustina would have been inside of the cella. Fragments of this statue and one of Antoninus Pius, which was added later, were discovered in front of the Temple.

properties.name: Templum Apollonis Medici (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Apollo Medicus, Rome.

The Temple of Apollo, specifically of Apollo Medicus, was situated outside the Servian Wall ‘between the Forum Holitorium and the Circus Flaminius’. It was ‘by the Theater of Marcellus’.

 Lavishly rebuilt in the Augustan period by C. Sosius (cos. 32 BC), thus also known as Apollo Sosianus, the temple was one of the most richly-decorated in Rome.

The cult of Apollo Medicus had long been an architectural presence on the site, since in 433-431 BC it was vowed and dedicated by the consul C. Iulius following a plague. It has been proposed that in the early 2nd c. BC the temple was substantially rebuilt in relation to the construction of a new theatre in the area in 179 BC. This tetrastyle-diastyle Temple of Apollo was excavated in part below the Augustan phase of the temple.

Well-preserved remains document, indisputably, the complete rebuilding of the temple by C. Sosius following a new design, probably after his victory in Judea in 34 BC. The pictorial narratives of the internal frieze suggest that Augustus may have been responsible for the completion of the project, presumably after his triumphs in 29 BC; otherwise C. Sosius must have re-oriented his ideology for this narrative program.

properties.name: Templum Apollonis Palatini (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Apollo Palatinus, Rome.

Temple of Apollo built on the SW Palatine by Augustus and considered one of his most magnificent buildings. 

Construction probably began in 36 BC following Octavian’s victory at Naulochus over Sextus Pompey and was soon mirrored by C. Sosius, who rebuilt the Temple of Apollo Medicus around 34 BC. After the battle at Actium in 31 BC, Augustus’ temple became an ex voto of the victory of Octavian over Marc Antony and was dedicated on 9 October 28 BC.

Tradition holds that the temple was built on land Augustus had intended for his residence, but consecrated to Apollo following the interpretation of the haruspices (soothsayers) after the spot had been struck by a thunderbolt.

The temple is hexastyle, pseudo-peripteral, and has an almost square cella (20.5 x 19 m). Elevated on a high podium of opus caementicium and opus quadratum of tufa and travertine, the temple was reached by a lengthy staircase. The opus quadratum superstructure was constructed entirely of Carrara (Luna) marble. The early-Augustan date suggested by the literary evidence is supported by the archaeological finds; for instance, a Corinthian column fragment dates stylistically to the beginning of the Augustan era. Further, either the temple or the Portico of the Danaids was adorned with polychrome terracotta relief plaques dating to 36-28 BC. The pediment was decorated with Archaic Greek statues made of Parian marble attributed to the 6th c. BC Chian sculptors Bupalos and Athenis. Additional decoration is attested in Propertius , who reports that the central acroteria represented the chariot of Helios, and that the double doors of the cella were decorated with ivory reliefs depicting the Celtic attack on Delphi and the myth of the Niobids. The altar of the temple may have been located to the S in the Area Apollinis, where the Severan Marble Plan preserves an image of a cruciform monument.

The temple formed an integral part of a group of Augustan buildings on the SW Palatine, which included his own residence, an open terraced area framed by porticoes, and the Greek and Latin Library. Excavations revealed that the temple was situated just E of Augustus’ residence which physically embraced it on the N and W, while on a lower S terrace private vaulted ramps connected the domus to the level of the sanctuary. The temple and its surrounding buildings formed a complex overlooking the Circus Maximus that emulated the Hellenistic palace-sanctuary scheme exemplified in Attalid Pergamon.

properties.name: Templum Bacchi (Roma, Italia)
properties.description: Temple of Bacchus, Rome

properties.name: Templum Bellonae (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Bellona, Rome.

A large Temple of Bellona, the archaic Roman goddess of war, stood immediately E of the Temple of Apollo Medicus. The temple was vowed in 296 BC by Appius Claudius Caecus during a battle with the Etruscans and Samnites and dedicated after his victory.

 Archaeological evidence suggests that the temple was rebuilt at the time of Augustus, probably along with the aedes Apollinis. Located just outside the city walls, it was a favourable place for the senate to meet, especially to receive generals on their return from military campaigns. 

In 79 BC, the consuls Appius Claudius Pulcher and P. Servilius Vatia Isauricus placed the imagines clipeatae of their ancestors in the temple. The special connection between the temple and the Claudian family is perhaps further supported by the proximity of their tombs on the W slope of the Capitolium, but the location of this sepulcrum is not certain.

The remains of the temple were discovered in Piazza Montanara in the course of demolition work in 1932-33, and were excavated in 1938-39. They were convincingly identified with the Temple of Bellona by Coarelli through an association with fragments of the Severan Marble Plan depicting the temple. 

The peripteral, hexastyle temple had a deep pronaos and was raised on a high platform. The podium had a concrete core with a mixed aggregate of tufa, attributed to the Augustan period; its encasing opus quadratum masonry has been completely robbed, and very little survives of the marble architectural decoration of the superstructure. An L-shaped peperino portico enveloped the NW edge of the precinct, both defining the compound of the Temples of Apollo and Bellona, and screening the rising slopes of the Capitoline hill. Based on the dating of the sporadic pieces of architectural decoration, it is suggested that the temple was reconstructed roughly in the same years with the renovations of the Temple of Apollo Medicus, and was probably dedicated by Appius Claudius Pulcher, consul of 38 BC, in the year 33 or 32 BC after his triumph over Spain.

On the Augustan travertine pavement directly in front of the platform of the Temple of Bellona, and adjacent to the porticoes of the Theatrum Marcelli, the footprint of a “roughly circular” monument was traced by La Rocca, who identifies this spot with the Columna Bellica. Literary sources associate this column with middle- and late-Republican fetiales, a ritual declaration of war, which took place before the Temple of Bellona, since that area was considered foreign territory after the collective memory of the 3rd c. BC war against Pyrrhus. The ritual was revived at the time of Augustus and involved throwing a spear, presumably over the column, which marked Rome’s border with the symbolic foreign territory.

properties.name: Templum Bellonae Pulvinensis (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Bellona Pulvinensis, Rome.

Sanctuary of the Cappadocian goddess Ma, who was assimilated to Bellona in Rome, located inside the Porta Collina and known only from epigraphic and literary evidence. 

The goddess Bellona of this temple was known by two epithets: PVLVINENSIS and PEDISEQVA. Palmer plausibly argues that the temple was dedicated by L. Cornelius Sulla to commemorate his victory over the Samnites at the Colline Gate in 82 BC. Martial complains that the noisy racket of an inspired throng of Bellona’s worshippers on the Quirinal deprived him of sleep.

Inscriptions uncovered during the 1872 excavations for the Ministero delle Finanze locate the Vicus Bellonae near the Porta Collina, and it is likely that the temple stood near the eponymous neighborhood. The shrine was located within a grove and placed on a pulvinus, “a terraced embankment with building and plantings”, near the Porta Collina and Campus Sceleratus.

properties.name: Templum Bellonae Rufiliae (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Bellona Rufilia, Rome.

The Temple of Bellona Rufilia is attested on the tombstone set up by C. Calidius Custos for L. Cornelius Ianuarius, who is described as a ‘devotee of the Temple of Bellona Rufilia in the region of Isis and Serapis’. 

It is argued that the deceased was a descendant of a freedman of L. Cornelius Sulla, who had been put in charge of a temple first erected by P. Cornelius Rufinus, the last of Sulla’s ancestors to hold the consulship, after his triumph over the Samnites in 290 BC. The inscription mentions ISIS ET SERAPIS, the temple from which Regio III: Isis et Serapis took its name; the Temple of Bellona Rufilia may thus be located close by. Since the inscription was found in the Villa Palombara, just E of the Servian Wall, it seems best to place this temple near the Wall, between the Iseum and the road leading out of the Colosseum Valley (“Via Tusculana”).

properties.name: Templum Bonae Deae (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of the Bona Dea, Rome.

The old sanctuary to Bona Dea ‘below the Rock’ on the Aventine, the “principal sanctuary of the region”, without identified remains, was of high repute and reserved for women only. 

It was restored by Livia, in perceived emulation of Augustus’ work. While the precise place of the cult site is not clear, a location in Regio XII is attested by the late-antique Regionary Catalogues; further, it was situated below the mighty ‘Rock’ of its mons, the Saxum from which Remus was thought to have taken his auspices for Rome’s foundation. For convincing reasons, the Saxum is identified with the cliff which forms the conspicuous N angle of the SE summit, the “Lesser Aventine” a point whose strategic importance led to its inclusion within the Servian Wall. Thus, a sanctuary right below this prominent rocky face seems warranted.

properties.name: Templum Castoris et Pollucis (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Castor and Pollux, Rome.

The Temple of Castor on the S side of the Forum, between the Basilica Iulia and the Lacus Iuturnae, dedicated in 484 BC by the son of the dictator Postumius who, according to Roman tradition, had vowed the temple at the battle of Lake Regillus in 493 BC.

 The temple was rebuilt by L. Caecilius Metellus Delmaticus in 117 BC, and Cicero notes that Verres made certain repairs to it. The Metellan temple may have burned in the fire of either 14 or 9 BC, but the sources do not record this; in any case the temple was completely rebuilt by Tiberius and dedicated in the names of Tiberius and his dead brother Drusus in 6 AD.

Caligula converted the temple into a vestibule for his palace, an arrangement which Claudius eradicated, and Domitian is credited with a restoration, but there are no further traces of major renovations and scholars agree that the existing remains are mainly Augustan.

The temple, which was octastyle and peripteral in its Augustan phase, was approached by one frontal and two lateral staircases; in the Augustan period the platform to which the lateral staircases provided access served as a speaker’s platform. At a later date this arrangement was modified and the staircase became a single frontal flight, as shown on the Severan Marble Plan.

properties.name: Templum Castoris et Pollucis (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Castor & Pollux, Rome.

Tetrastyle, prostyle temple along the SW side of the Circus Flaminius dedicated to Castor and Pollux, characterized by an unusual transverse cella, similar to the Tiberian Temple of Concordia Augusta or the Temple of Veiovis. 

The limited space available for the construction of the temple between the Circus Flaminius and the Tiber may have dictated this plan, though it should be noted that no archaeological evidence of contemporaneous structures on the W side of the Circus Flaminius has been uncovered.

Only three literary sources mention the structure: Vitruvius, the calendars (fasti), and Plutarch, who mentions that a Caecilius Metellus decorated the Temple of the Dioscuri with statues and images; this person may have also donated the temple itself. Since the name of this temple is present in the fasti Amiternini and Antiati, both written before the Caesarian change of the calendar in 46 BC, that year should be taken as terminus ante quem. Therefore, Plutarch’s Metellus must be identified with Q. Caecilius Metellus Pius who triumphed in Spain in 71 BC and built the temple using war booty (ex manubiis) soon after.

properties.name: Templum Cereris, Libri Patris et Liberae (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Ceres, Liber Pater and Libera, Rome.

Joint temple to Ceres, Liber Pater, and Libera, usually abbreviated to ‘aedes Cereris’, located close by the Circus Maximus and near the temples of Flora and Luna; no physical remains have been identified. 

Reputed for its image of Ceres, the ‘first bronze image of a divinity at Rome’, and for the exquisite artworks displayed there, the temple also served as the headquarters of the plebeian aediles and housed their archive, with copies of the Senate’s decrees. In addition, the temple possessed the asylum Cereris, a place of refuge where bread was distributed to the poor.

 Thus, the Temple of Ceres formed a defining place of plebeian self-identification. The building had a strikingly old-fashioned appearance and Vitruvius cites it as the primary example of the Tuscan style soon before it was destroyed by fire in 31 BC. Remarkably, Augustus only began its rebuilding (along with the nearby Temple of Flora, and the Temple of Ianus at the Forum Holitorium), and its rededication did not take place before 17 AD, which means that this important sanctuary remained both a ruin and a construction site throughout the Augustan period.

properties.name: Templum Concordiae (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Concordia, Rome.

The first temple to Concord, dedicated in 216 BC, stood on the Arx.

properties.name: Templum Concordiae Augustae (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Concordia Augusta, Rome.

The Temple of Augustan Concord at the foot of the Capitolium overlooking the Forum. 

According to Roman tradition, the Temple of Concord was originally vowed by Camillus during patrician-plebeian struggles in 367 BC. Although the people voted to build the temple on behalf of Camillus, it is unclear whether this temple was ever built, though recent excavations have uncovered 4th c. BC remains on the site.

 A temple to Concordia was definitely built by L. Opimius in 121 BC following the death of C. Gracchus, but this temple burned, perhaps in 9 BC. Tiberius vowed to restore the temple in 7 BC and the rebuilt temple, now to Augustan Concord, was dedicated in the names of Tiberius and his dead brother Drusus.

The visible remains of the temple are from the Augustan phase. The cella, which abuts the Tabularium, has a transverse axis, an unusual design that maximizes the available space. The new temple probably covered the Volcanal, an altar to Vulcan said to have been erected by Titus Tatius. The NE façade of the pronaos and the NE half of the cella, now underneath the adjacent staircase ascending the Capitolium, are restored on the principle of symmetry.

properties.name: Templum Dianae (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Diana, Rome.

Temple vowed during the Ligurian war in 187 BC and dedicated in 179 BC by M. Aemilius Lepidus in conjunction with his Temple to Iuno Regina, both located in circo Flaminio. 

Unfortunately, neither the remains nor the exact location of the Temple of Diana have been positively identified. Augustus does not mention restoring the Aemilian shrine in his Res Gestae, though it could have been among the 82 buildings he restored but did not name individually. 

Coarelli postulates an Augustan restoration of Diana’s shrine based on aurei of c. 29-27 BC which depicts Diana on the obverse and a small distyle, prostyle Tuscan shrine with a naval trophy in the cella on the reverse. Coarelli equates the numismatic depiction of this shrine with one of the two small, square sacella depicted in the exedra behind the Theatrum Marcelli on the Severan Marble Plan.

properties.name: Templum Dianae Aventinae (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Diana Aventina, Rome.

Temple precinct of Diana Aventina in the Lauretum on the Aventine, the main sanctuary of the goddess in Rome and a place of strong plebeian self-representation. 

Allegedly founded by the slave-born Servius Tullius, the sanctuary was once the assembly-place of the Latin cities under Rome’s leadership and also a notable asylum; its festival on the Ides of August continued to be the holiday of slaves. Further, the sanctuary served as an important archive for legislation; a bronze pillar, still standing in the Augustan period, included the Icilian law of the mid-5th c. BC de Aventino publicando which provided allotments of Aventine land to the plebs.

No remains of this temple have been identified, yet the building and its precinct are represented on fragment 22 of the Severan Marble Plan, next to the Temple of Minerva. 

Under the Augustan program of ‘adorning the city’, the temple was rebuilt or restored by L. Cornificius. Since the name DIANA CORNIF. is attested independently, the label CORNIFICIA[... on the Marble Plan clearly refers to Diana Cornificia or Cornificiana and thus establishes the identification. The footprint of the octostyle podium temple shown on the 3rd c. AD fragment is presumably still that of Cornificius’ building; it is surrounded by a precinct with a double-colonnaded portico along its flank.

properties.name: Templum Dianae Plancianae (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Diana Planciana, Rome.

Republican temple of Diana Planciana on the collis Latiaris of the Quirinal; its name and probable location are known from inscriptions commemorating an AEDITVMVS (temple keeper) of the sanctuary. 

The temple has been linked to Cn. Plancius (curule aedile in 55 or 54 BC), an affiliation possibly supported by the appearance of Diana in his coinage. L. Munatius Plancus is another possible donour for the temple. Either way, the temple was certainly erected before Augustus ended the senatorial tradition of eponymous temple dedications.

The temple was located near the intersection of Via Panisperna and Salita del Grillo, where fragments of an archaistic female statue, perhaps the cult statue, were recovered along with the two inscriptions. Since the travertine architectural remains found on this site have been lost we must still be cautious, but the mention of imperial freedmen as AEDITVI suggests that the cult site was of some size.

properties.name: Templum Dii Fidii (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Dius Fidius, Rome.

Temple of Dius Fidius, the god of oaths and treaties, located on the Quirinal near the Porta Sanqualis and Temple of Quirinus.

 It was believed to have been built by Tarquinius Priscus and later dedicated by Spurius Postumius Albinus, though no remains of the temple survive; the structure would have been open to the sky, given the nature of the deity. An inscription found near S. Silvestro allows the sanctuary to be located in the vicinity of the church.

properties.name: Templum Divi Claudii (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of the Divine Claudius, Rome.

Construction of the Temple of Claudius on the Caelian Hill was begun by Agrippina, the fourth wife of the Emperor Claudius, after his death in 54 AD. 

In 59 AD, Agrippina was murdered by her son, the Emperor Nero, who immediately destroyed the unfinished temple and converted the massive podium built to support it to his own uses. The eastern wall was transformed into a grand nymphaeum to embellish the view from Nero's new palace, the Domus Aurea, on the adjacent Oppian Hill. The nymphaeum was made up of tiered columns and semicircular and rectangular niches; it likely would have contained a large sculptural group at the center. Archaeological excavations confirm that the water cascaded from the top of the nymphaeum down into 4 basins, which in turn fed into the huge pool in the valley now occupied by the Colosseum, which was in the time of Nero the centerpiece of the gardens belonging to the Domus Aurea.

To supply his nymphaeum with water, Nero constructed reservoirs within the Caelian and built a new branch aqueduct to carry water to the hill from the Aqua Claudia. This branch, known as the Arcus Neroniani, accessed the Claudia at Porta Maggiore and ran 2 kilometers west to the southern side of the Caelian Hill, where it terminated at a structure called the Aqueductium. From there conduits branched off along the hill to the north, bringing water to the nymphaeum and the temple. Another conduit was carried to the western edge of the hill and ended right beside the Temple of Claudius.

Vespasian reconstructed the Temple of Claudius and established an association dedicated to the worship of the numen of Claudius, known as the Augustales, adjacent to the temple on its southern side. A fragment of the Forma Urbis which depicts the southern end of the temple complex shows an apsidal building in front of the stairs and rampway which accessed the temple, which was likely the home of this association. The last mention of the temple is from the fourth century and nothing is known of what happened to it after Vespasian’s reconstruction.

properties.name: Templum Divi Iulii (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of the Divine Julius, Rome.

The Temple of the Deified Julius Caesar on the E side of the Forum. Erected on the site where the people had burned Caesar’s corpse, the temple was begun in 42 BC by the Triumvirs and completed by Octavian. It was dedicated on 18 August 29 BC. 

The temple stood on a platform c. 3.5 m high to which lateral ramps on either side of the structure provided access. These ramps, which continued as arcuated porches along the sides of the structure and along the NE wall of the Regia, have been identified as the porticus Iulia . The ramps may have been connected behind the temple by means of a cryptoporticus. A semicircular exedra in the center of the platform contains the remains of a small circular structure, probably the altar built by Octavian to replace the original altar and column marking the site of Caesar’s funeral pyre (which the consul P. Cornelius Dolabella had removed in 42 BC. This exedra was subsequently walled off, an action Coarelli connects with Augustus’ decision to restrict the temple’s right of asylum by denying access to the altar. Most scholars identify the platform on which the temple stood as the rostra aedis Divi Iulii, also known as the rostra Iulia.

 The combination of temple and speaker’s platform was very common, however, and the plan for the Temple of Divus Julius seems to have been modelled closely on that of the Temple of Venus Genetrix.

The temple itself rose on a second platform, approached by a frontal staircase. Very little of the temple has survived, but extensive excavations of 1950-54 uncovered most of the structure’s ground-plan.

properties.name: Templum Divi Romuli (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of the Divine Romulus, Rome.

The Temple is traditionally held to have been dedicated by Emperor Maxentius to his son and co-consul Valerius Romulus, who died in 309 AD and was given divine honours. The temple building was probably part of a rebuilding program of "incredible intensity" undertaken by Maxentius in the area, following a disastrous fire in 306 AD; the project was only part-complete at his death. 

The temple's identification with Valerius Romulus is tentative, based on the spot-find of a coin dated to 307 AD showing the distinctive shape of the building, and a nearby dedication to Valerius Romulus as a divinised mortal.

 The temple has also been speculated as a rebuilding of the original temple of "Jupiter Stator", or one dedicated to Penates, restored by Maxentius.

properties.name: Templum Fauni (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Faunus, Rome.

A temple was dedicated to Faunus, an ancient Latin god of the forest and its prophetic voices, in 196 BC at the N end of the Tiber island. 

It was vowed by the tribuni plebis, Cn. Domitius Ahenobarbus and C. Scribonius Curio, and dedicated by the praetor urbanus of the time. Vitruvius mentions the building as an example of the tetrastyle, prostyle temple.

properties.name: Templum Febris (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Febris, Rome.

A minor sanctuary dedicated to Febris on the Quirinal, situated at the highest point of the Vicus Longus.

 Its date, form, size and exact location are unknown, and no archaeological remains are associated with it.

properties.name: Templum Felicitatis (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Felicitas, Rome.

A Temple of Felicitas in the NW corner of the Forum, planned by Caesar and built by M. Aemilius Lepidus in 44 BC. 

According to Dio, the temple was erected on the site of the old Curia Hostilia as the formal justification for the Curia’s demolition. Although it is often assumed that this temple was itself destroyed soon after its erection, there is no evidence for its destruction before or during the Augustan period, and monumental remains discovered under the Church of SS. Luca e Martina adjacent to the Forum Iulium are now thought to belong to this structure.

properties.name: Templum Feroniae (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Feronia, Rome.

One of the four known temples in the sacral area near Largo Argentina, Temple C was perhaps the oldest, originally built in the first half of the 3rd c. BC concurrently with, or slightly earlier than, Temple A. 

The temple was prostyle, tetrastyle sine postico, with widely-spaced façade columns perhaps of the Tuscan order. The massive tufa podium, with heavy moldings typical of the early 3rd c. BC, still stands, though the visible remains of the cella floor and superstructure are Domitianic in date.

Before the mid-2nd c. BC, a new altar built on a large platform in front of the temple, and inscribed A. POSTVMIVS A. F. A. N. ALBINVS DVOVIR LEGE PLAETORIA REFICIVNDAM COERAVIT, replacing the original. The altar was still a prominent feature in the Augustan era, for even though the installation of the first tufa pavement engulfed the platform, care was taken to leave the altar exposed; it was finally buried by a second pavement dating to 80 AD.

properties.name: Templum Fidei (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Fides, Rome. 

The Temple of Fides, also known as Fides Publica and Fides populi Romani, was built between 258 and 247 BC and rebuilt between 115 and 109 BC. It stood in Capitolio and near the Temple of Iuppiter Optimus Maximus, hence in the Area Capitolina. 

A military diploma set up ‘on a wall behind the Temple of Fides suggests that it stood near the outer temenos wall. It may be placed on the SW edge of the Area Capitolina on the basis of archaeological remains found in the Piazza della Consolazione and the Vico Iugario. These finds, which are believed to have slipped down from the Capitol in the Middle Ages, included the base of a statue of Fides and fragmentary inscriptions of treaties of friendship and alliance with foreign communities; these were perhaps originally posted on or near this temple, for the goddess Fides took treaties between Rome and foreign nations in her charge.

 Architectural fragments found at the foot of the Capitol suggest that it was a large temple, with a podium at least 2 m high and with dimensions of c. 20 x 30-35 m.

properties.name: Templum Florae (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Flora, Rome.

Temple of Flora on the slope of the Aventine by the Circus Maximus. Featuring a distinctly plebeian cult, the sanctuary was founded by the plebeian aediles L. and M. Publicii, probably concurrent with the institution of the Floralia in c. 240 BC and the construction of the Clivus Publicius, the Aventine’s main access from the N. 

The temple is without identified remains and its placement on Coarelli’s plan is certainly too detailed. But since it stood ‘on the same site’ as the Temple of Ceres, its place in the immediate vicinity of Ceres’ aedes is assured; thus, Flora’s temple can be located on the slope of the Aventine’s N tip, just above the head of the Circus Maximus. 

As with the Temple of Ceres, Flora’s temple was rather dilapidated when Augustus began to restore or rebuild it, and its rededication did not take place before the early years of Tiberius’ reign.

properties.name: Templum Florae (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Flora, Rome.

A Republican temple to the goddess Flora was located in a valley of the Quirinal, probably on the site of an earlier altar to the Sabine goddess dedicated by Titus Tatius. 

Since no archaeological remains survive, its location can only be estimated from ancient texts that associate it with other monuments on the Quirinal. Vitruvius notes that the cinnabar workshops of Rome, the “Officinae Minii”, were located between the temples of Flora and Quirinus, which establishes the proximity of the aedes Florae to the collis Quirinalis. Varro describes a clivus, or steep road, linking the Temple of Flora to the Capitolium Vetus; thus the temple must have been positioned along the side or at the foot of a hill. Martial also associates the Temple of Flora with the Capitolium Vetus; his wording suggests a clear line of sight between the two sanctuaries. 

The Temple of Flora was probably situated within the Servian Wall, as would befit an archaic foundation of Titus Tatius and a cult led by a flamen.

properties.name: Templum Fortis Fortunae (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Fors Fortuna, Rome.

A Republican temple, or temples, dedicated to Fors Fortuna in Trans Tiberim, presumably somewhere along the Via Campana (later via Portuensis), which presents severe topographical problems. 

Two archaic temples of Fors Fortuna are known to have been built on the Via Campana, one founded by Servius Tullius at the first milestone, and the other by an unknown dedicator at the sixth milestone. The latter is not to be considered here, since it falls well outside the city. Two later temples to Fors Fortuna followed the early foundations mentioned above. The first one is known from a contract dating to 293 BC by Spurius Carvilius which specifically mentions a temple near that of Servius Tullius. The second was a new temple, or restoration, dedicated in 16 AD by Tiberius within the confines of Horti Caesaris.

Since the first milestone on Via Campana (as measured from the Pons Aemilius) would fall within the limits of the Horti Caesaris, it is reasonable to think that all three temples to the cult (i.e., those of Servius Tullius, Sp. Carvilius and Tiberius) may have been built within the same neighborhood in S Trans Tiberim; the later ones may even represent the rebuilding(s) of the same fanum. Tiberius’ rebuilding also shows that the cult was active upon the same site into the early 1st c. AD.

properties.name: Templum Fortunae (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Fortuna, Rome.

Twin temples dedicated to Fortuna and Mater Matuta located at the N border of the Forum Boarium, just inside the Porta Carmentalis.

 Tradition held that both were founded by Servius Tullius, and the temples are often mentioned together, even sharing a dedication day. 

Since both temples burned in the fire of 213 BC, which also damaged the Forum Holitorium and Porta Carmentalis, a location in that vicinity seems likely. These factors led scholars to identify the twin temples discovered in 1937 near the Church of S. Omobono as those of Fortuna and Mater Matuta; further, archaeological evidence dates this site back to the Archaic period, which corresponds well with the tradition of the temples’ foundation. The temples share a single, large platform and each has an altar in front of it. Under the nave of S. Omobono is the aedes of Mater Matuta, while the temple of Fortuna lay further S. The visible temple remains seem to belong to the reconstruction in 212 BC.

properties.name: Templum Fortunae (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Fortuna, Rome.

A religious sanctuary standing in the horti of Lucullus, perhaps dedicated to Fortuna, which dates to the 3rd or 2nd c. BC.

 It appears to have been entirely rebuilt by Valerius Asiaticus during the Julio-Claudian period as part of a complete overhaul of the estate’s design. The association of this sanctuary with Fortuna is based upon a dedicatory inscription discovered in the nearby monastery of Trinità dei Monti. The garden complex built by Valerius Asiaticus also bears a striking resemblance to the famous tiered sanctuary of Fortuna at Praeneste. Republican remains recovered from this site consist of a wall in opus quadratum and some tufa columns with Tuscan capitals.

properties.name: Templum Fortunae Equestris (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Fortuna Equestris, Rome.

Temple vowed and dedicated in the 2nd c. BC near the Theatre of Pompey in the Campus Martius; no archaeological remains are extant and its exact location is a matter of debate.

Q. Fulvius Flaccus vowed the temple in 180 BC, when his Roman cavalry bravely turned the tide in a battle against the Celtiberians, and dedicated it at the end of his term as censor on 13 August 173 BC. 

Vitruvius locates it near the stone theatre; since he wrote before the mid-20s BC, this could only have been the Theatrum Pompeium.

properties.name: Templum Fortunae Huiusce Diei (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Fortuna Huiusce Diei, Rome.

The round, columned temple vowed by Q. Lutatius Catulus to ‘this day’s Fortune’, on 30 June 101 BC, during a battle at Vercellae against the Cimbri; it was dedicated on the anniversary of the conflict sometime before 87 BC. 

 The fasti Allifani locate the temple in Campo. Corroboration comes from Varro, who describes the ‘Catulan temple’, aedes Catuli, as a ‘columned tholos’, tholos columnatus. This temple must have stood near the Villa Publica, since Varro’s description is part of a ‘conversation’ held in the latter building, itself located ‘on the edge of the Campus [Martius]’. This description accords well with the tholos temple located in the “Area Sacra” in Largo Argentina, commonly known as Temple B, which was built in the first quarter of the 1st c. BC.

One of the four known temples in the sacral area near Largo Argentina, Temple B is the latest dedication and the only one with a firm identification. The original temple had a circular cella surrounded by a ring of 18 stuccoed tufa columns with travertine bases and capitals (diam. 9.3 m). The façade was marked by a shallow porch, flanked by two long bases (podia) for the display of statues (6.66 x 2.10 m). Traces of a 3rd c. BC cappellaccio wall, probably the temenos wall marking the boundary between Temples A and C, were found underneath Temple B and suggest that Catulus took near-equal amounts of consecrated space from Temples A and C to build his new monument; this encroachment was masked when he installed an expansive tufa pavement, which unified the sacral area.

In the mid-1st c. BC the temple was extensively renovated: the podium was enlarged (by a layer of rubble fill faced with thin peperino slabs), the old cella wall was removed, and new tufa walls were built between the columns to create a pseudo-monopteros (diam. 15.5 m). Inside the new cella, a base for a colossal statue was set up. The head of an immense acrolithic statue (H. 8 m) depicting Fortuna was unearthed between Temples B and C in 1929 (now in the Palazzo dei Conservatori). This sculptural find offers further support for the identification of Temple B as that of Fortuna Huiusce Diei. The podia flanking the façade stairway were well suited for the display of statuary, and Pliny records 13 statues ‘ad aedem Fortunae Huiusce Diei’; many of these were dedicated by Catulus, though some were donated by an Aemilius Paulus.

The temple was not modified again until after the fire of 80 AD, when the fire-damaged tufa walls and column shafts of the cella were covered by a layer of brick; this renovation did not alter the temple’s plan, thus the Severan Marble Plan preserves a fairly accurate image of the original temple.

properties.name: Templum Fortunae Primigeniae (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Fortuna Primigenia , Rome.

Shrine or sanctuary of Fortuna Primigenia on the Capitol, attributed to Servius Tullius, and located close to the Temple of Iuppiter Tonans.

properties.name: Templum Fortunae Primigeniae (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Fortuna Primigenia, Rome.

A trio of Republican temples dedicated to Fortuna and known as the Tres Fortunae was located near the Porta Collina on the Quirinal.

 One was dedicated to Fortuna Primigenia in 194 BC by Q. Marcius Ralla to fulfill a vow made 10 years earlier by P. Sempronius Tuditanus. 

Ovid records a second temple, this dedicated to Fortuna Publica; Fortuna Publica Citerior may have been the full name of this temple which the fasti Praenestini locate on the Quirinal. 

A third temple honoured Fortuna Publica Populi Romani Quiritium, which the calendars also locate IN COLLE QVIRINALI.

Thus, three temples of Fortuna are known to have been located on the collis Quirinalis near the Porta Collina.

properties.name: Templum Fortunae Publicae Citerioris (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Fortuna Publica Citerior, Rome.

A trio of Republican temples dedicated to Fortuna and known as the Tres Fortunae was located near the Porta Collina on the Quirinal.

One was dedicated to Fortuna Primigenia in 194 BC by Q. Marcius Ralla to fulfill a vow made 10 years earlier by P. Sempronius Tuditanus.

Ovid records a second temple, this dedicated to Fortuna Publica; Fortuna Publica Citerior may have been the full name of this temple which the fasti Praenestini locate on the Quirinal.

A third temple honoured Fortuna Publica Populi Romani Quiritium, which the calendars also locate IN COLLE QVIRINALI.

Thus, three temples of Fortuna are known to have been located on the collis Quirinalis near the Porta Collina.

properties.name: Templum Fortunae Publicae Populorum Romanorum Quiritium (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Fortuna Publica Populi Romani Quiritium, Rome.

A trio of Republican temples dedicated to Fortuna and known as the Tres Fortunae was located near the Porta Collina on the Quirinal.

One was dedicated to Fortuna Primigenia in 194 BC by Q. Marcius Ralla to fulfill a vow made 10 years earlier by P. Sempronius Tuditanus.

Ovid records a second temple, this dedicated to Fortuna Publica; Fortuna Publica Citerior may have been the full name of this temple which the fasti Praenestini locate on the Quirinal.

A third temple honoured Fortuna Publica Populi Romani Quiritium, which the calendars also locate IN COLLE QVIRINALI.

Thus, three temples of Fortuna are known to have been located on the collis Quirinalis near the Porta Collina.

properties.name: Templum Fortunae Respicientis (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Fortuna Respiciens, Rome.

Sanctuary of Fortuna Respiciens (‘Solicitous Fortune’) located on the E slopes of the Palatine.

 The cult site is associated with a 2nd c. BC terracotta pediment depicting the goddess seated on an altar. This pediment was recovered in the late 1800s along the Via di S. Gregorio, between the Claudian-Neronian aqueduct and the Portale del Vignola (now the E entrance to the Palatine archaeological site) at a level predating the fire of 64 AD.

 Though no building remains can be associated with the pedimental sculptures (which indicate a pediment of some size: 15-16 m across, 2 m high), the temple was surely in the area of its findspot, as the region was known as the vicus Fortunae Respicientis by 2nd c. AD, and the 4th-c. Regionary Catalogues list Fortuna Respiciens between the Curiae Veteres (at the NE corner of the Palatine) and the Severan Septizodium (at the SE corner of the Palatine).

properties.name: Templum Hadriani (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Hadrian, Rome.

The Temple of Hadrian was dedicated to the deified emperor Hadrian on the Campus Martius by his adoptive son and successor Antoninus Pius in 145 AD. 

This temple was previously known as the Basilica of Neptune but has since been properly attributed as the Temple of Hadrian completed under Antoninus Pius. With one cella wall and eleven columns from the external colonnade surviving, the remains of the temple have been incorporated into a later building in the Piazza di Pietra (Piazza of Stone – derived from use of the temple's stones to build the piazza), whereby its facade, alongside the architrave which was reconstructed later on, was incorporated into a 17th-century papal palace by Carlo Fontana, now occupied by the Borsa Italiana, Italy's main stock exchange. While only part of the structure remains, excavations and scholarship have provided us with information regarding its construction techniques and stylistic influences, helping us recreate the building dynamics and significance of the Temple of Hadrian in Imperial Rome.

properties.name: Templum Herculis (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Hercules, Rome.

Round temple in the Forum Bovarium near S. Maria in Cosmedin, probably located north of the church. Torn down in the 15th c., it is known in some detail through reconstruction drawings of the Renaissance, which show an exterior colonnade in the Tuscan order, possibly the result of an Augustan-period renovation. 

This temple may have been larger than the well-preserved Round Temple by the Tiber. Its location at the Forum Boarium near the Circus Maximus is undisputed and must have distinguished its location from the Round Temple by the Tiber, which stood apart from the Forum Boarium.

 Found at this site was a bronze statue of a young Hercules and a series of praetorian inscriptions (the earliest dated to 193 AD) mostly addressed to HERCVLES INVICTVS.

properties.name: Templum Herculis Cubantis (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Hercules Cubans, Rome.

A small aedicular sanctuary dedicated to Hercules Cubans in Trans Tiberim, listed in the Notitia and the Curiosum for Regio XIV: Transtiberim.

 In 1889, along Viale Trastevere some 600 m N of the Trastevere train station, a rock-carved aedicular shrine of Hercules was excavated along with two inscribed altars and numerous sculptures. The inscriptions on the altars and on the epistyle of the rock-cut niche mention the dedication by L. Domitius Permissus to Hercules. A series of small tufa sculptures further secures the identification of the cult with Hercules Cubans; the wider sculptural assemblage from the area suggests that the sanctuary existed from the 1st c. BC through the end of the 3rd c. AD. This area is thought to have been situated within the limits of the Horti Caesaris.

properties.name: Templum Herculis Invicti (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Hercules Invictus, Rome.

A Temple to Hercules near the Circus Maximus, without identified remains, was rebuilt or restored by Pompey the Great (according to both the epithet Pompeianus used by Vitruvius and Pliny’s specification in aede Pompei Magni).

 Vitruvius mentions the temple as an example of the old-fashioned, Tuscan style, so a rectangular ground-plan is certain and a rather early date for the original structure can be assumed. The temple stood by the Circus Maximus, perhaps not too far from the Temple of Ceres near the Circus’ W end, since Vitruviusdescribes both as ad circum Maximum.

properties.name: Templum Herculis Magni Custodis (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Hercules Magnus Custos, Rome.

Sanctuary, and probably temple, in the area of the Circus Flaminius that was dedicated to Hercules as protector of the circus.

 Ovid relates that the opus was sanctioned by Sulla, and that it was located after consultation with the Sibylline Books in the opposite part of the Circus Flaminius from the Temple of Bellona. Yet Sulla may have only restored a cult site originally built during the 3rd c. BC.

 An inscription found in the Circus Flaminius area attests to the existence, already in the early Republican period, of a collegium in charge of the organization of games (ludi) in honour of Hercules.

properties.name: Templum Herculis Musarum (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Hercules Musarum, Rome.

The Temple of Hercules Musarum was a temple dedicated to Hercules in ancient Rome, near the Circus Flaminius.

It was built by Marcus Fulvius Nobilior, who conquered of the Greek city of Ambracia in 189 BC. It was probably completed and dedicated during his triumph in 187 BC. The epithet 'Musarum' means 'of the Muses' and refers to Nobilior's discovery that Hercules was known in Greece as 'Musagetes' or 'leader of the Muses'. The temple contained copies of the fasti and statues taken from Ambracia, including statues of the Muses. The Portico of Metellus was later built near the temple.

In 29 BC Lucius Marcius Philippus restored the temple and built a portico around it, later known as the Portico of Philippus. Part of the temple's floorplan is known from a fragment of the 3rd century Forma Urbis Romae.

properties.name: Templum Herculis Primigenii (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Hercules Primigenius, Rome.

Sanctuary of Hercules Primigenius, located outside the Servian Wall, along the Via Salaria.

 Hannibal camped here in 211 BC. 

Though no archaeological evidence survives, the location of this cult site can safely be inferred from the shrine of Hercules Primigenius, known from Augustan and Julio-Claudian funerary inscriptions and a marble cippus inscribed to Hercules Primigenius, found in the area of Piazza Fiume.

properties.name: Templum Herculis Victoris (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Hercules Victor, Rome.

The well-preserved Round Temple by the Tiber, with its ring of 20 Corinthian columns surrounding a circular cella, had been attributed to the first half of the 1st c. BC, and intensive re-examination of its architecture has suggested a more precise date in the early 1st c. BC. 

Sometime in the decades after Augustus, major repair work was carried out on about half of the colonnade; at this point Luna marble was used in place of the original, imported Pentelic marble — a remarkably luxurious material at the time of its construction. Further, the presence of Greek masons can be plausibly deduced from the workmanship of the original capitals, whereas other details of the temple’s execution are at odds with Greek practices (esp. the flat, not curved, ends of the fluting on the column shafts) and are ascribed to local workshops. 

The temple was elevated on an artificial platform, some 12 m above the Tiber and 2-3 m above the Forum Boarium; it stood outside the Forum Boarium, and probably just beyond the Republican circuit wall as well. In addition to the Greek marble and workmen, an inscribed statue base found next to the temple attests to the presence of a work by the 2nd c. BC Greek sculptor Scopas the Younger, possibly the Hercules Olivarius listed by the late-antique Regionary Catalogues (Regio XI) in the area NW of the Circus Maximus.

properties.name: Templum Honoris (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Honos, Rome.

Double Temple to Honos and Virtus built ex manubiis by C. Marius in 101 BC; no archaeological remains are known, but Vitruvius describes it as a peristyle temple without a portico in the rear.

properties.name: Templum Honoris (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Honos, Rome.

Double Temple to Honos and Virtus, without archaeological remains, close by the Porta Capena and the sanctuary of the Camenae in the vicinity of the Vicus Honoris et Virtutis of Regio I.

 M. Claudius Marcellus, the conqueror of Syracuse, is reported to have restored an older Temple of Honos as well as added a new cella for Virtus; these were dedicated in 205 BC by his son. 

The temple was renowned for its superb artworks dedicated by Marcellus from the spoils of Syracuse, many of which had disappeared by Livy’s time. The sanctuary received a new and specifically Augustan meaning in 19 BC when the senate erected the Altar of Fortuna Redux in front of the temple; there, by the gate where Augustus entered the city, the altar commemorated his safe and singularly successful return from the East with the Roman standards regained from the Parthians.

properties.name: Templum Honoris (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Honos, Rome.

Temple dedicated to Honos, possibly also to Virtus, located outside the Porta Collina, and known only through literary and epigraphic evidence.

 A dedication to Honos found c. 35m from the Colline Gate confirms the location given by Cicero. An inscription to Virtus, found between the Baths of Diocletian and Via XX Settembre, may point to the presence of a double cult at this site, as seen at the city’s two other temples to Honos. No archaeological remains have been found and the exact site, form and size of the temple are unknown.

properties.name: Templum Iani (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Janus, Rome.

The northernmost of the three preserved temples in the Forum Holitorium, dedicated to Ianus and located outside the Porta Carmentalis.

 The identification is based on the description of the temple as ‘iuxta’ or ‘ad’ the Theatre of Marcellus. Built by C. Duilius soon after 260 BC, Augustus began to reconstruct the temple, but the project was only completed by Tiberius who rededicated the temple in 17 AD.

 The S side of the temple is partly incorporated into the Church of S. Nicola in Carcere and the ground-plan can easily be restored, as remains of the temple have also been excavated outside the church. These remains have been dated to the Augustan period on the basis of their architectural decoration.

properties.name: Templum Iunonis Lucinae (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Juno Lucina, Rome.

This Temple to Iuno Lucina on the Esquiline was founded by Roman matrons in 375 BC and only later became an aedes publica. 

It was restored in 190 and 41 BC. It was situated in a small grove, or lucus on the Cispian as listed in the sacraria Argeorum. The general consensus thus places this temple just N of the Clivus Suburanus on the S slopes of the Cispian. But this location is not consistent with an inscription relating to the restoration of the perimeter wall by Q. Pedius in 41 BC, found under the Monastery of S. Francisco de Paula, apparently in situ. The monastery lies S of Via di S. Lucia in Selci (the Clivus Suburanus), and so on the Oppian, not the Cispian. Unfortunately, this ambiguity cannot be resolved.

properties.name: Templum Iunonis Monetae (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Juno Moneta, Rome.

The Temple of Iuno Moneta on the Arx was vowed by L. Camillus and dedicated in 345/43 BC.

 Ovid states that it was located ‘on the summit of the Arx’. This puts the temple under the Church of S. Maria in Aracoeli.

properties.name: Templum Iunonis Reginae (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Juno Regina, Rome.

The Temple of Juno Regina was a temple dedicated to "Queen Juno". It was near the Circus Flaminius in the southern half of the Campus Martius.

 It was vowed by consul Marcus Aemilius Lepidus in 187 BC during his final battle against the Liguri and dedicated on 23 December 179 BC, whilst he was censor. It was linked by a portico to a temple of Fortuna, possibly the temple of Fortuna Equestris. It was probably to the south of the Portico of Pompey, on the western side of the circus Flaminius.

A Temple of Jupiter Stator was later built next to it. Both temples were surrounded by the Portico of Metellus and this portico and both temples were later rebuilt and rededicated by Octavian as the Porticus Octaviae.

properties.name: Templum Iunonis Sospitae (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Juno Sospita, Rome.

One of three adjacent temples preserved in the Forum Holitorium, the Temple of Iuno Sospita is probably situated between those of Ianus and Spes.

 The well-preserved remains attest to two building phases: the 2nd c. BC original construction, and a second phase in the 1st c. BC, corresponding to the reconstruction by L. Iulius in 90 BC. 

This identification is made by process of elimination: the Temples of Ianus and Spes are plausibly identified as the two temples flanking it; and the fourth known temple in the Forum Holitorium, the Temple of Pietas, had already been destroyed by Caesar.
