The Temple to Iuno Sospita was vowed by C. Cornelius in 197 BC and dedicated three years later. It is extraordinarily well preserved due to its integration into the Church of S. Nicola in Carcere. The plan of the temple is indicated on the Severan Marble Plan.

properties.name: Templum Iovis Optimi Maximi Capitolini (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus Capitolinus, Rome.

The Temple of Iuppiter Optimus Maximus has been identified, since 1683, with the foundations under Palazzo Caffarelli in the Area Capitolina. 

Originally dating from the Archaic period, this huge temple was arguably the most important and revered sacred building in Rome. It was dedicated to the Capitoline Triad: Iuppiter Optimus Maximus, Iuno Regina, and Minerva, and incorporated preexisting shrines to Terminus, Iuventas, and Mars.

 Excavations undertaken since 1865 have revealed enough to reconstruct a rectangular podium c. 62 x 53 m in area and 3.6 m high. North of the rear side of the podium is a parallel foundation which was part of the temenos wall of the Area Capitolina, not part of the temple. 

Several construction phases are visible: a layer of capellaccio tufa blocks (H. c. 30-32 cm) set into the bedrock, 5 layers of the same tufa (H. c. 40 cm) set back slightly from the course below and, on top, a layer of concrete. However, there are fewer distinct construction phases than known restorations, and the dating of these levels is disputed. 

The Archaic temple burned in 83 BC. The new temple was started by L. Cornelius Sulla and dedicated by Q. Lutatius Catulus in 69 BC. It was subsequently damaged by lightning on a number of occasions and restored by Augustus at great expense, perhaps after a fire in 9 BC. It is fairly certain from the existing podium remains that the Augustan temple as well as its antecedents and successors all stood on the same foundations. Above the level of the podium, the Temple of Iuppiter Optimus Maximus is generally restored in the Tuscan order, with three narrow cellae set behind a deep porch supported by three rows of 6 columns in a peripteros sine postico arrangement. In addition, there must have been a flight of steps in front of the façade, yet nothing survives of these steps in the archaeological record.

properties.name: Templum Iovis Optimi Maximi Heliopolitani (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus Heliopolitanus, Rome.

A sanctuary dedicated to Iuppiter Optimus Maximus Heliopolitanus, the chief god of the Syrian solar triad of Heliopolis-Baalbek, within the limits of the Lucus Furrinae on the SE slopes of the Ianiculum.

The precinct wall was discovered in 1906 and excavated in 1908-9 on the fringes of the present-day Villa Sciarra-Wurts, along the edge of a ravine, right below the curve of Via Dandolo.

 While the major phase of the temple (with its peculiar eclectic architecture) was dated to the 4th c. AD, the excavators identified two earlier phases, which were probably not more than open-air precincts with similar layouts. The earliest phase was associated only with the remains of a perimeter wall, and was assigned an insecure mid 1st c. AD date based on construction techniques. The second phase, a rebuilding by M. Antonius Gaionas, is well dated to 176-181 AD by inscriptions.

Although the dating and architecture of the first phase of the temple remain unclear, there seems to be good reason to assume the presence of the sacred spot and associated cultic activity in the time of Augustus, since both the location of the temple in the Lucus Furrinae and the cult itself were popular in the late-Republican period.

properties.name: Templum Iovis Statoris (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Jupiter Stator, Rome.

The Temple of Jupiter Stator was a temple named after the god Jupiter, in his form of Jupiter Stator (Jupiter the stayer). Together with the Temple of Juno Regina (Juno in the form of "Queen Juno") and the enclosing Porticus Metelli (later rebuilt as the Porticus Octaviae), it was built by Quintus Caecilius Metellus Macedonicus after his triumph, in 146 BC. 

It is referred to as aedes Iovis Metellina and aedes Metelli. It was inside the porticus Metelli, close to the Circus Flaminius, and its exact site is known to have been beneath the church of Santa Maria in Campitelli. The Temple of Juno Regina was just west of it, on the opposite side of the Via della Tribuna di Campitelli.

It is not stated in explicitly by Velleius that Metellus built both temples, but that is the natural inference from the passage. He is also said to have been the first to build a temple in Rome entirely of marble, and which probably applies to both structures. In front of the temples Metellus placed Lysippus' equestrian statues of Alexander the Great's generals, and in them were several famous works of art.

properties.name: Templum Iovis Statoris (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Jupiter Stator, Rome.

Temple to Iuppiter Stator (‘Stayer’) said to be vowed by Romulus during a battle with the Sabines near the Porta Mugonia.

 According to Livy, the Romulean temple was never built, and the site remained a fanum (consecrated location) until 294 BC when the consul M. Atilius Regulus vowed a temple to Iuppiter Stator in the heat of battle. The Roman Senate, having twice been obligated to erect a temple, now ordered the aedes built. 

In the late-Republican period Cicero convened the Senate there, and Ovid records its dedication day as June 27.

The location of this temple has been subject to heated debate. Literary sources frequently connect it with the Porta Mugonia, a Palatine gate which can be placed with some confidence along the “Clivus Palatinus” S of the Sacra Via. The temple was also near the Nova Via and the house of Tarquinius Priscus. Ovid places it ‘in front of the Palatine’, and Plutarch at ‘the beginning of the Sacra Via as you ascend the Palatine hill’. Combined, these sources suggest the area around the Arch of Titus, and traditionally the temple has been associated with a concrete podium found just E of that arch.

properties.name: Templum Iovis Tonantis (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Jupiter Tonans, Rome.

The Temple of Iuppiter Tonans was vowed by Augustus in 26 BC after he narrowly escaped lightning and dedicated in 22 BC. 

It was located in Capitolio, and is humorously described as the gatekeeper for the Temple of Iuppiter Optimus Maximus. It is thus generally placed at the entrance to the Area Capitolina at the top of the Clivus Capitolinus.

properties.name: Templum Iovis Victoris (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Jupiter Victor, Rome.

An early-Republican cult site of Iuppiter Victor on the collis Quirinalis near the Temple of Quirinus. 

The dies natalis of the ‘templum’ was April 13. A 3rd c. BC inscription found in the papal gardens on the Quirinal during the 17th c. records the restoration of a shrine to Iuppiter Victor: [D]IOVEI VICTORE T.MEFV[…] M. F. III VIR [RESTI]TVIT and suggests the location of the cult site. 

This sanctuary may have been vowed in 295 BC by Q. Fabius Maximus Rullianus, and dedicated a few years later, perhaps in 289 BC by Q. Fabius Maximus Gurges, who was the son of Rullianus and consul that year.

properties.name: Templum Iuturnae (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Juturna, Rome.

Temple to Iuturna of uncertain appearance located in the Campus Martius, perhaps near the terminus of the Aqua Virgo.

 The temple was built by a Lutatius Catulus in c. 241 BC and dedicated on 11 January. In the late 70s or early 60s BC, C. Aelius Staienus set up before the temple gilt-bronze statues and a titulus recording the number of kings he restored to friendship with Rome.

Ovid gives the temple’s location at the terminus of the Aqua Virgo. Frontinus locates the end of the Virgo’s arcade ‘alongside the front of the Saepta’. Since the aqueduct entered the city, and the Campus Martius, from the N, it seems reasonable to assume that the temple of Iuturna was located near the N end of the Saepta.

properties.name: Templum Larium (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of the Lares, Rome.

Temple of the Lares on the Velia or on the lower Palatine, restored by Augustus in 4 BC.

 The aedes was located in summa Sacra via, ‘at the heights of the Sacra Via’, and ‘on the Palatine near the Porta Mugionia’. Combined, these suggest that the area near the Arch of Titus, just W of the Sacra Via, was home to the Lares cult.

 Also nearby was the fanum Orbonae and the Temple of Iuppiter Stator, which shared a dies natalis with the Temple of the Lares . Coarelli proposes that the Temple to the Lares would have been small, perhaps no larger than a compital shrine.

properties.name: Templum Larium Permarini (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of the Lares Permarini, Rome.

Votive temple of the 2nd c. BC to the Lares Permarini located in campo Martio, and more specifically by the fasti Praenestini in the Porticus Minucia ([LARIBVS PERM]ARINIS IN PORTI[CV MI]NVCIA. 

Remnants of this temple were discovered in 1938 near the intersection of Via delle Botteghe Oscure and Via Celsa during a road-widening project; the remains, dating to the late 1st c. BC, correspond to a depiction of the temple on the Severan Marble Plan near the legend MINI[CIA].

The praetor L. Aemilius Regillus vowed the temple in 190 BC and L. Aemilius Lepidus dedicated it on 22 December 179 BC, along with his own temples in the Campus. Part of the dedicatory inscription affixed above the temple doors is preserved in Livy. Note that this temple stood immediately W of the point where the Porticus Aemilia (Campus Martius), which began at the Porta Fontinalis, debouched onto the Campus Martius; such a collocation of Aemilian dedications would easily explain the application of the name Aemiliana to this area.

properties.name: Templum Lunae (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Luna, Rome.

Temple of Luna on the Aventine, without identified remains. 

Its site depends on that of the Temple of Ceres, whose location, though not known with certainty, can reasonably be narrowed to the lower slope of the Aventine’s N tip, just above the head of the Circus Maximus. Luna’s temple stood in the immediate vicinity of Ceres’, since its doors are reported to have been dislodged by a storm in 182 BC and hurled into the rear wall of the Temple of Ceres; further, both temples were hit by lightning — presumably the same bolt — on the same day in 84 BC. 

 The importance of a cult to Luna and the proximity of her temple to those of Ceres and Flora may appear less “obscure” when one takes into account the potentially destructive effect on crops and vegetation that the full moon was considered to have.

properties.name: Templum Magnae Matris (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of the Magna Mater, Rome.

Temple on the Palatine dedicated to the Phrygian mother-goddess Magna Mater, also known as Cybele, and home to the sacred black stone which represented the deity. 

Begun in 204 and dedicated in 191 BC, the temple burned twice before it was restored by Augustus after the second fire of 3 AD.

Excavations on the SW corner of the Palatine in 1809 first brought the temple to light, while more recent investigations have clarified the architectural development of the structure. The extant remains, located just above the Scalae Caci and adjacent to the Temple of Victoria, indicate that the Augustan rebuilding utilized the earlier Republican foundations and high concrete podium (c. 33 x 17 m) to support a prostyle, hexastyle superstructure in the Corinthian order with a sculpted pediment. A statue of Magna Mater and inscriptions pertaining to her cult found in the vicinity allow these remains to be identified as her sanctuary.

Extending across the façade of the temple was a broad staircase, which led down to a large, paved platform where the ludi Megalenses, dramatic performances and games in honour of Cybele, were held; these steps would have seated spectators. Sometime after the fire of 111 BC, modest vaults extended this precinct across a street, here identified as the Clivus Victoriae, that had previously limited the platform on the SW; tabernae (small shops and offices) opening onto the street were located within the barrel-vaulted spaces below the platform.

properties.name: Templum Martis (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Mars, Rome.

Livy affiliates a temple of Mars with the Porta Capena.

properties.name: Templum Martis (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Mars, Rome.

Republican Temple to Mars located near the Circus Flaminius, erected ex manubiis by D. Brutus Callaicus between 135 and 130 BC, after his Spanish triumph.

 The temple was planned by Hermodorus of Salamis and contained the cult statues of both Mars and Venus.

Remains of a hexastyle peripteral temple near the Church of S. Salvatore in Campo (in the N Circus Flaminius) were first identified in 1838; its architectural elements are assigned to the early Republican period on account of their mixture of native Italic and Hellenistic Greek features. A fragment of the Severan Marble Plan that depicts part of a peripteral temple with a long, narrow cella and an aditus — just as Cicero describes the aedes Martis— is placed in the area of S. Salvatore in Campo. Moreover, archival documents found by Tortorici report the discovery in S. Salvatore of fragments of a colossal statue depicting a goddess, perhaps the cult statue of Venus described by Pliny.

properties.name: Templum Martis (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Mars, Rome.

Rome’s main Temple of Mars was situated outside the city on the N side of the Via Appia between its first and second milestones. It was vowed in 388 BC by T. Quinctius.

The Temple of Mars was an important landmark in ancient Rome; it is frequently mentioned in connection with the paving and repaving of the Via Appia and the surrounding neighborhood was known as ‘ad Martis’. Further, the sloped section of the Via Appia leading up to the temple was known as the clivus Martis.

properties.name: Templum Martis Ultoris (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Mars Ultor, Rome.

The triumvir Octavian vowed to build a temple honoring Mars, the Roman God of War, during the battle of Philippi in 42 BC.

It was dedicated in 2 BC and in 19 AD Tiberius added two triumphal arches either side of the temple in honour of Drusus the Younger and Germanicus and their victories in Germania.

Before battle, generals set off from the Temple of Mars, after attending an inaugural ceremony. Other ceremonies took place in the temple including the assumption of the toga virilis by young men. The Senate met at the Temple when discussing war and the victorious generals dedicated their spoils from their triumphs to Mars at the altar. Arms or booty recovered from battle were often stored in the Forum as well.[6] Another use that Augustus made of the Temple was to store the standards taken by the Parthians from Crassus during his failed campaign, after their retrieval through Augustus' diplomacy in 20 BC, as depicted by the Augustus of Prima Porta. Three Aquilae were lost in 9 AD in the Battle of the Teutoburg Forest of the Legions Legio XVII, Legio XVIII and Legio XIX; all three were recovered-one in 14 AD from the Marsi and one in 15 AD from the Bructeri; the 3rd was recovered in 41 AD from the Chauci-and all three placed within the Temple of Mars the Avenger.

properties.name: Templum Matris Matutae (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Mater Matuta, Rome.

Twin temples dedicated to Fortuna and Mater Matuta located at the N border of the Forum Boarium, just inside the Porta Carmentalis.

Tradition held that both were founded by Servius Tullius, and the temples are often mentioned together, even sharing a dedication day. 

Since both temples burned in the fire of 213 BC, which also damaged the Forum Holitorium and Porta Carmentalis, a location in that vicinity seems likely. These factors led scholars to identify the twin temples discovered in 1937 near the Church of S. Omobono as those of Fortuna and Mater Matuta; further, archaeological evidence dates this site back to the Archaic period, which corresponds well with the tradition of the temples’ foundation. The temples share a single, large platform and each has an altar in front of it. Under the nave of S. Omobono is the aedes of Mater Matuta, while the temple of Fortuna lay further S. The visible temple remains seem to belong to the reconstruction in 212 BC.

properties.name: Templum Matidiae (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Matidia, Rome.

The Temple of Matidia was a temple on the Campus Martius dedicated to Salonia Matidia, who was deified after her death in 119 AD by her son-in-law Hadrian. 

He began construction immediately after her deification, choosing a site near the Pantheon and the Saepta Julia, both of which he restored or rebuilt. A lead water pipe inscribed 'templo matidiae' ('from the temple of Matidia') was found near Sant'Ignazio, which may indicate the temple's location. After Hadrian died and was deified, his own temple was built next to that of Matidia.

properties.name: Templum Mefitis (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Mefitis, Rome.

Temple on the Cispian overlooking the Vicus Patricius. It is best located on the high ground at the S end of the Vicus Patricius where the valley is deepest, rather than further N on the more level ground near Piazzale Esquilino.

 Coarelli suggests that a domus belonging to the Papirii also stood in this area, on the site of Vigna Santarelli, and that this may have belonged to a Republican branch of the family, either the Papirii Cursores or Papirii Carbones; he also argues that an early member of this family established the cult of Mefitis.

properties.name: Templum Mentis (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Mens, Rome.

Twin temples are known only from a Severan Marble Plan fragment of the S slopes of the Area Capitolina.

 Nothing remains in the archaeological record since this part of the hill has been lost through landslides. The names of these temples, one a narrow apsidal temple and the other a larger hexastyle podium temple, are not shown on the Marble Plan. Sometimes they appear on modern maps but are not identified. However, the fact that the temples are adjacent provides a clue as to their identity, for several Capitoline temples were regarded as pairs. 

Two strong candidates for the Marble Plan Temples remain: Mens and Venus Erycina. These temples stood in Capitolio, probably in the Area Capitolina. They were vowed in 217 and dedicated in 215 BC. Most importantly, they stood next to each other, separated only by a small drain. Livy’s description fits the Marble Plan Temples especially well.

properties.name: Templum Minervae (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Minerva, Rome.

The Temple of Minerva was a temple on the short side of the Forum of Nerva in Rome. It was completed by Nerva in 97 AD - who harboured a particular devotion for goddess.

 It was still well-preserved in the 16th century, when pope Paul V took materials from it for his fontana dell'Acqua Paola on the Janiculum Hill and for the Borghese chapel in Santa Maria Maggiore.

properties.name: Templum Minervae (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Minerva, Rome.

Temple of Minerva on the Aventine, apparently in a prominent place, but without identified remains.

 It is mentioned in reference to events of the late 3rd c. BC and depicted on the Severan Marble Plan. 

The temple was rebuilt by Augustus, together with (on the Aventine) the temples of Iuppiter Libertas and Iuno Regina. Its precise location depends on the position of the Marble Plan’s fragment, which has recently been disputed, but the most plausible solution still speaks for the traditional placement in the N center of the hill.

properties.name: Templum Minervae Captae (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Minerva Capta, Rome.

A shrine of Minerva, is mentioned by Varro, who places it on a road leading up to the Caelian, and a shrine or sanctuary of Minerva Capta is mentioned by Ovid, who puts it on the crest of the same hill.

 It seems likely that both authors refer to the same place. Following the discovery of a statue of Minerva and an inscription recording a dedication to Minerva on the N slopes of the Caelian, this shrine has generally been placed on the “Via Tusculana” in the area of SS. Quattro Coronati.

properties.name: Templum Minervae Medicae (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Minerva Medica, Rome.

This temple is listed in the Notitia and Curiosum within Regio V: Esquiliae.

Its location has been determined on the basis of votive deposits found in Via Carlo Botta between Via Buonarotti and Via Machiavelli, but there are no surviving architectural remains. The votive offerings, found in situ in the storage chambers of the temple, included a dedication to Minerva, representations of the goddess, and dedications to a healing deity, all dated from the 4th to 1st c. BC. An Imperial-period statue of Minerva was discovered nearby, along with statues of other deities.

properties.name: Templum Neptuni (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Neptune, Rome.

Tetrastyle temple dedicated to Neptune, located in the area of the Circus Flaminius and recently identified with the remains of a tufa opus quadratum podium, of which only the W flank is preserved.

 Additional archaeological remains found nearby in Piazza Costaguti substantiate this location and suggest a 2nd c. BC date. A fragmentary relief from Ostia, which depicts a temple to Neptune next to a shrine of Hercules, had been used to locate the former in the NW corner of the Circus Flaminius, next to the sanctuary of Hercules Musarum, placing the Temple of Neptune in the exact place in which the recent remains were found.

 The podium recently found in Piazza Costaguti should be connected to this structure. Pliny mentions cult statues of Neptune, Thetis, Achilles and the Nereids, all by Scopas, a 2nd-c. Greek artist working in Rome. The so-called Altar of Domitius Ahenobarbus, in actuality a large base for statuary honoring its donour Marcus Antonius, was erected in the vicinity of the temple sometime in the early 1st c. BC.

properties.name: Templum Opis (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Ops, Rome. 

A mid-Republican temple of Ops, the goddess of wealth, stood in Capitolio and was struck by lightning in 186 BC. It was probably dedicated by L. Caecilius Metellus in 250 BC.

 It existed in the Augustan period, for it was here that women and children assembled for the celebration of the ludi Saeculares of 17 BC. The Temple of Ops is believed to have stood next to the Temple of Fides: military diplomas of the 1st c. AD were attached to both temples; a storm in 44 BC damaged both temples, and the concepts of fides and ops (faith and wealth) were closely related.

properties.name: Templum Pacis (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Pax, Rome.

The Temple of Peace, also known as the Forum of Vespasian, was built in Rome in 71 AD under Emperor Vespasian in honour to Pax, the Roman goddess of peace. It faces the Velian Hill, toward the famous Colosseum, and was on the southeast side of the Argiletum.

The funds to create this grand monument were acquired through Vespasian's sacking of Jerusalem during the Jewish-Roman Wars. The interior and surrounding buildings were decorated with the treasures collected there by the Roman army.

Because Vespasian was both a leading general and later appointed emperor during civil war, the Temple of Peace was especially important to him as a leader. A grand and significant monument such as this is vital to the promotion of a powerful, strong public image of the emperor, and is a symbol of the peace and prosperity Vespasian was able to bring the empire.

properties.name: Templum Penatium Publici (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of the Penates Publici, Rome.

Temple to the Penates Publici, located on the Velia, was rebuilt by Augustus. 

The Altar of Pax Augusta may offer visual evidence for the appearance of the shrine; the relief of Aeneas sacrificing includes an image of the enshrined Lavinian Penates in the background which closely corresponds to the description of the Roman Temple of the Penates Publici found in Dionysius of Halicarnassus; perhaps the sculptors found their model for the relief in the recently renewed temple.

The temple was probably destroyed during the fire of 64 AD and subsequent Neronian rebuilding on the Velia.

properties.name: Templum Portuni (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Portunus, Rome.

The well-preserved Ionic temple between the Tiber and the Forum Boarium, formerly attributed to Fortuna Virilis, is now widely agreed to be that of Portunus, a divinity whose temple was near the Portus Tiberinus and whose festival, held on the same day as the temple’s foundation day, was celebrated at the Pons Aemilius.

 The structure attests to two phases: the earlier dates to the late 4th or early 3rd c. BC, had a 6-m-tall podium of Grotta Oscura blocks, and was fronted by a tall, arched passageway (H. 6 m, also in Grotta Oscura tufa) at its N-facing façade. The current temple was built on the same podium around 80/70 BC; the new building was surrounded by much higher terrain (probably a result of the artificial elevation of the area in the early 2nd c. B.C.), and it kept, though at a slightly different angle, the unusual N orientation towards both the viaduct leading to the Pons Aemilius and, more importantly, the Portus Tiberinus which was just N of this street.

 Tetrastyle and pseudoperipteral in its arrangement, the temple is essentially built of Anio tufa, with special elements articulated in travertine. In the immediate vicinity stood two identical travertine bases erected for C. and L. Caesar which may have flanked the temple or the nearby “Fornix Augusti”.

properties.name: Templum Quirini (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Quirinus, Rome.

Temple to Quirinus located atop the collis Quirinalis. First built in the 4th c. BC, the temple burned in 49 BC and was restored by 45 BC.

 Augustus rebuilt and rededicated the monumental aedes in 16 BC. Quirinus was a deity of special interest to the gens Iulia, and a statue of Julius Caesar was erected in the precinct. Vitruvius describes the temple as dipteral, octastyle and Doric, with a pronaos and posticum; given the time at which he wrote (c. 30 B.C.), Vitruvius probably would have seen the restoration of 45 BC. Since Dio relates that the Augustan temple had 76 columns, it must have been dipteral like its predecessor. The temple precinct was enclosed by a portico known as the porticus Quirini, and was home to a shrine of Quirinus’ consort Hora as well as Rome’s first sundial, a gift of L. Papirius Cursor in 293 BC.

properties.name: Temple of Salutis (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Salus, Rome.

Temple to Salus, dedicated by C. Iunius Bubulcus Brutus in 302 BC and built atop the collis Salutaris, one of the four peaks of the Quirinal. 

Though the temple suffered from frequent lightning strikes and fires, the original 4th c. BC paintings by Fabius Pictor survived until the reign of Claudius; this suggests that the temple weathered the damage well, and may have retained an Archaic appearance, with proportions and decoration suitable to its late 4th c. dedication, through the Augustan period. As with the other major temples of the Quirinal, no architectural remains survive and the temple’s location is debated.

The place name vicus Salutis is known from an inscription dating to 33 BC found beneath S. Maria Maddelena which names the neighborhood. Its findspot is in close proximity to the Porta Salutaris (c. 150 m distant); together, the place names suggest that the temple, the aedes Salutis, stood nearby in the E section of the Palazzo del Quirinale, a locale well within the bounds of the collis Salutaris.

properties.name: Templum Saturni (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Saturn, Rome.

The Temple of Saturn stood in the SW corner of the Forum, between the Vicus Iugarius and the Clivus Capitolinus. 

There were a number of traditions about its foundation, all of which assigned the temple to the earliest years of the Republic. The rebuilding of the temple by L. Munatius Plancus must have begun in the late 40s BC; it became one of the last great monuments paid for by an individual outside the imperial family.

 There is broad consensus among scholars that the massive podium visible today is that of Plancus. The architrave records the Senate’s restoration of the temple after it had burned, probably in the 4th c. AD, and the surviving superstructure dates to this later period. Very little remains of the original staircase, which probably contained the state treasury (aerarium Saturni or aerarium populi Roman. The stair has been restored on the basis of the Severan Marble Plan.

properties.name: Templum Solis (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Sol, Rome.

Archaic temple within the Circus Maximus dedicated to the sun-god Sol, to whom the Circus as a whole was consecrated; the temple was embedded in the seating on the Aventine side, just opposite the finish line and across from the Pulvinar.

 Tacitus, in the first secure reference to the temple, calls it a vetus aedes in 65 AD; earlier numismatic testimony may be found on a denarius of Mark Antony dated to 42 BC, which depicts a small, distyle shrine to Sol.

properties.name: Templum Spei (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Spes, Rome.

One of the group of three temples on the W side of the Forum Holitorium, probably the one furthest S. Since the temple of Spes burned in the fire of 213 BC, it must have stood in the vicinity of the Porta Carmentalis and the “Area Sacra” of S. Omobono.

 In addition, if it was the southernmost temple, it would not have been connected to the other temple buildings in 213 BC, a fact which explains why the neighboring Temple of Ianus did not catch fire.

After a fire in 31 BC, damaged the building, Augustus began its restoration, and Germanicus rededicated it in 17 AD. Though the date the restoration work began, and how much was completed by 14 AD, cannot be known, it seems unlikely that Augustus left the temple in ruins for very long. Substantial remains of the aedes, a Doric hexastyle temple, are preserved in the Church of S. Nicola in Carcere.

properties.name: Templum Telli (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Tellus, Rome.

Temple dedicated to Tellus, located on the Carinae. 

No archaeological remains survive, though its 3rd c. AD form is depicted on the Severan Marble Plan. 

Originally vowed by P. Sempronius Sophus in 268 BC, the temple was built by the Roman people. For a time Cicero lived in close proximity to the temple, and he reports that some Romans asserted that he was responsible for safeguarding it.

properties.name: Templum Tempestatis (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Tempestas, Rome.

Temple to the Tempestates, or Tempestas, vowed by L. Cornelius Scipio, which stood on the Via Appia near the Temple of Mars; its exact site is not known. 

Two dedication days, one preserved in the fasti Antiates maiores (December 23) and the other in Ovid (June 1), suggest that the temple may have been refounded by Augustus. 

The temple probably stood near the family tomb of the Cornelii Scipiones, where its founder was interred; this connection between family tomb and temple is mirrored further N on the Via Appia, where the Temple of Honos et Virtus, dedicated by the son of M. Claudius Marcellus, stands in close proximity to his family monumenta.

properties.name: Templum Traiani (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Trajan, Rome.

The Temple of Trajan was dedicated to the emperor Trajan and his wife Plotina after his deification by the Roman Senate. It was built in the Forum of Trajan, by Trajan's adoptive son and successor Hadrian, between 125 and 138 AD. The architect was Apollodorus of Damascus.

properties.name: Templum Vediovis (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Vediovis, Rome.

A temple dedicated to Vediovis on the Tiber island, known only from literary sources and epigraphic evidence.

 The shrine was vowed by the praetor L. Furius Purpurio in 200 BC and dedicated by C. Servilius in 194 BC.

properties.name: Templum Veiovis (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Veiovis, Rome.

The temple dedicated to the ‘young’ or ‘bad’ Jupiter in 192 BC and rebuilt in the early 1st c. BC was located inter duos lucos, in the same area as the Asylum. 

It has been identified with the remains of a small temple under the SW corner of Palazzo Senatorio on the Capitol, nestled into a corner of the later Tabularium. Its ground-plan, unusual on account of its transverse cella fronted by a tetrastyle pronaos, is well established through excavations.

properties.name: Templum Veneris Erycinae (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Venus Erycina, Rome.

Twin temples are known only from a Severan Marble Plan fragment of the S slopes of the Area Capitolina.

Nothing remains in the archaeological record since this part of the hill has been lost through landslides. The names of these temples, one a narrow apsidal temple and the other a larger hexastyle podium temple, are not shown on the Marble Plan. Sometimes they appear on modern maps but are not identified. However, the fact that the temples are adjacent provides a clue as to their identity, for several Capitoline temples were regarded as pairs. 

Two strong candidates for the Marble Plan Temples remain: Mens and Venus Erycina. These temples stood in Capitolio, probably in the Area Capitolina. They were vowed in 217 and dedicated in 215 BC. Most importantly, they stood next to each other, separated only by a small drain. Livy’s description fits the Marble Plan Temples especially well.

properties.name: Templum Veneris Erycinae (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Venus Erycina, Rome.

Extra-urban Temple to Venus Erycina near the Porta Collina, vowed in 184 BC by L. Porcius Licinius and dedicated in 181 BC by his son of the same name.

The extramural location would have facilitated the celebration of erotic cult practices, including the presence of cult prostitutes. Though no architectural remains survive, a denarius minted by C. Considius Nonianus at Rome in 57 BC, which depicts the Sicilian shrine with a tetrastyle façade and triangular pediment, is suggestive.

The temple was the site of the Vinalia festival held on April 23. The fasti list both April 23 and October 24 as the dies natalis.

properties.name: Templum Veneris Genetricis (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Venus Genetrix, Rome.

The Temple of Venus Genetrix in the Forum of Caesar, was dedicated to Venus Genetrix, the goddess of motherhood and domesticity. It was dedicated in 46 BC by Julius Caesar.

On the eve of the Battle of Pharsalus, Caesar vowed the temple to Venus Victrix. He eventually decided to dedicate the temple to Venus Genetrix, the mother of Aeneas, and the mythical ancestress of the Julian family.

properties.name: Templum Veneris Libitinae (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Venus Libitina, Rome.

The Esquiline grove of Libitina, a goddess associated with funerals and with Venus; the name is derived from libido, ‘desire’. It included a templum to Venus-Libitina. 

This grove was probably the headquarters of the libitinarii, professional undertakers. An inscription found outside the Porta Esquilina, which mentions a guild of flute-players, who also took part in funerals, puts this grove in the Campus Esquilinus just S of the Macellum Liviae; archaic architectural terracottas have been discovered in this area. 

The temple seems to have been an early Republican foundation and its survival into the Imperial period is attested. In the Augustan period this was also a commercial area. Late-Republican tombstones attest that two freedmen, a butcher and a clothes-dealer, had businesses here.

properties.name: Templum Veneris Victricis (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Venus Victrix, Rome.

Pompey had a temple to Venus Victrix built near the top of his theatre's seating; Pompey then claimed that he had "not [built] a theatre, but rather a temple of Venus to which I have added the steps of a theatre".

It was dedicated in 55 BC.

properties.name: Templum Veneris et Romae (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Venus and Roma, Rome.

The Temple of Venus and Roma is thought to have been the largest temple in Ancient Rome.

 Located on the Velian Hill, between the eastern edge of the Forum Romanum and the Colosseum, it was dedicated to the goddesses Venus Felix ("Venus the Bringer of Good Fortune") and Roma Aeterna ("Eternal Rome"). The architect was the emperor Hadrian and construction began in 121 AD. It was officially inaugurated by Hadrian in 135 AD, and finished in 141 AD under Antoninus Pius. Damaged by fire in 307 AD, it was restored with alterations by the emperor Maxentius.

properties.name: Templum Vespasiani et Titi (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Vespasian & Titus, Rome.

The Temple of Vespasian and Titus was located at the western end of the Roman Forum between the Temple of Concordia and the Temple of Saturn. 

It is dedicated to the deified emperor Vespasian and his son, the deified Titus. It was begun by Titus in 79 AD after Vespasian's death and Titus's succession. Titus’ brother, Domitian, completed and dedicated the temple to Titus and Vespasian in approximately 87 AD.

It was in the Corinthian order, hexastyle, and prostyle. It was particularly narrow due to the limited space, measuring 33 meters long and 22 wide.

properties.name: Templum Vestae (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Vesta, Rome.

The circular temple of Vesta, located between the “Arcus Augusti” and the Atrium Vestae, which Roman tradition assigned either to Romulus or to Numa.

 The temple burned down frequently, at least once during the Augustan period. During the Imperial period the temple was a typical domed tholos. Most scholars agree that, while the existing superstructure is Severan, the podium is Augustan.

properties.name: Templum Victoriae (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Victoria, Rome.

Temple to Victory on the SW Palatine adjacent to the Temple of Magna Mater and the shrine to Victoria Virgo.

 Dedicated in 294 BC by L. Postumius Megillus, the temple was substantially restored in the late-Republican or early-Augustan era, perhaps in the wake of the fire of 3 AD. 

Substantial architectural remains, identified as the Temple of Victoria due to their location, size, and close relation to epigraphic material pertaining to Victoria, include fragments of Corinthian capitals and other elements in travertine, which suggest a restoration during the third quarter of the 1st c. BC. The temple’s opus quadratum podium (c. 33 x 19 m) originally supported a hexastyle, peripteral sine postico temple with a double row of columns along the façade. The restoration retained the same plan, while augmenting the cella foundations to support an internal colonnade, and replacing the tufa superstructure with a Corinthian columnar order.

properties.name: Templum Virtutis (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Virtus, Rome.

Double Temple to Honos and Virtus built ex manubiis by C. Marius in 101 BC; no archaeological remains are known, but Vitruvius describes it as a peristyle temple without a portico in the rear.

properties.name: Templum Virtutis (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Virtus, Rome.

Double Temple to Honos and Virtus, without archaeological remains, close by the Porta Capena and the sanctuary of the Camenae in the vicinity of the Vicus Honoris et Virtutis of Regio I.

M. Claudius Marcellus, the conqueror of Syracuse, is reported to have restored an older Temple of Honos as well as added a new cella for Virtus; these were dedicated in 205 BC by his son. 

The temple was renowned for its superb artworks dedicated by Marcellus from the spoils of Syracuse, many of which had disappeared by Livy’s time. The sanctuary received a new and specifically Augustan meaning in 19 BC when the senate erected the Altar of Fortuna Redux in front of the temple; there, by the gate where Augustus entered the city, the altar commemorated his safe and singularly successful return from the East with the Roman standards regained from the Parthians.

properties.name: Templum Virtutis (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Temple of Virtus, Rome.

Temple dedicated to Honos, possibly also to Virtus, located outside the Porta Collina, and known only through literary and epigraphic evidence.

A dedication to Honos found c. 35m from the Colline Gate confirms the location given by Cicero. An inscription to Virtus, found between the Baths of Diocletian and Via XX Settembre, may point to the presence of a double cult at this site, as seen at the city’s two other temples to Honos. No archaeological remains have been found and the exact site, form and size of the temple are unknown.

properties.name: Domus (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Residence, Rome.

Scant remains of a late-Republican or Augustan residence on the Vicus Tuscus just N of the Horrea Agrippiana were recovered beneath S. Maria Antiqua during excavations in the 1980s; in an initial report, the finds (reticulate walls and opus spicatum pavements) were cautiously identified with either a commercial or residential structure.

 After further study, Hurst has characterized the material as the atrium of “a grand house of late-Republican or Augustan date” that may have been home to Germanicus during the Augustan era. Regardless of the suggested proprietor, the home did not survive long after the Augustan period, as it was built over by 25-30 AD.

properties.name: Domus (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Residence, Rome.

Large residence along the lower W slope of the Palatine, located just above and S of the Horrea Agrippiana.

 Remains include a reticulate foundation wall parallel to the W side of the hill, as well as other foundation and dividing walls in tufa blocks that Krause interprets as tabernae (shops or stalls) opening onto a street, and Papi as two cryptoportici. Carandini has associated this residence with that of M. Antony, which burned in 25 BC, though this is far from universally accepted.

properties.name: Domus (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Residence, Rome.

Recent excavations on the NW Palatine in the area of the Domus Tiberiana have revealed a long reticulate retaining wall (L. 59.30 m) parallel to the W side of the hill as well as two walls running perpendicular to it (L. 10.5 and 14.4 m; Krause 192: sectors 3-6-9, at level V); the excavators identify these as probable foundations of a late-Republican house which would have faced the Velabrum.

properties.name: Domus (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Residence, Rome.

Remains of a large residence and bath complex dated to the late 1st c. BC were recovered on the NW Palatine.

 A heated room (c. 21 x 30 m) cut into the living rock and paved with mosaics had plastered walls and vaults decorated with stuccos; at a higher level of the same area reticulate remains of an indeterminate plan have been documented. The residence occupied at least 600 sq. m.

properties.name: Domus (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Residence, Rome.

Residence on the NW corner of the Palatine dated to the mid 1st c. BC.

 Excavated just N of an Imperial-era street (often labeled the ‘Clivus Victoriae’) within three Hadrianic tabernae were cement and opus reticulatum substructures belonging to a series of rectangular rooms.

properties.name: Domus (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Residence, Rome.

A luxurious late-Republican or Augustan residence on the NW Palatine was recovered during recent excavations; unearthed were three vaulted rooms revetted in marble and mosaics and, behind these, a brief (c. 5 m) segment of a cryptoporticus cut into the tufa hillside. Some 19 m distant are remains in opus reticulatum associated with the same house.

properties.name: Domus (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Residence, Rome.

A lavishly decorated, rectangular hall of a late-Republican/early-Augustan residence, commonly known as the “Aula Isiaca”, is located on the Palatine beneath the “Basilica” of the Flavian Palace; the room, which features an apsidal E end and a barrel-vaulted ceiling, is the only portion of the domus which survives the later Neronian and Flavian interventions on the site. 

While the opus caementicium and opus reticulatum walls provide a general late-Republican/early-Augustan timeframe, the late Second-Style wall-paintings, which cover the extant walls and vault, allow for a date c. 19 BC. There is surprisingly little scholarly speculation as to the proprietor of this once-prominent residence, though Coarelli hypothesizes Mark Antony may have owned it and, after his death, Agrippa; meanwhile, Ling speculates that the room may have been part of the *Domus of Augustus.

properties.name: Domus (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Residence, Rome.

The cryptoporticus and peristyle of a luxurious early 1st c. AD residence were found on the NE Palatine below the present-day Vigna Barberini.

 Extant is one corner of a marble-clad gallery fronted by a colonnade and paved in opus sectile; perhaps this peristyle enclosed a garden. Under the gallery is a cryptoporticus which follows the same orientation. The excavators date the residence to the Julio-Claudian period, while Papi suggests an Augustan date. Other remains of late-Republican/Augustan date recovered nearby may also belong to this residence.

properties.name: Domus (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Residence, Rome.

Late-Republican residence on the lower slopes of the N Palatine, located at the intersection of the Nova Via and “Clivus Palatinus”, next to the Domus of M. Aemilius Scaurus.

 Excavations in 1983-85 unearthed remains of a house with an irregular rectangular ground-plan (c. 33 x 25 m) that was entered from the Nova Via . Walls in opus reticulatum and a black-and-white mosaic date the residence to the late 1st c. BC. The house shows evidence of fire damage, perhaps incurred during the Neronian blaze of 64 AD.

properties.name: Domus (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Residence, Rome.

Remains of a large residence along the Sacra Via between the Domus Publica and the Domus of M. Aemilius Scaurus, dating to the 1st c. BC (area of c. 1000 sq. m); extant are a number of subterranean rooms, probably servants’ quarters, a large garden, and fragmentary remains of the living area on the ground floor. The entrance to the residence, which was from the Sacra Via, was flanked by two tabernae (shops).

properties.name: Domus (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Residence, Rome.

A well-appointed residence located beneath the NW corner of the platform of the Temple of Venus and Roma.

 Extant remains include a circular hall flanked by four rectangular galleries, each preserving rich marble and mosaic pavements; their design and workmanship suggest a late-Republican or Augustan date. Recently Cn. Domitius Ahenobarbus (cos. 32 AD) has been proposed as one proprietor of this elegant and prominent residence. Previously, these remains were identified with Nero’s Domus Transitoria, but this association has been conclusively rejected.

properties.name: Domus (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Residence, Rome.

Large Republican-era residence built on the Velia; excavated and destroyed in 1931 during construction of Via dell’Impero. 

The ruins included a circular room designed as either a water basin or nymphaeum joined to four parallel rectangular rooms. Aligned with the N border of this structure, and following the same orientation, was a cryptoporticus which framed a rectangular garden. The walls of this domus were of opus incertum, which points to a Republican date.

properties.name: Domus (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Residence, Rome.

Remains of a Republican residence were unearthed at the E foot of the Velia during the construction of the modern subway system. 

Though destroyed soon after their discovery, archival documents attest to walls of opus quadratum in tufa and a fine mosaic pavement, which probably belonged to a residence. The location of the remains suggests the domus may have fronted onto the eponymous street of the Vicus Compiti Acili).

properties.name: Domus (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Residence, Rome.

Republican residence on the W slope of the Caelian discovered and destroyed in 1939-40 during construction of Rome’s subway system.

 The house is notable for its Third-Style wall-paintings; also recovered are walls of large tufa blocks, a black-and-white mosaic pavement, and a small marble staircase. These remains offer precious testimony of the luxurious residences that dotted the hill in the Augustan period.

properties.name: Domus (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Residence, Rome.

Extensive remains of house walls have been found on the SW edge of the Aventine plateau, under the Convent of S. Anselmo.

 Based on a inscribed lead pipe, the residence has been associated with a Pactumeia Lucilia (c. 100-150 AD); while specific chronological elements for interpreting the complex walls are lacking, they belong to “numerous phases, from the 1st c. BC to the 3rd, and perhaps 4th, c. AD”.

properties.name: Domus (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Residence, Rome.

Recent excavations on the S slope of the Caelian, outside the Servian Wall, have revealed walls in opus reticulatum and a mosaic pavement.

 The mosaic is dated to the Augustan era through a stylistic comparison to one recovered from the Domus of Augustus on the Palatine. While the remains are too scant to determine reliably the building’s original form, this structure, along with the Domus: Caelius Mons, offers valuable testimony of the presence of luxury architecture on the hill during the Augustan era.

properties.name: Domus (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Residence, Rome.

Augustan-era residence on the E Caelian, located outside the Servian Wall near the “Via Caelimontana”.

 Excavations in 1989-91 unearthed portions of two large structures, perhaps insulae, built in opus reticulatum that faced a row of small shops across a street. The E edifice housed a luxurious, ample residence; remains of a central impluvium (perhaps part of an atrium), two fine pavements, a small courtyard with a fountain, and a large underground cistern suggest that the domus was well-appointed. The W structure, which was separated from the E domus by a small alleyway, has rather scant remains that defy easy interpretation, though one room may have served as a shop. In addition, the NE sides of these two buildings, which are in perfect alignment with the row of shops opposite, suggest the axis of an Augustan-era street, which probably continued E to intersect the “Via Caelimontana”, which lay some 50 m distant; while the excavators hypothetically extend this street across the Caelian.

properties.name: Domus (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Residence, Rome.

Two rooms, probably belonging to a Republican residence on the Caelian, were recovered in 1958 during street work E of the Lateran Basilica.

 The walls were built of opus mixtum, and one room was revetted in marble; both rooms had fine polychrome mosaic floors. No elements allowing for a precise date were recovered, but the building technique of the walls is ascribed to the mid-1st c. BC.

properties.name: Domus (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Residence, Rome.

This large residence in Via Buonarroti near the Chiesa Cluny was excavated and drawn in the late 19th c. 

On the basis of several walls in opus reticulatum, it is dated to the Augustan period. Due to its location E of the Servian Wall, it seems to have been part of the Horti Maecenatis.

properties.name: Domus (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Residence, Rome.

The residential quarters of the horti of Maecenas, adjacent to the “Auditorium Maecenatis”, may be identified with the series of rooms discovered under the Cinema Brancaccio on the W side of the Servian Wall. 

An Augustan date is suggested by the use of opus reticulatum, and by sculptural finds which included marble column capitals from the Augustan period. The (partial) ground-plan is taken from 19th-c. excavation drawings. The S and N parts stood on slightly different axes, but both may be integrated with the orientation of the “Auditorium”.

properties.name: Domus (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Residence, Rome.

Substantial remains of a mid-1st c. BC residence stand at the foot of the Viminal near the intersection of Via Cimarra and Via dei Ciancaleoni, c. 3 m below the present ground level.

 Excavated in 1969-70, extant portions of the luxurious home include a peristyle and cryptoporticus, as well as fragmentary wall-paintings and floors of black-and-white mosaic and opus sectile. The building is dated to c. 50 BC by the construction techniques and by comparing its hellenistic plan with other late-Republican structures.

properties.name: Domus (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Residence, Rome.

This late-Republican house on the Cispian was discovered in 1847 at the corner of Via Sforza and Via dei Quattro Cantoni. Its modern name ‘Casa dei Paesaggi dell’Odissea’ is derived from a fresco featuring the adventures of Odysseus. 

This house is only partially known, but excavations suggest that the Odyssey frieze was part of a portico or cryptoportico, and that the house was developed in terraces on the crest of the hill. The house is dated to the late Republic on the basis of opus reticulatum walls of the same type as the Theatrum Pompeium, and on the basis of a stylistic analysis of the frieze itself.

properties.name: Domus (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Residence, Rome.

Remains of an extremely long-lived residence have been located beneath S. Pudenziana on the Viminalis. 

Though most of the walls date to the 2nd c. AD, a portion in opus reticulatum, as well as substantial remains of late-Republican or Augustan mosaics, suggest a residence of the early-Augustan era. One room preserves indications of an earlier pavement of hydraulic cement with inserted fragments of colored marble; Coarelli dates this floor to the 2nd c. BC, which suggests the residence was continuously inhabited for c. 400 years.

properties.name: Domus (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Residence, Rome.

Several partial opus reticulatum walls of late-Republican or Augustan date abut the Agger near the Porta Viminalis and have been identified as a residence. 

This identification seems based upon the preconception of the Viminalis as a “residential quarter” rather than on the extant physical evidence, which is quite fragmented. Even if one elects not to accept this as a residence, the walls offer valuable testimony for the intrusion of buildings into the Agger by the Augustan era.

properties.name: Domus (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Residence, Rome.

Remains of a private residence built in opus reticulatum featuring mosaic pavements, stucco decorations, and wall-paintings, were excavated just W of the Via Salaria, E of the “Sepulcra Salaria”, and N of the *Horti Sallustiani.

properties.name: Domus (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Residence, Rome.

Remains of a late-Republican residence on the Alta Semita within the Horti Sallustiani were recovered beneath the basement of the Caserma dei Corazzieri, once part of the convent of S. Susanna. 

Abutting the tufa remains of the Servian Wall were two levels of walls in opus reticulatum; these belonged to a balneum (bath) or nymphaeum. The complex was substantially rebuilt after the Augustan era.

properties.name: Domus (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Residence, Rome.

Remains of a mid-1st c. BC residence standing along the N face of the Viminalis. 

Excavations in 1871 recovered portions of 6 parallel rooms facing SE with walls of opus reticulatum and black-and-white mosaic floors. The construction technique and the mosaic designs are similar to those of the Domus of Livia on the Palatine, and suggest a date of the mid-1st c. BC for the complex. Associated brick walls with Flavian-era wall-paintings reveal that the domus remained active sometime after the Augustan period.

properties.name: Domus Augustana (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Imperial Palace, Rome.

The Domus Augustana is the modern name for the so-called domestic wing of the vast Palace of Domitian on the Palatine Hill.  It was the official residence in the city of the emperors from the late 1st to the 3rd c. AD.

Its name is not directly related to Augustus and should not be confused with the Domus Augusti.

The central section consists of at least four main parts: the "2nd Peristyle" to the northeast, the central "3rd Peristyle", the courtyard complex and the exedra on the southwest. The two peristyles to the north may have had public functions.

The 2nd Peristyle garden is partly exposed but little is known of its architecture.

The 3rd Peristyle was filled almost completely with a huge pool as wide as that of the Domus Flavia and included a seascape perhaps of Greek mythology on an island and with sculpture in the water. Other sources say that a temple was built on the island, namely a temple of Minerva. On its southwest side the walls still stand to a considerable height with several rooms around a semicircular hall.

"Courtyard" garden of the Domus Augustana looking east to the Severan Baths
The great exedra is a long curving arcaded gallery linking the two wings and overlooking the Circus Maximus allowing the emperor to watch the races. It may have been an ornamental façade, perhaps added by Trajan when the seats of the circus were carried up thus far.

From this curved terrace on the south-west, a large arched opening led into a courtyard, surrounded by a colonnade, behind which were rooms of elaborate plan. It seems that this complex was reserved for the private quarters of the emperor. This hypothesis is reinforced by the fact that the southern section was built a little later and some details suggest that it was not Rabirius who directed the work. The courtyard complex has two levels, the upper containing complex sets of rooms and the lower, 10 m below, consists of a pool with an unusual design of islands.

properties.name: Domus Augusti (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Palace of Augustus, Rome. 

The house of Augustus stood on the SW Palatine slope which rose above the Circus Maximus between Scalae Caci, the Temple of Apollo, and the house of Livia, from which it was separated by a narrow alley.

 The residence itself occupies an area of c. 350 sq. m. and forms part of a larger complex, over 12,000 sq. m., which included a Latin and a Greek library, porticoes and the dominating Temple of Apollo. 

The house was conceived in such a way as to embrace the temple on the N, W and S, so that the residence of the princeps and his protective god were visually perceived as one and the same. The house was probably one of many occupied by the imperial family on the SW Palatine, and its construction reflects the planning and restructuring of the zone under Augustus who transformed the area into an urban block with streets and passages.

Augustus, who once lived in a house which belonged to orator C. Licinius Macer Calvus next to the Forum Romanum and later resided in the house of Hortensius, had his Palatine residence built after he returned to Rome from his victory at Naulochos in 36 BC. His domus incorporated late-Republican houses, including those of the families of Q. Hortensius Hortalus and Q. Lutatius Catulus. Suetonius reports that the house of Hortensius was small and modest without marble revetment or mosaics; the residence may have been destroyed during the construction of the Temple of Apollo and the house of Augustus. The house of Catulus, on the other hand, was considered one of the finest houses of its time; Augustus acquired this residence perhaps as early as 36 BC but certainly by 29 BC, when he gave it to Agrippa. Since Augustus’ grandsons Gaius and Lucius were tutored in the atrium of the Catulinae domus, this house almost certainly belonged to their parents Julia and Agrippa and formed part of Augustus’ Palatine residence. The domus has been identified with the remains of a late 2nd- to early 1st c. BC house (extant are a peristyle, early Second-Style frescoes resembling those of the *“Casa dei Grifi”, a fine mosaic pavement, and a basin for fish) discovered immediately SW of the house of Livia and extending toward the Scalae Caci.

properties.name: Domus Aurea (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Imperial Palace, Rome.

Construction for the Golden Palace of Nero began after the great fire of 64 AD and was nearly completed before Nero's death in 68 AD, a remarkably short time for such an enormous project.

The Domus Aurea complex covered parts of the slopes of the Palatine, Oppian and Caelian hills, with a man-made lake in the marshy valley. Its size can only be approximated, as much of it has not been excavated. Some scholars place it at over 300 acres (1.2 km2), while others estimate its size to have been under 100 acres (0.40 km2). Suetonius describes the complex as "ruinously prodigal" as it included groves of trees, pastures with flocks, vineyards and an artificial lake—rus in urbe, "countryside in the city".

The Golden House was designed as a place of entertainment, as shown by the presence of 300 rooms without any sleeping quarters. The main palace building was on the Esquiline Hill. No kitchens or latrines have been discovered. Contemporary conveniences such as heating pipes have also not been discovered.

Rooms sheathed in dazzling polished white marble had richly varied floor plans, complete with niches and exedras that concentrated or dispersed the daylight. There were pools in the floors and fountains splashing in the corridors.

Some of the extravagances of the Domus Aurea had repercussions for the future. The architects designed two of the principal dining rooms to flank an octagonal court, surmounted by a dome with a giant central oculus to let in light. It was an early use of Roman concrete construction. One innovation was destined to have an enormous influence on the art of the future: Nero placed mosaics, previously restricted to floors, in the vaulted ceilings. Only fragments have survived, but that technique was to be copied extensively, eventually ending up as a fundamental feature of Christian art: the apse mosaics that decorate so many churches in Rome, Ravenna, Sicily and Constantinople.

Celer and Severus, his engineers, also created an ingenious mechanism, cranked by slaves, that made the ceiling underneath the dome revolve like the heavens, while perfume was sprayed and rose petals were dropped on the assembled diners.

properties.name: Domus C. Sestii (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Residence, Rome.

Republican residence of C. Sestius located in the Subura on the Argiletum, and known from an inscription marking the extent of the property that was found in situ in the basement of a house near S. Maria dei Monti in 1628. A wall of opus reticulatum was seen adjacent to the inscription.

properties.name: Domus Cn. Calpurnii Pisonis (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Residence, Rome.

The home of the prominent Augustan consular and longtime friend of Tiberius, Cn. Calpurnius Piso, described by Tacitus as ‘overhanging the Forum’.

 A recently-published inscription from Spain refers to certain structures ‘which Piso built over the Porta Fontinalis in order to join private houses’, which were demolished by the decree of the Senate in 20 AD in the wake of Piso’s disgrace following the death of Germanicus. This location fits well with Tacitus’ wording, since the pre-Trajanic geography of the area between the Quirinal and the Arx, where the Porta Fontinalis stood, was high enough in relation to the neighbouring Forum to provide the visual prominence that a powerful Senator’s residence required.

It is unclear how we should reconstruct this structure’s ground-plan from its description. The inscription refers specifically to additions built by Piso to merge more than one separate domus into a single complex. The language used seems to suggest something built over, i.e. on top of, the gate itself, perhaps connecting houses on either side of the city wall. Alternatively, the preposition ‘supra’ may simply refer to the general location of the structures in question, and need not suggest that Piso’s domicile actually impinged upon a public structure. In either case, no remains have yet been found.

properties.name: Domus Corneliae L. f. (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Residence, Rome.

Residence of Cornelia from the Augustan period located on the Quirinal under the large exedra of the thermae Diocletianae. The name is attested on a fistula aquaria recovered with the remains of an early-Imperial building, which Coarelli dates to the Augustan period. This Cornelia was probably the wife of L. Volusius Saturninus, cos. suff. in  3 AD and later praefectus urbi.

properties.name: Domus Flavia (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Imperial Palace, Rome.

The Flavian Palace, normally known as the Domus Flavia, is part of the vast residential complex of the Palace of Domitian on the Palatine Hill in Rome. It was completed in 92 AD by Emperor Domitian, and attributed to his master architect, Rabirius.

The term Domus Flavia is a modern designation used to describe the northwestern section of the Palace where the bulk of the large public rooms for entertaining and ceremony are concentrated. It is interconnected with the domestic wing to the southeast, the Domus Augustana, which descends from the summit of the Palatine down to wings specially constructed within the hill to the south and southwest.

The imposing ruins which flank the southeastern side of the Palace above the Circus Maximus are a later addition built by Septimius Severus; they are the supporting piers for a large extension which completely covered the eastern slope.

properties.name: Domus Gryphorum (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Residence, Rome.

Remains of the House of the Gryphons, a luxurious Republican residence, are extant on the Palatine under the “Lararium” of the Flavian Palace.

 Commonly known as the “Casa dei Grifi” after its stucco decorations, the house is admired for its fine early Second Style wall-paintings. Originally constructed in opus incertum during the mid-2nd c. BC, the building received various modifications in opus quasi reticulatum afterwards, perhaps as a consequence of the same fire in 111 BC that ravaged the Temple of Magna Mater.

 A number of proprietors have been proposed for the residence, though none persuasively enough to adopt here: Numerius Fabius Pictor (c. 93 BC) and the Fabii in general, Q. Hortensius, a Catiline.

 Only a few subterranean rooms survive the numerous interventions on the site; Nero and the Flavian emperors took a great toll on the residence, but even by the Augustan era the subterranean rooms had been infilled and foundations for a new residence “ruthlessly driven through” their vaults.

properties.name: Domus Liviae (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Imperial Palace of Livia, Rome.

A late-Republican house on the SW Palatine is attributed to Livia based upon a lead pipe inscribed IVLIA AVG[VSTA] discovered on the site and its proximity to the domus of Augustus; this identification is supported by a passage in Suetonius naming the Palatine as the birthplace of Tiberius.

 The residence stood on the slope of the SW Palatine just below the terrace of the Temple of Victoria, and was just N of the Palatine residence of Augustus; since only a narrow alley separated the two houses, these remains have been interpreted as apartments reserved for Livia after her marriage to Augustus.

Excavations carried out in 1722-24 by the Farnese family, in 1869 by P. Rosa, and in the 1950s by G. Carettoni have clarified the building phases of the residence. Originally, the one-storey residence was built in somewhat irregular reticulate masonry; this phase dates from the first half of the 1st c. BC, perhaps from 75-50 BC. Many associate this phase of the house with Hortensius, which Augustus is known to have incorporated into his own residence. Livia’s house was organized in two sections, each centered on a courtyard. The focal point of the residence in the pre-Augustan era was the subterranean W atrium; opening onto this space were three large rooms: a central triclinium  flanked by two alae; to the SW lay a fourth room, commonly called the tablinum. The use of these terms is purely conventional, and the attributed functions are not supported by archaeological evidence. A stairway and ramped corridor paved with a black-and-white mosaic provided access to this courtyard from the exterior; the original entrance to the house, however, must have been from the E. A long corridor connected the W wing to the E half of the residence, which was located on a higher level; a series of small service rooms lined the S side of this connecting passageway. The E courtyardhad an impluvium and was surrounded by small service rooms.

After Augustus acquired this section of the Palatine, substantial renovations were made to the house, including the restructuring of its W half, which was decorated with advanced Second-Style wall-paintings; especial attention was paid to the rooms situated on the S and E sides, though the alterations to the E portion of the house remain obscure. The chambers around the E court were rebuilt and a second, perhaps also a third, storey was added above the rooms surrounding the E atrium. The second phase is characterized by typical Augustan dusky-red concrete faced with opus quasi reticulatum. Coarelli proposes that restorations were made to the house after the fire of  3 AD, which damaged other buildings in the region.

properties.name: Domus M. Aemilii Scauri (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Residence, Rome.

M. Aemilius Scaurus (pr. 56 BC) was the mid-1st c. BC proprietor of a magnificent aristocratic residence on the lower Palatine, at the intersection of the Sacra Via and Clivus Palatinus. 

Excavations in 1983-85 unearthed remains of at least one, possibly two houses, in this area. The house dates to the second quarter of the 1st c. BC based upon its building materials and mosaics; its atrium and portions of a series of heated bathing rooms are preserved. Carandini connected the Asconius passage with these remains convincingly to identify them as the domus of M. Aemilius Scaurus. In 53 BC Scaurus sold the house to P. Clodius Pulcher and in 17 BC the famed Hymettan marble columns of its atrium were transferred from the domus to the Theatre of Marcellus. Its owner in the Augustan era remains unknown, though Clodius’ heir P. Claudius Pulcher (cos. 21/22 AD), is one possibility. By the mid-1st c. AD C. Caecina Largus (cos. 43 AD) was proprietor.

properties.name: Domus Sessoriana (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Imperial Palace, Rome.

The Sessorium, a building known in later times as the palatium Sessorianum, was standing in the 1st c. AD when it is mentioned as being near the spot where the execution of criminals took place. The origin of the name is unexplained, but the building became an imperial residence in the 4th c. AD and was a favourite home of Helena, the mother Constantine.

properties.name: Domus Severiana (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Imperial Palace, Rome.

The Domus Severiana is the modern name given to the final extension to the imperial palaces on the Palatine Hill in Rome, built to the south-east of the Stadium Palatinum in the Domus Augustana of Septimius Severus. It included the Baths of Septimius Severus.

All that remains of the building are the imposing brick substructures at the corner of the hill, which created an artificial platform at the same level as the palace of Domitian, extending it, since the emperors had run out of space on the hill. There are very few remains of the building itself, which was then built on the terrace under the substructures. It had a view of Rome from the Circus Maximus and the Aventine Hill to the Caelian Hill and the Baths of Caracalla. They were part of an imperial baths complex or thermae, now visible in the remains below the exedra of the Stadium Palatinum, which may have been built under Domitian and which was rebuilt by Maxentius. They were fed by a branch of the Aqua Claudia, which spanned the valley between the Palatine Hill and the Caelian Hill and whose arches are still visible.

On the side facing the via Appia, Septimius Severus commissioned an impressive three-level facade akin to the scaena in a theatre, with fountains and colonnades. This became known as the Septizodium. It is said that the emperor monumentalised this side of the building to impress his fellow Africans, who would arrive in Rome along the via Appia. The Septizodium's remains were demolished in the 16th century and it is only known from Renaissance drawings.

properties.name: Domus Sexti Pompeii (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Residence, Rome.

House of Sextus Pompeius.

properties.name: Domus T. Pomponii Attici (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Residence, Rome.

Republican-era residence of T. Pomponius Atticus, located somewhere near the Temple of Quirinus  and not far from the Temple of Salus.

 No archaeological remains of the domus survive but it was said to have been a tasteful rather than a costly home, with charming gardens.

properties.name: Domus Tiberiana (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Imperial Palace, Rome.

Despite its name, this palace on the northwest sector of the Palatine was not erected by Tiberius but by his successors, Caligula and Nero. Very little is known about its design and phases because it is still buried beneath the Farnese Gardens, laid out in the 16th century by Cardinal Alessandro Farnese. The mad emperor Caligula, linked the palace to the Temple of Castor and Pollux by a bridge. The emperor would appear there and receive divine honors along with the cult statues of the Dioscuri. After Caligula's assassination, Claudius removed the bridge.

properties.name: Domus (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Residences, Rome.

Opus incertum walls belonging to several houses of the 2nd c. BC have been found inside the Servian Wall on the brow of the Aventine overlooking the Tiber (just NW of S. Sabina). 

Nearby, reticulate walls, of late-Republican or early-Imperial date, reach into the area just outside the wall; to facilitate circulation, four passageways were opened in the wall, and thus the wall’s defensive function had clearly been abandoned.

properties.name: Domus (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Residences, Rome.

Housing remains of Republican-Augustan date have come to light at the S foot of the Oppian under the Nuova Esattoria to the E of the ludus Magnus in the Colosseum valley.

 Pavements and walls, destroyed in the Neronian fire of 64 AD, were found just S of the modern Via Labicana; a black mosaic pavement with marble insets from a domus of Republican/Augustan date, also destroyed by fire, was found in the S part of the Nuova Esattoria.

properties.name: Domus (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Residences, Rome.

Remains of two Republican-era houses have been unearthed on the Carinae beneath the nave of S. Pietro in Vincoli. The first was originally built as early as the 3rd c. BC in opus quadratum, and then remodeled during the 1st c. BC when it was fitted with mosaic pavements. Remains of several rooms, an atrium and a cistern survive beneath the nave of the church.

 Adjacent to and just W of this house stood a second residence which was built during the 1st c. BC on a larger and more luxurious scale. This home had walls in opus incertum and opus reticulatum as well as beautiful mosaics and striking opus signinum pavements. Though the two residences share the same orientation, the differences in the building techniques and in the elevation of their pavements suggest that the two were separate structures, rather than a unified complex.

properties.name: Insula (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Apartment block, Rome.

The Insula dell'Ara Coeli is a rare surviving example of an insula, the kind of apartment blocks where many Roman city dwellers resided. It was built during the 2nd c. AD, and rediscovered, under an old church, when Benito Mussolini initiated a plan for massive urban renewal of Rome's historic Capitoline Hill neighbourhood.

Four floors remain. The ground floor consisted of shops that faced the surrounding streets, with the owners using ladders to access living quarters immediately above. A mezzanine lay above the shop level. The two remaining floors seem to have been designed for human residence. The third floor seemed to be large, spacious apartments. The fourth floor had a corridor with a series of three room suites leading off of it. Archeologist Andrew Wallace-Hadrill suggested that with a little imagination, these suites are comparable to apartments in which many 21st century Roman families live. Archeologists believe the structure was originally built with at least five stories.

properties.name: Villa (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Country house, Rome

A fairly large and prosperous villa on the W bank of the Tiber, excavated in the gardens of Villa Farnesina during the construction of the Tiber embankments in 1879. Remains of a vast complex of wine-cellars, the cellae Vinariae Nova et Arruntiana lay immediately to its SE.

The monumental villa was symmetrically planned with a hemispherical extension and a set of terraces and gardens cascading toward the Tiber. The villa is often associated with contemporary Augustan monuments to its SE along the river: the Sepulcrum: C. Sulpicius Platorinus (18 BC) and the Pons Agrippae.

The building complex is dated on stylistic grounds by its well-preserved late Second-Style wall-decorations which the most recent art-historical scholarship assigns to the early part of the Augustan period, c. 20 BC. However, the Farnesina wall-paintings are also referred to as transitional or early Third Style, in which case their date ranges from 20 to 10 BC. Bragantini and de Vos suggest a particular Augustan-Agrippan workshop initiated the Egyptianizing Third Style.

 Based upon its construction techniques, a slightly higher date for the building complex is proposed, of 35-25 BC. Its architectural design is often found as innovative as its paintings. Due in part to its proximity in date and location to the Pons Agrippae, the villa may have belonged to Agrippa and Julia, thereby dating its construction to 19 BC, but there is no conclusive evidence to prove this hypothesis.

properties.name: Villa Capitis Tauri (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Country house, Rome.

The villa was owned by Herodes Atticus and his wife Annia Regilla. The excavations revealed thermal baths dating back to the middle of the 2nd c. AD. These baths were used until at least the 4th c.
