AD and were almost certainly for private use. Greek inscriptions found there remind us of the Greek origins of Herodes Atticus. There are several well-preserved mosaics and the high quality of building materials used suggest a very elegant environment. Water was provided by two large cisterns.

properties.name: Villa Quintiliorum (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Country house, Rome.

The Villa of the Quintilii is a villa beyond the fifth milestone along the Via Appia just outside the traditional boundaries of Rome. It was built by the rich and cultured brothers Sextus Quintilius Valerius Maximus and Sextus Quintilius Condianus (cos. in 151 AD).

The ruins of this villa suburbana are of such an extent that when they were first excavated, the site was called Roma Vecchia ("Old Rome") by the locals, as they occupied too great a ground, it seemed, to have been anything less than a town. The nucleus of the villa was constructed in the time of Hadrian. The villa included extensive thermae fed by its own aqueduct, and, what was even more unusual, a hippodrome, which dates to the fourth century, when the villa was Imperial property: the emperor Commodus coveted the villa strongly enough to put to death its owners in 182 AD and confiscate it for himself.

properties.name: Atria Licinia (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Auction halls, Rome.

Auction halls near the entrance of the Macellum mentioned by Cicero.

 No remains of the Atria Licinia have been found, but Cicero’s reference to the fauces Macelli implies a location somewhere behind the E façade of the Basilica Paulli.

properties.name: Forum Boarium (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Cattle market, Rome.

The Forum Boarium was the cattle forum. It was located on a level piece of land near the Tiber between the Capitoline, the Palatine and Aventine hills. As the site of the original docks of Rome (Portus Tiberinus), the Forum Boarium experienced intense commercial activity.

The Forum Boarium was the site of the first gladiatorial contest at Rome which took place in 264 BC as part of aristocratic funerary ritual—a munus or funeral gift for the dead. Marcus and Decimus Junius Brutus Scaeva put on a gladiatorial combat in honour of their deceased father with three pairs of gladiators.

The site was also a religious centre housing the Temple of Hercules Victor, the Temple of Portunus, and the massive 6th or 5th c. BC Great Altar of Hercules.

properties.name: Forum Espuilinum (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Commerical area, Rome.

Commercial space on the S Cispian. 

Appian’s description of a battle said to have taken place here in 88 BC between C. Marius and L. Sulla implies that the Forum Esquilinum was a large open space, located just inside the Porta Esquilina. It is mentioned in several funerary inscriptions. An inscription discovered by the Church of S. Vito, built on the site of the Porta Esquilina, mentions a forum restored by Fl. Eurycles Epitychianus in 450 AD. The findspot of this inscription suggests that the Forum Esquilinum stood inside the Porta Esquilina, N of the Clivus Suburanus. The Macellum Liviae, which was built outside the Porta Esquilina during the Augustan period, confirms the commercial nature of this area.

properties.name: Forum Holitorium (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Vegetable market, Rome.

The Forum Holitorium was the site of a commercial marketplace for vegetables, herbs and oil. 

It was "oddly located" outside the Porta Carmentalis in the Campus Martius, crowded between the Forum Boarium and buildings located in the Circus Flaminius.

properties.name: Horrea Agrippiana (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Warehouse of Agrippa, Rome.

A massive warehouse built by Agrippa on the NW slope of the Palatine. 

Carandini has recently argued that this complex is in fact the later horrea Germaniciana et Agrippiniana, but the inscription to the Genius horreorum Agrippianorum found in the center of the courtyard secures the traditional identification. The excavated portion of the Horrea Agrippiana indicates that its shape was rectangular, not trapezoidal, and that it was multi-storeyed. 

Excavations in 1983-85 in the area to the N of the Horrea Agrippiana, underneath the Church of S. Maria Antiqua, uncovered a late-Republican structure, either a house or a commercial building of some sort, and a later pavement in opus spicatum. Because the Horrea Agrippiana also had a pavement in opus spicatum, it has been suggested that this correspondence implies a thorough reworking of the whole area in the Augustan period, but only further excavation will be able to confirm this hypothesis.

properties.name: Horrea Galbana (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Warehouses of Galba, Rome.

Extensive late-Republican warehouses that define the urban topography of the SE Emporium area. 

The identification of the monumental complex is well established, and the late 2nd c. BC. date for its construction is not debated. The broad district SW of the Aventine, bordered by the Via Ostiensis to the NE, the so-called “Porticus Aemilia” to the NW, and the Monte Testaccio to the S, was known as the praedia Galbana in the Republican period, and the name may be preserved in the Marble Plan : [PRAED]IA ET HORREA [G]ALB[ANA]). 

The land in this area belonged to the Sulpicii Galbae. The spacious warehouses were organized around three rectangular courtyards immediately SE of the Porticus Aemilia, as shown on the Marble Plan.

The small-scale excavations in 1955 revealed concrete walls “faced with slightly irregular opus reticulatum” that were dated to mid-1st c. BC. Coarelli has recently suggested a late 2nd c. BC date for the same evidence. Confirmation of the earlier construction date for the warehouses comes from the nearby Sepulcrum of Ser. Sulpicius Galba, consul of 144 or 108 BC, who is often associated with the construction of the horrea.

Careful examination of the architecture of the three units shows that they are not identical, while the structures that occupied the E courtyard remain unknown. Rodríguez Almeida convincingly argued for a triple-cohors social organization of the warehouse workers, evident from numerous inscriptions and reflected in the structure of the monument (e.g., the inscription, dated to the time of Galba, from an altar to Bona Dea Galbilla mentioning a dedication by the VILICVS HORREORVM GALBIANORVM COHORTIVM TRIVM: CIL VI 30855).

properties.name: Horrea Lolliana (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Warehouses of Lollius, Rome.

Courtyard-type late-Republican warehouse complex in the S Emporium area, known primarily from a large fragment of the Severan Marble Plan since archaeological evidence for the horrea is scanty. The completely preserved label on the Marble Plan makes the identification of the structure certain. This fragment is firmly located S of, and downstream from, the Emporium area, where the Tiber bends to the SE.

On the lower part of the fragment, the Horrea Lolliana are represented as organized around two courtyards with porticoes. The two units are dissimilar in the overall size of the courtyards and the arrangement of the rooms around them. The horrea are linked to the Tiber by means of a wide quay and stairs. On the upper half of the fragment, a narrow set of courtyard structures and a small bath-house “similar to the Stabian baths at Pompei” are shown with the same rectilinear orientation as the horrea.

The construction of the horrea was associated with the gens Lollia, whose commercial relations with Delos are known from epigraphic evidence. As for the specific individual from the Lollii family responsible for the construction, Coarelli suggests M. Lollius Palicanus, a follower of Pompey, based upon the slim archaeological evidence suggesting a date of the mid-1st c. BC for the structures. Epigraphic evidence demonstrates that the horrea became imperial property at the time of Claudius.

properties.name: Horrea Seiana (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Warehouse of Seius, Rome.

A prominent Republican warehouse complex in the Emporium area, not far from the Tiber, known only from epigraphic evidence.

 Based on the findspots of a number of inscriptions which were excavated in situ, Lanciani located the horrea just SE of the so-called Porticus Aemilia. Based on the name of the monument, the foundation of the horrea is associated with the Seii family-clan, and specifically with M. Seius, who was an aedile in 74 BC. During building construction in 1911 between Via G. Branca, Via G. Battista Bodoni and Via Beniamino Franklin, remains of possible warehouse structures showing extensive use of opus reticulatum were uncovered. Even if the Horrea Seiana can be associated with these scanty remains, no coherent plan can be deduced without further systematic excavations in the area.

properties.name: Macellum (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Market, Rome.

Food market rebuilt by M. Fulvius Nobilior in 179 BC near the Forum Romanum and the busy commercial area of the Argiletum.

 The exact location of the Macellum was debated until Morselli and Tortorici identified architectural remains belonging to the structure. It is now securely placed behind the Basilica Paulli in the region later occupied by the Forum Transitorium and Templum Pacis.

 The archaeological remains, however, are too scant to restore fully the Macellum’s ground-plan or elevation. An indication of the structure’s extent is provided by literary accounts which suggest that the macellum stretched from the Argiletum to the Corneta, a small alley NE of the Basilica Paulli.

properties.name: Macellum Liviae (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Market of Livia, Rome.

The Macellum Liviae, a market building on the Esquiline, is mentioned only by late-antique and mediaeval sources, which place it near the Church of S. Vito, the arch of Gallienus , the Nymphaeum Alexandri and S. Eusebio.

 It was thus identified by Lanciani with remains that came to light in Via Principe Amedeo and Via Napoleone III outside the Servian Wall, just N of the Porta Esquilina. This structure consists of a rectangular open court (in which stood a fountain) surrounded by porticoes and shops; the walls date from different periods, but one wall of opus reticulatum may be dated to the 1st c. AD. However, the strong connection between the macellum and Livia in the later literary sources dates the first phase of this structure to the Augustan period. It is not mentioned by Augustan sources. 

The identification of the structure outside the Servian Wall as the Macellum Liviae follows both the mediaeval and modern communis opinio; the remains date mostly from the mid-2nd c. AD, but given the survival of one wall in opus reticulatum, it is possible that later renovations followed the original Augustan ground-plan.

properties.name: Macellum Traiani (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Market of Trajan, Rome.

Thought to be the world's oldest shopping mall, the arcades in Trajan's Market are now believed by many to be administrative offices for Emperor Trajan. The shops and apartments were built in a multi-level structure and it is still possible to visit several of the levels. Highlights include delicate marble floors and the remains of a library.

properties.name: Mons Testarum (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Monte Testaccio, Rome.

The artificial hill of modern-day Monte Testaccio lies S of the Horrea Galbana in the Emporium area, bordered by Via Galvani, Via Zabaglia, Ex-Mattatoio Comunale and the 3rd c. AD Aurelian Wall, occupying an c. 22,000 sq. m. triangular area (on average: 180 m N–S x 250 m E–W), with a maximum height of 49 m asl and 36 m above the surrounding street level. The elevation of this area was 5 to 6 m lower in antiquity.

The hill was created by the systematic deposition of amphora sherds to form a terraced pyramidal structure, beginning early in the Augustan era and continuing until its abandonment in 257 AD.

Though recent archaeological investigations at the Monte Testaccio have not yet found sherds pre-dating 144 AD, it is assumed that the deposition must have started when the Roman province of Baetica was integrated into the Roman economy early during the reign of Augustus, since a large proportion of amphoras uncovered on the site are Baetican olive-oil types. Further, by the late-Republican period the Emporium was already well developed with massive warehouses as well as a monumental tomb structure of the Rusticelii family immediately to the S of the hill'', that demarcated its limits.

properties.name: Officina Metallorum (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Metal Workshop, Rome.

Two series of walls, one dating to the Republican period, the other possibly to the Augustan era, were recovered during recent excavations inside the “Arcus Dolabellae et Silani” near the present-day Piazza Celimontana. 

The earliest walls on the site are built in opus quasi reticulatum, and thus may date to c. 125-75 BC; one was unearthed in 1977-82, the other reported seen in 1908. The N–S orientation of one wall parallels the eventual course of the so-called vicus Capitis Africae, and suggests to the excavators that a street may have run in the area as early as the Republican period, yet they cautiously recall that the structure of the region was radically altered between the Republic and the early-Imperial period. The second set of walls on the site is built of opus mixtum, and dated to the reign of Augustus by the characteristic cement employed; these walls follow the same N–S orientation as the Republican opus quasi reticulatum ones, and the excavators once again postulate that these flanked a street, perhaps even serving to limit the roadway itself (Pavolini 113-14: again, noting the limited data and possibility that the street was not affiliated with the vicus Capitis Africae but rather a nameless road). In 1893, a group of similar opus mixtum walls was recovered in the immediate vicinity along with an opus spicatum pavement and numerous fragments of bronze vessels, which suggest that in antiquity a metalworking facility stood on the site.

properties.name: Officinae Minii (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Rome.

Workshops located on the slope of the collis Quirinalis between the Temple of Quirinus and Temple of Flora where mercury ore imported from Spain was refined to produce minium (cinnabar, a red pigment). 

This artisanal process is described in some detail by Pliny. The workshops were probably established during the second half of the 1st c. BC. Though mentioned by both Vitruvius and Pliny, neither author preserves the ancient name of the workshops. Current scholarship typically employs the name “Officinae Minii”.

properties.name: Porticus Aemilia (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Warehouses of Aemilius, Rome.

The portico was built in 193 BC by aediles Marcus Aemilius Lepidus and Lucius Aemilius Paulus from which the name of the structure and association to the gens Aemilia is derived. It was subsequently rebuilt in 174 BC by censors Quintus Fulvius Flaccus and Aulus Postumius Albinus.

The development of the Porticus coincided with the rapid growth of the city after the Second Punic War. This increase, in both trade and population, placed stresses on the limited space available in the Forum Boarium and underlined the importance of the river link to Rome's main port at Ostia. The Porticus and the Emporium appear to have worked together to facilitate the unloading, storage, and possibly redistribution of goods and foodstuffs, including imported grain for the corn dole, and appear to have been in continuous operation until the 6th century AD.

The opus incertum building, in the form of a thin rectangle running parallel to the Tiber, was very large; approximately 487 metres (1,598 ft) long, 60 metres (200 ft) deep and subdivided by 294 pillars in rows of seven. These created a series of 50 aisles, each 8.30 metres (27.2 ft) across. They were roofed by a series of overlapping vaults that rose in line with the slope of the hill, offering protection from the elements while allowing in light and air. The total covered surface was 25,000 square metres (270,000 sq ft).

The building was set back approximately 90 metres (300 ft) from the Emporium and river access, possibly to mitigate the effects of seasonal flooding. By the Trajanic period this space was filled with additional commercial structures, and the large utilitarian spaces in the Porticus were put to a variety of uses, often modified or subdivided to suit the needs of their users.

properties.name: Tabernae (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Shops, Rome.

A line of tabernae preceded by a portico located just N of the Column of Trajan were brought to light during excavations in 1929-34; they showed signs of having been destroyed to make way for the construction of the Forum of Trajan. The shops were built of brick with a travertine socle, yet at least one wall rested on opus incertum ruins with the same orientation. These shops are difficult to date (c. 1st c. AD), but even if later than 14 AD, the earlier remains indicate a late-Republican structure of the same orientation and perhaps function. The tabernae fronted a paved street, of which a few pavers were recovered. Also nearby were traces of an early structure built of tufa; though oriented along the same street, the ruins are too fragmentary to reconstruct.

properties.name: Tabernae (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Shops, Rome.

Residence on the NW corner of the Palatine dated to the mid-1st c. BC. Excavated just N of an Imperial-era street (often labeled the 'Clivus Victoriae’) within three Hadrianic tabernae were cement and opus reticulatum substructures belonging to a series of rectangular rooms.

properties.name: Tabernae (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Shops, Rome.

A row of spacious tabernae nearly 50 m long stretched along the N slope of the Caelius Mons, just W of the apse of SS. Quattro Coronati.

 Built in opus reticulatum with a limited use of brick, the structure dates to the early-Imperial period. Fragments of walls along the rear of the shops indicate that the building joined other structures to the NW, though the form of these is unknown. Portions of walls in front of the tabernae suggest that they faced onto a second row of shops, and perhaps served as a market building. Note that these tabernae extend into the hypothetical course of Colini’s Vicus Statae Matris, thus excluding the adoption of this 2nd c. AD street plan for the Augustan era .

properties.name: Tabernae (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Shops, Rome.

A row of tabernae over 40 m long was excavated in 1989-91 on the E slope of the Caelian well outside the Servian Wall. The heavy reticulate rear wall of the shops served to retain the hillside. The remains suggest that each shop was c. 5 m wide and 7 to 10 m deep, with the larger ones divided into two rooms. The roofing technique remains unknown, as does the full extent of the row, since it may continue at both ends. These shops, along with an adjacent residence, define the axis of an Augustan-era street.

properties.name: Castra Cohortum Urbanae (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Urban Cohorts barracks, Rome.

Three permanent urban cohorts, established by Augustus and reorganized by Tiberius, constituted the body in charge of maintaining public order in the city and were commanded by the praefectus urbi.

Initially they were perhaps also housed in the Castra praetoria, since in emergencies they were used as auxiliary troops of the praetorian cohorts for the defense of the Emperor. Subsequently, at least from the time of the Emperor Septimius Severus , they had their own barracks. We know from sources that this was in the VII Augustan region (Via Lata), probably in the area of the current Piazza di Spagna .

properties.name: Castra Misenatium (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Sailors barracks, Rome.

A special detachment of the sailors (classiarii) of the military fleet stationed in Miseno was used for the maneuver of the velarium which protected the spectators of the Colosseum from the sun or rain and probably also for the naumachias .

The detachment was housed in a barracks near the amphitheater, which was probably located at the thermal baths of Trajan , on the slopes of Opium, where an inscription was found relating to an extension of the barracks in the 3rd c. AD.

properties.name: Castra Nova Equitum Singularium Augusti (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Imperial Cavalry Guard barracks, Rome.

The Castra Nova was so-called because it was the newer of the two forts, built to house an enlargement of the cavalry guard. Their previous fort Castra Prioria which lay not far away to the north had been built earlier, possibly under the emperor Domitian, and still housed the original force of 1500 mounted troopers.

The fort can be precisely dated to 193 AD, at the beginning of the reign of Septimius Severus. The new camp was necessitated by this emperor's increase of the size of his cavalry guard from 1,500 to 2,000 men.

The site of the camp was always speculated as being beneath the cathedral of St John Lateran (Basilica di San Giovanni in Laterano), but it was identified definitively by excavations between 1934 and 1938 undertaken by Enrico Josi. Josi had obtained permission to explore the area of the basilica’s nave in advance of the construction of a new reinforced concrete floor. Within days it became clear that the remains of the Castra Nova existed in good condition just below the floor level and that the excavation was including a large part of the principia (headquarters) building. The completed excavations were then published by Colini.

A large two-storey storage building and two barracks were also uncovered, but the greatest interest centered around the principia as its two strong rooms were very well preserved as were several office rooms. On the completion of the investigation the remains were preserved beneath the basilica (along with the remains of the Constantinian cathedral and a Neronian domus) in a spectacular underground archaeological park.

properties.name: Castra Peregrina (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Peregrini barracks, Rome.

he barracks are situated on the Caelian Hill between the Temple of Claudius and Nero's Macellum Magnum. It is centrally located on a hill known for its housing of wealthy Romans. The fourth-century Regionaries list the Castra Peregrina in Regio II.

The remains of the camp were discovered during digging for the foundations of a convent and hospital and partially excavated from 1904-1909. It can now be found just south-east of the well preserved church Santo Stefano al Monte Celio.

As the name suggests, the barracks housed a garrison of peregrini; soldiers from the provincial armies detached for special services in Rome. These consisted of a majority of frumentarii[and inscriptions suggest that the Castra Peregrina acted as a central base for the distribution of these men throughout the unarmed provinces (inermes). The frumentarii, who were likely based, and not only housed, at the Castra Peregrina, were initially involved in the provision supply service of Rome, but were later employed as military couriers and members of the secret service.

Richardson suggests that the brickwork demonstrates an Augustan origin with a 2nd c. AD rebuilding, probably under Severus, and another rebuilding in 3rd c. AD, however the earliest mention of the princeps peregrinorum (camp-commandant) in Rome was during the reign of Trajan. It is also mentioned by Ammianus Marcellinus, showing that it was in use as late as the 4th c. AD.

properties.name: Castra Peregrina (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Peregrini barracks, Rome.

The Castra were found during the archaeological excavations, conducted in the Amba Aradam-Ipponio station, in November-December 2015 and resumed in March 2016. The area occupies 1750 square meters, and, at ܃9meters deep, part of a castrum was found, dating back to the first half 2nd c. AD, probably at the time of Hadrian. The castrum is composed of a long central corridor with 39 rooms of 16 sq m, 25 of which are quadrangular, with mosaic floors with white/black tesserae and frescoed plaster walls.

properties.name: Castra Praetoria (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Praetorian Guard Fortress, Rome.

According to the Roman historian Tacitus, the barracks were built in 23 AD by Lucius Aelius Sejanus, the praetorian prefect serving under the emperor Tiberius, in an effort to consolidate the several divisions of the guards.

The barracks were erected just outside the city of Rome and surrounded by solid masonry walls, measuring a total of 440 by 380 metres (1,440 ft × 1,250 ft). Three of the four sides of the walls were later incorporated in the Aurelian Walls, and parts of them are clearly visible today.

The Castra Praetoria was the site of the murder of the Emperor Elagabalus, and his mother Julia Soaemias by the Praetorian Guard in 222 AD.

The Castra Praetoria was destroyed by Constantine I, who also disbanded the Praetorian Guard upon his conquest of Italy while Maxentius ruled as the Western Roman Emperor in Italy.

properties.name: Castra Priora Equitum Singularium Augusti
properties.description:
Imperial Cavalry Guard barracks, Rome.

The remains of the oldest one were found in 1885-1889 on the Caelian (via Tasso), together with numerous inscriptions dedicated to different deities that were to be housed in the barracks sanctuary.

properties.name: Navalia (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Naval arsenal, Rome.

Naval arsenal, with rows of warship sheds, along the Tiber bank of the SW Campus Martius, stretching opposite the transtiberine prata Quinctia and thus upstream from the Insula Tiberina, but not too far away from the city walls since the porta Navalis was ‘in the vicinity of the Navalia’.

 No remnants are known, unless a sizeable portico of the Republican period belonged, in some way, to the facilities.

 The Navalia complex was already fully established by the 3rd/2nd c. BC, with additional work carried out in the later 2nd c. BC by the prestigious architect Hermodoros of Salamis. The naval arsenal was in regular use when Cato the Younger returned from his Cypriot mission in 56 BC. Its buildings could also be used to keep wild animals until needed in circus games. They were damaged by lightning in 44 BC. The testimonies of Livyand Pliny, both of whom use the navalia as an unqualified point of reference during their lifetimes, contradict the inference of Coarelli that the arsenal had fallen out of use by the mid-1st c. BC. Moreover, Procopius’ 6th-c. AD eyewitness account of a ‘ship of Aeneas’ faithfully preserved in a shipshed ‘in the middle of the city along the Tiber’ seems to apply to the Navalia.

The Marble Plan fragment from Via Anicia shows part of an edifice situated along the Tiber bank near the Temple of Castor and Pollux in the SW Campus Martius; the structure also appears on the Severan Marble Plan and has been connected with the Navalia.

properties.name: Columbaria (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Tomb, Rome. 

A well-preserved reticulate columbarium of square plan (c. 6 x 5 m, 7 m deep) with over 300 loculi was excavated near the Via Appia in 1847.

 An inscription dated to 10 AD provides a terminus ante quem for the tomb. Inscribed cinerary urns recovered from the site confirm that it was opened under Augustus, and indicate that the tomb continued to receive burials through the Julio-Claudian period. Many of the deceased freedmen and slaves interred here served the imperial household, so it is sometimes called the “Monumentum Marcellae”.

In the decades following Augustus’ death, two other large columbaria (one of 450 loculi, the other with 800) were opened in the immediate vicinity of this tomb; these three monuments are often grouped as the “Columbaria of the Vigna Codini”. These tombs attest to the continuing popularity of the Via Appia as a burial site, yet witness a changing demographic: the distinctive family tombs of the Republican élite were soon surrounded and far outnumbered by columbaria filled with Rome’s middle and lower classes.

properties.name: Columbaria Statiliorum Taurorum (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Tombs of the Statilii Tauri, Rome.

The agglomeration of columbarium-tombs of the Statilii Tauri, their freedmen and slaves, formed the core of a large necropolis N of the ”Via Labicana-Praenestina”, close to Spes Vetus. 

Excavations from 1875 to 1877 have resulted in an extensive collection of funerary inscriptions and an overall ground-plan. Some parts of the necropolis may be dated with certainty to the Augustan period or earlier. A small columbarium in opus reticulatum may be dated, on the basis of wall frescoes with scenes from the Aeneas legend, to the 1st c. BC. 

The tomb of Q. Pompeius Sosus, whose name appears on the epitaph, dates to around 50 BC; its peperino blocks were reused as foundations for later columbaria. The funerary inscription of two slaves of Autronius Paetus was found in the area; their master was either the consul of 66 BC or his son, the consul of 33 BC, hence we can be sure that this area was in use during the Augustan period. 

Close by stood the main columbarium of the Statilii Tauri, in use from the time of Augustus to Claudius. Slaves and freedmen of the Statilii are attested nearby; it is likely that these columbaria were built at the same time. 

As for the rest of the necropolis, the evidence is less clear. Some columbaria remained in use until the time of Nero, yet this does not rule out an earlier construction date. As a general rule, those areas discovered at a depth of c. 9 m are considered Augustan or earlier, while those at c. 6 m are early Imperial.

properties.name: Columbarium (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Tomb, Rome.

A columbarium was unearthed in 1936 during works to expand the modern Via Nomentana near its intersection with Via Asmara. 

The remains included a series of structures in opus reticulatum pertaining to an underground sepulchral chamber with niches for cinerary urns. The names of the deceased are not preserved.

properties.name: Columbarium Libertorum Augusti (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Tomb of Augustus' freedmen, Rome.

It was discovered on the second mile of via Appia in 1724-26 in the course of excavations of the columbarium of the freedmen of Livia.

An overground construction of 3 adjacent chambers was coated with bricks and covered with plaster. It housed c. 3000 niches, each for 2 ceramic urns in the form of pots.

In 1747 the current state of the building was studied and fixed in a series of etchings by G. B. Piranesi.

In 1790 Carlo Labruzzi made another etching of the monument.

In 1796 the Vatican made a census of the taverns of the city for defining a number of tax-payers. According to this census the taverna inside the ruins of the columbarium was named Hosteria del colombario. At the present time the ruins are occupied by a restoraunt “Hostaria Antica Roma”.

properties.name: Columbarium Libertorum Liviae (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Tomb of Livia's freedmen, Rome.

Close to the columbarium of her husband, it could also hold 3,000 urns.

Unfortunately it was destroyed shorly after it was discovered on the second mile of via Appia in 1724-26.

properties.name: Columbarium Pomponii Hylae (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Tomb of Pomponius Hylas, Rome.

The columbarium of Pomponio Hylas is a 1st c. AD columbarium, discovered completely intact, located near Porta Latina on the Via Appia , shortly after leaving the city, with entrance from the Parco degli Scipioni. It was discovered in 1831 by Giampietro Campana.

Although it takes its name from Pomponius Hylas, who lived in the Flavian period, the building was dated between 14-54 AD thanks to two of its niches (one dedicated to a freedman of Tiberius and l other to a freedman of Claudia Ottavia, daughter of Claudius and Messalina). It was later bought by Pomponius for himself and his wife; he added a mosaic panel on the entrance steps, which is decorated with griffins and an incription.

properties.name: Mausoleum Augusti (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Tomb of Augustus, Rome.

One of the few surviving Augustan monuments is the monumental tomb built by Octavian early in his reign for both his own burial as well as the interment of other members of gens Iulia and his notable friends.

 In 1934, the environs of the ancient structure were cleared of residential urban fabric as part of the creation of a Fascist architectural ensemble at Piazzale Augusto Imperatore. The archaeological excavations and primary architectural restorations were completed in 1938.

In antiquity, the location of the Mausoleum, immediately W of the Via Flaminia, fell within the N limits of the Campus Martius. Its colossal architectural form marked the N entrance to the marshland of the Campus, having been built at the mouth of the isthmus created between Collis Hortulorum and the Tiber.

According to Suetonius, the building was already completed by 28 BC, but perhaps only to a certain extent, since at the time of the first burial at the Mausoleum (that of Marcellus in 23 BC), the construction may not have been complete.

properties.name: Mausoleum Caeciliae Metellae (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Tomb of Caecilia Metella, Rome.

The Tomb of Caecilia Metella is a mausoleum located just outside Rome at the three mile marker of the Via Appia. 

It was built during the 1st c. BC to honour Caecilia Metella, who was the daughter of Q. Caecilius Metellus Creticus, a consul in 69 BC, and wife of M. Licinius Crassus who served under Julius Caesar and was the son of the famous triumvir Marcus Crassus.

Located on top of a hill along the Via Appia, the Tomb of Caecilia Metella consists of a cylindrical drum, or rotunda, atop a square podium with the Caetani Castle (Castrum) attached at the rear. The square podium stands at 8.3 meters tall with the cylindrical drum standing at 12 m. The monument in totality stands at a height of 21.7 meters tall. The diameter of the circular drum is 29.5 m, equivalent to 100 Roman feet.

On the outside of the monument, an inscription can be seen reading "CAECILIAE |Q·CRETICI·F | METELLAE·CRASSI" indicating to whom this tomb was dedicated. Further up the monument, decorations can be seen depicting festoons and bucrania, heads of bulls, which were the inspiration for the area being named Capo Di Bove, meaning head of the bovine. 

At the top of the monument, medieval battlements can be seen from the time when the tomb was used as a fortress.

properties.name: Mausoleum Hadriani (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Tomb of Hadrian, Rome.

The tomb of the emperor Hadrian was erected on the right bank of the Tiber, between 134-139 AD.

 Originally the mausoleum was a decorated cylinder, with a garden top and golden quadriga. Hadrian's ashes were placed here a year after his death in Baiae in 138 AD, together with those of his wife Sabina, and his first adopted son, Lucius Aelius, who also died in 138.

 Following this, the remains of succeeding emperors were also placed here, the last recorded deposition being Caracalla in 217 AD. The urns containing these ashes were probably placed in what is now known as the Treasury room deep within the building. Hadrian also built the Pons Aelius facing straight onto the mausoleum – it still provides a scenic approach from the center of Rome and the left bank of the Tiber, and is renowned for the Baroque additions of statues of angels holding aloft instruments of the Passion of Christ.

properties.name: Mausoleum Romuli (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Tomb of Romulus, Rome.

The large circular tomb was built by the emperor Maxentius in the early 4th c. AD, probably with himself in mind and as a family tomb, but when his young son Valerius Romulus died he was buried there first and it was dedicated to him.

properties.name: Necropolis (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Cemetary, Rome.

Expansive Republican and early-Imperial necropolis on the Collis Hortulorum N of the Horti Sallustiani and clustered around the “Via Sepulcra Salaria”, the cemetery extended as far N as the Sepulcrum: M. Lucilius Paetus, which was easily the largest and most luxurious tomb in the area. 

Many columbaria in opus reticulatum are known to have stood in the area. Buried in these modest tombs were soldiers, merchants, freedmen, and the like. While most of the remains can be dated by their building material to the late-Republican or early-Imperial periods, sporadic depositions continued through the 4th c. AD. 

Despite excavations in the 1960s, evidence for the cemetery is scant, since the ancient remains were largely destroyed by late 19th-c. development.

properties.name: Pyramis C. Cestii (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Pyramid tomb of C. Cestius, Rome.

The Egyptianizing pyramid tomb of C. Cestius is located at a prominent intersection of the Via Ostiensis and the street which ran S from the central Aventine; it survives almost in its original state after being incorporated into the 3rd c. AD Aurelian Wall near the Porta Ostiensis.

 One of the inscriptions associated with the tomb provides an identification, and states that the tomb was constructed by Cestius’ heirs according to his will. The inscription on it mentions that Cestius was a praetor, a tribune of the plebs, and a septemvir of the Epulones. The heirs themselves are listed on two inscribed statue bases found nearby; the most prominent figure is Agrippa and his presence allows for a terminus ante quem of 12 BC (the year of his death). A terminus post quem is given by the connection of Cestius with the lex Iulia sumptuaria of 18 BC.

The sharply pointed shape of the pyramid is strongly reminiscent of the pyramids of Nubia, in particular of the kingdom of Meroë, which had been attacked by Rome in 23 BC. The similarity suggests that Cestius had possibly served in that campaign and perhaps intended the pyramid to serve as a commemoration.

properties.name: Remoria (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Tomb of Remus, Rome.

A site placed by most ancient sources on the Aventine and connected with Remus’ rival city foundation, specifically as the point where he was thought to have taken auspices and, later, to have been buried.

Ovid presents what may have been an Augustan-period mainstream view: that Remus took his ill-fated auspices on the mighty Saxum above the Bona Dea sanctuary. It is the location of the Saxum that allows the area of the Remoria to be specified. Since Bona Dea’s sanctuary is listed by the Regionary Catalogues in Regio XII, its location on the Aventine’s SE height (the “Lesser Aventine”) is certain, and the prominent cliff forming its N angle — a strategic point included within the Servian Wall.

properties.name: Sepulcra (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Tombs, Rome.

Remains of several tombs were brought to light in the 1920s near the intersection of Viale Regina Margherita and the Via Nomentana. 

Three rectangular tombs, two in opus reticulatum (c. 5.5 x 4.0 m and 4.5 x 3.5 m) and one of opus latericium (c. 3.5 x 3.5 m), were unearthed on the N side of the Via Nomentana. Also in the area was a tomb with two rooms in opus reticulatum, enclosed by a perimeter wall in opus quadratum of tufa blocks. Just S of this were walls of another Republican-era structure and the Aletii monument.

properties.name: Sepulcra (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Tombs, Rome.

Republican burials found on the S slope of the Caelius Mons, outside the Servian Wall.

 Three tile graves and a tufa sarcophagus, all dated to the Republic, were discovered in virgin earth below remains of the Imperial castra Peregrina during construction of the Convent and Hospital of the Little Company of Mary in 1905-9. Also recovered during the work were two sepulchral inscriptions. These burials offer rare evidence for the course of the Republican defenses across the Caelian.

properties.name: Sepulcra (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Tombs, Rome.

A group of five Republican tombs on the E heights of the Caelius Mons, located outside the Servian Wall.

 Three Republican chamber tombs were found during the construction of the Hospital of S. Giovanni; the tombs are situated along the “Via Caelimontana”, just outside the line of the Aqua Appia. One of the tombs has an especially well-preserved chamber cut into the living tufa rock (c. 3 x 2.5 m), and the finds associated with it suggest a date in the late 4th to early 3rd c. BC. Fragmentary remains uncovered during the same campaign suggest a fourth tomb stood nearby, while a fifth Republican tomb was found in 1887. These tombs are important, both as rare examples of pre-Imperial building on the Caelius Mons, and as data pertaining to the debated course of the Servian Wall.

properties.name: Sepulcrum (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Tomb, Rome.

Huge circular tomb, some 40 m in diameter, situated prominently on the Aventine’s extramural SE lobe in the former Vigna Cavalieri, perhaps not far from a regional road.

 The exterior of the cylinder, whose core of opus caementicium still stands 5.5 m high, was revetted with travertine blocks (of which some fragmented headers are still preserved). A barrel-vaulted radial tunnel, built mainly in opus reticulatum, still provides access to the center tomb where a vaulted ring chamber with 5 niches is constructed around a central pillar; its function may have been to support a cippus or statue on top of the tumulus’ mound. Because of its type and grand size, along with the use of opus reticulatum, the tomb has been attributed to the last years of Republic or first decades of the Principate. No clue exists as to its ancient owner.

properties.name: Sepulcrum (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Tomb, Rome.

This funerary monument, known as the Casa Tonda, was located on the Via Labicana-Praenestina 360 m outside the Porta Esquilina, now beneath Piazza Vittorio Emanuele. 

It consists of a cylinder (diam. 20 m) mounted on a square base (24 m), and is universally dated to the late 1st c. BC. The identity of the tomb’s occupant remains a matter of speculation. Maecenas is a possible candidate, given the proximity of the Horti Maecenatis and the fact that one tradition placed the final resting spot of both Horace and Maecenas ‘on the furthest edges of the Esquiline’.

properties.name: Sepulcrum (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Tomb, Rome.

Republican opus quadratum tomb in tufa and peperino (c. 8 x 8 m) located well outside the Servian Wall on the Via Nomentana.

 The tomb was on the same level as the pre-viaduct remains of the Via Nomentana, though not aligned with the street. The deceased is unknown.

properties.name: Sepulcrum (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Tomb, Rome.

Republican tomb on the W side of the Via Salaria located between the Sepulcrum: M. Aemilius Dulio and the Sepulcrum: Cornelia L. Scipionis f.

 The monument was built in opus quadratum of tufa with a caementicium nucleus (c. 10 x 8 m); a second tomb of the same style may have been built 8 m to the N. Neither tomb owner is known.

properties.name: Sepulcrum (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Tomb, Rome.

Partial remains of a monumental tomb discovered at the NW corner of the Collis Hortulorum on the grounds of the convent of S. Maria del Popolo.

 Foundations of Anio tufa and opus caementicium suggest an Augustan date. These remains have been tentatively associated with the Sepulcrum of the Domitii, but not enough is known about that monument to warrant any firm identification.

properties.name: Sepulcrum A. Hirtii (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Tomb of A. Hirtius, Rome.

Burial monument in the W Campus Martius, built for A. Hirtius, consul in 43 BC and killed during the battle of Mutina the same year. 

A public burial in the Campus Martius was granted to him and his co-consul of 43 BC, C. Vibius Pansa Caetronianus. 

Remains of the tomb precinct have been identified with brick walls (H. 2.65 m) covered by a course of slanted travertine blocks standing beneath Palazzo della Cancelleria at the Euripus. The actual burial chamber inside the precinct has disappeared, perhaps reused as building material (intensive activity of marmorari has been revealed by numerous late-antique inscriptions and the presence in the tomb of fragmentary sculptures from later periods).

 The identification of the structure as the sepulcrum of Hirtius is supported by the presence of three cippi carrying the inscription A. HIRTIVS A. F. which were inserted at the corners of the brick precinct wall. From a passage of Cicero it can be assumed that Hirtius and Pansa found their resting place in the Horti of Mark Antony.

properties.name: Sepulcrum Aletiorum (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Tomb of the Aletii, Rome.

An inscribed funerary relief of the Aletii family found on the S side of the Via Nomentana. 

The late-Republican travertine relief depicts three male (all labeled C. ALETIVS) and one female (inscribed ALETIA) portrait busts; their hairstyles and garments suggest a Caesarian date. Since this type of sculpture was designed to be encased in the façade of a tomb, it is likely that the monument of this family was located in the vicinity.

properties.name: Sepulcrum Arruntiorum (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Tomb of the Arruntii, Rome.

This tomb structure lay N of the ”Via Labicana-Praenestina” and W of the Porta Maggiore, between Via Giolitti and Via di Porta Maggiore; it consisted of three rooms in opus reticulatum with a vaulted stuccoed roof.

 These walls are dated to the Augustan period. Discovered in 1733 and demolished c. 1900, its ground-plan is known from various 18th-c. drawings. An inscription over the entrance drawn by Piranesi records that it was constructed by L. Arruntius (cos. 6 AD) to house the funerary urns of his dependents and descendants.

properties.name: Sepulcrum C. Cornelii Galli (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Tomb of C. Cornelius Gallus, Rome.

Early Imperial pyramidal tomb located on the E side of the Tiber, at the intersection of the post-Augustan Via Cornelia and the Via Triumphalis.

 In the Middle Ages, it remained a major topographic landmark, known as the “Romuli sepulcrum”. The actual tomb was destroyed by Pope Alexander VI in 1499 and only the foundations are now preserved.

The clear Egyptian typology of this tomb easily allows for a date in the Augustan period, a time when an Egyptianizing style strongly influenced architecture in Rome. Most probably its owner was Cornelius Gallus, the first prefect of Egypt. This identification is strengthened by the name of the later street passing nearby, Via Cornelia. A similar pyramidal tomb, the Sepulcrum: C. Cestius, still stands on the S periphery of the city.

properties.name: Sepulcrum C. Publii Bibuli (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Tomb of C. Publius Bibulus, Rome.

The façade of this tomb still stands in situ at the foot of the Arx next to the Victor Emanuel Monument; originally, it faced onto the Via Flaminia. 

The structure is dated to the early 1st c. BC, but prosopographical considerations suggest that Bibulus himself lived in the 2nd c. BC and that this is a rebuilding of an earlier tomb. The façade remains, but the rear of the tomb is not known.

properties.name: Sepulcrum C. Sulpicii Platorini (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Tomb of C. Sulpicius Platorinus, Rome

The monumental clan tomb of the Sulpicii Platorini at the Transtiberine head of the Pons Agrippae, immediately inside the Aurelian Wall, probably of late-Augustan date.

 Discovered and excavated during the construction of the modern Tiber embankments in 188, it was reconstructed in the Museo Nazionale Romano in 1911. It was a squarish structure, 7.44 x 7.12 m in plan, raised on a travertine podium.

Surviving are several inscriptions associated with the burials accommodated within the tomb, which date from the Augustan to Flavian periods. The building inscription over the entrance mentions C. Sulpicius Platorinus, who is widely accepted as the triumvir monetalis of 18 BC, although the construction of the tomb could also be attributed to a grandson.

properties.name: Sepulcrum C. Vibii Pansae (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Tomb of C. Vibius Pansa, Rome.

Funerary monument dedicated to C. Vibius Pansa Cetronianus, consul in 43 BC with A. Hirtius, who died the same year. 

The actual structure has not been found, but a large travertine slab, carrying the dedicatory inscription EX S(ENATVS) C(ONSVLTO) C. VIBIO C.F. CETRONIAN(O) CO(N)S(VLI) was uncovered beneath Palazzo Italiani in the W Campus Martius. The proximity of the Sepulcrum: A. Hirtius to the findspot of Pansa’s dedicatory inscription indicates that the latter had his resting place nearby and shared the honour of a public burial.

Whether the structure was located inside or outside the pomerium in the Augustan period has been speculated. An inscription dedicated by C. Vibius T.f., a nephew of C. Vibius Pansa Cetronianus, once suggested that he may have built a monumental funerary structure for his wife and brother-in-law in the Campus Martius.

properties.name: Sepulcrum Corneliae L. Scipionis f. (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Tomb of Cornelia, Rome.

Tomb for Cornelia, daughter of L. Scipio, and wife to a Vatienus, located well outside the Servian Wall along the Via Salaria.

 Traditionally, the tomb inscription is associated with a circular Augustan tumulus monument revetted in marble, which was uncovered when the porta Salaria was destroyed in 1871. The demolition work revealed extensive remains, including an opus caementicium nucleus and numerous carved elements of the superstructure in travertine and marble. The style of the bucrania and lettering suggest a date of c. 40-30 BC.

properties.name: Sepulcrum Corneliorum Scipionum (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Tomb of the Cornelii Scipiones, Rome.

Family tomb of the Cornelii Scipiones, which faced onto a minor cross street connecting the Via Appia with the Via Latina, about 1 km outside the Porta Capena.

 One of the most illustrious tombs of the city, it was originally built in the 3rd c. BC, when an irregular square chamber (c. 13.5 x 14.5 m) was cut into the living rock to house the family’s sarcophagi, many of which survive.

 Over time, the internal chambers of the tomb were expanded (to hold over 30 burials), and in the 2nd c. BC a new, monumental columnar façade was erected. It was probably at that point that the tomb was adorned with statues of P. Cornelius Scipio Africanus (cos. 205, 194 BC), L. Cornelius Scipio Asiaticus (cos. 190 BC), and the poet Q. Ennius.

With the extinction of the Cornelii Scipiones in the early 1st c. BC, the tomb was inherited by the Cornelii Lentuli, who reused it briefly under Claudius for the burial of Cornelia Gaetulica and M. Iunius Silanus Lutatius Catulus, respectively the wife and nephew of Lentulus Gaetulicus (cos. 26 AD).

properties.name: Sepulcrum Hilarii Fusci (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Tomb of Hilarius Fuscus, Rome.

The Tomb of Hilarus Fuscus is a funerary monument, located near the fourth mile of the Appian Way.

 The tomb was restored by Luigi Canina in the mid-1800s. An inscription bearing the names of those represented on the masonry disappeared in the period between 1978 and 1998. The sculptures are copies: the originals are now in the National Museum of the Baths of Diocletian.

The architecture of the tomb and the analysis of figures (particularly the hairstyle of the women) suggests the tomb was built at end of the Republican period and the beginning of the Imperial age (c. 30 BC).

properties.name: Sepulcrum Horatiorum et Curiatiorum (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Tomb of the Horatii and Curiatii, Rome.

The mausoleum is situated on the southern boundary of the residential area, on the edge of Appian Way and is a unique example for its architecture reminding us of the Etruscan cinerary urns in Volterra.

Local history associates the mausoleum to the warriors Horatii and Curiatii, but historically speaking is more likely to be a reconstruction of the tomb of Arunte (an Etruscan leader) member of the ancient Arruntia family who had properties in the area. In fact, it was built in the first half of the 1st c. BC approximately six centuries after the famous battle of the Horatii and Curiatii.

It was built in huge peperino blocks; on a square base there are four truncated cones on the corners (only two remained intact) and probably a bigger fifth one stood on the drum-shaped central base containing the burial chamber of which only ruins can be found.

properties.name: Sepulcrum M. Aemilii Dulionis (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Tomb of M. Aemilius Dulio, Rome.

Remains of a tufa mausoleum in opus quadratum were found on the W side of Via Salaria along with an inscribed marble slab naming the tomb’s proprietor, M. Aemilius Dulio. The tomb lay at the far E edge of the “Sepulcra Salaria”.

properties.name: Sepulcrum M. Lucilii Paeti (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Tomb of M. Lucilius Paetus, Rome.

Tumulus-style tomb built on the Via Salaria by M. Lucilius Paetus, who held the offices of tribunus militum, praefectus fabrum and praefectus equitum under Augustus, for himself and his sister in c. 20 BC.

 A ring of travertine ashlar masonry (diam. 34.9 m) and a burial chamber survive; originally the tomb was crowned by an earthen tumulus akin to the Mausoleum of Augustus. The tomb is the largest and most luxurious monument known in the “Sepulcra Salaria”.

properties.name: Sepulcrum M. Servilii Quarti (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Tomb of M. Servilius Quartus, Rome.

The tomb of M. Servilius Quartus made on bricks on the Via Appia and was restored in 1808.

properties.name: Sepulcrum M. Vergilii Eurysacum (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Tomb of M. Vergilius Eurysaces, Rome.

Sepulchral monument erected by M. Vergilius Eurysaces, a wholesale baker, inside the fork of the Via Praenestina and Via Labicana just outside the line of aqueducts. 

It is dated to the decade 30-20 BC. In the 3rd c. AD it was enclosed within one of the semicircular towers of the porta Praenestina of the Aurelian Wall, hence its exceptional state of preservation. 

A relief representing various stages of bread production runs along the top of the tomb. The relief depicts, on the south side, the delivery and grinding of grain and sifting of flour; on the north, the mixing and kneading of dough, forming of round loaves, and baking in a domed "pizza-type" oven; and, on the west, the stacking of loaves in baskets and their being taken for weighing.

In 1838 it was again exposed. Excavations have established its ground-plan as trapezoidal in shape, with a sharp apex (destroyed with the construction of the semicircular tower). There were many other tombs which lined Via Labicana E of the Porta Maggiore, some of which have been excavated but not identified or dated.

properties.name: Sepulcrum M. Vipsanii Agrippae (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Tomb of M. Vipsanius Agrippa, Rome

Tomb M. Vipsanius Agrippa built for himself in the Campus Martius before his ashes were interred in the Mausoleum of Augustus.

 Recently the tomb, which must have functioned as a cenotaph, has been tentatively associated with the remains of 5 parallel walls of peperino, each pierced by an opening 1.9 m wide, that were found in the 1880s under Via Vittorio Emanuele in the area of the Vallicella.

 A large fragment (L. 2.8 m) of a monumental altar pulvinus (bolster) was found within the trench. Recent reexamination of the building materials and techniques suggests a late-Republican or early-Augustan date for the structure, while the sculptural decoration of the pulvinus can be ascribed to a relatively narrow chronological period early in the Augustan principate. However, the pulvinus was not necessarily found in its original location; as no other altar remains were found, it may have been taken to the site as spolia, since several late-Imperial workshops where marble fragments were re-carved are known in the W Campus Martius. Given the uncertainties surrounding the pulvinus, the unusual building remains, and the absence of corroborative testimony to support that of Dio Cassius, it is ot certain that this is his tomb.

properties.name: Sepulcrum Octaviae M. f. (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Tomb of Octavia, Rome.

Marble tomb belonging to an Octavia, daughter of a Marcus Octavius (perhaps M. Octavius Cn. f.), and probably wife to an Appius, dating to the mid-1st c. BC.

 The tomb was discovered in 1616 near the intersection of Via di Porta Pinciana and Via Sistina; after it was drawn and recorded by Grimaldi, the tomb was dismantled for spolia.

 Grimaldi sketched a flat-roofed, rectangular façade preceded by a shallow, distyle, Ionic porch whose architrave bore the epitaph. The tomb probably had a rectangular plan with the inscription and entrance on opposite sides; Grimaldi did not include dimensions, so the tomb’s depth has been estimated (c. 5 m) based on comparison with similar tombs.

properties.name: Sepulcrum Priscillae (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Tomb of Priscilla, Rome.

The Tomb of Priscilla is a monumental tomb erected in the 1st c. AD on the Appian Way, situated opposite the Church of Domine Quo Vadis.

The Tomb belonged to Priscilla, wife of Titus Flavius Abascanto, a freedman of the emperor Domitian.

On a quadrangular base, covered with travertine blocks (opus quadratum), there were in the past two superimposed cylindrical towers, built in opus mixtum and opus reticulatum, the upper one with 13 niches designed to house statues of the dead.

The funerary cell covered by a barrel vault is entered via a corridor, currently accessible from the basement of one of the houses that are adjacent to the monument. The cell was coated within by blocks of travertine and included three niches designed to house sarcophagi.

The tomb was used in the 11th century and later as a fortress. It belonged to the counts of Tusculum, and later the Caetani.

properties.name: Sepulcrum Q. Terentii Rufi (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Tomb of Q. Terentius Rufus, Rome.

A Republican tomb in opus quadratum of tufa (c. 4 x 5 m), located along the N border of the Horti Sallustiani on the “Via Sepulcra Salaria”.

 Inscribed across the façade in large letters was the tomb owner’s name, Q. TERENTILIVS RVFVS, making this one of the few tombs within the “Sepulcra Salaria” whose proprietor is known.

properties.name: Sepulcrum Rusticelii (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Tomb fo Rusticelius, Rome.

Monumental tomb on the S side of Monte Testaccio which belonged to a member of the Rusticelii family and was built sometime between the mid-2nd and mid-1st c. BC.

 Excavated in the 1690s during the construction of a wine cellar, the monument’s precise topographical location seems not to have been properly surveyed.

The size of the monument was roughly 10 x 10 m in plan and constructed extensively in tufa stone; thus both in design and execution it must have been quite similar to the nearby Sepulcrum: Ser. Sulpicius Galba.

properties.name: Sepulcrum Semproniorum (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Tomb of the Sempronii, Rome.

Well-preserved chamber-tomb on the W slope of the Quirinal belonging to a C. Sempronius, his sister, and his mother Larcia. Now located in a cellar below Palazzo S. Felice, the tomb has a travertine façade with an arched entranceway leading to a vaulted tomb chamber carved into the tufa hillside. 

Much of the tomb’s superstructure is extant, including the façade which faced onto the Vicus Salutis, an important road from the Campus Martius to the Porta Sanqualis and the Quirinal. The tomb is dated to the second half of the 1st c. BC based upon the lettering of the inscription and style of the architectural decoration.

properties.name: Sepulcrum Ser. Sulpicii Galbae (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Tomb of Ser. Sulpicius Galba, Rome.

Monumental tomb structure of the late 2nd c. BC in the Emporium area, belonging to Servius Sulpicius Galba, a prominent member of the Sulpicii Galbae family, according to the building inscription; two men of this name are known, one of whom served as consul in 144 BC and the other in 108 BC. The later date is generally preferred for the tomb on the basis of its architectural type and construction technique. Constructed of fine Monte Verde tufa masonry with peperino blocks for its cornice, the monument should be dated to c. 100 BC.

The monument was erected in the urban ensemble of the Emporium between the Horrea Galbana structures and the vast warehouse called the “Porticus Aemilia”. As a small square structure in plan, it faced the street that connected the Via Ostiensis to the southerly structures of the Emporium area, marking a slight bend in its course. The tomb was excavated in 1885 and subsequently re-erected in the Antiquarium Comunale on the Caelian . The building can also be traced on the Severan Marble Plan, although it is not labeled.

properties.name: Ustrinum Domus Augustae (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Imperial Cremation Ground, Rome.

A modern term used to describe what was in fact a post-Augustan monument marking the site where the bodies of certain members of Augustus’ family were cremated.

 In 1777, six large travertine slabs bearing inscriptions which refer to different members of the imperial household came to light in the area of Piazza S. Carlo al Corso, near the Mausoleum of Augustus. Variously interpreted as orthostat cippi or as paving stones, three of them make use of the phrase HIC CREMATVS EST. For many years these inscriptions laid the basis for the unsupported assumption that this was the site of the funereal καύστρα described by Strabo, in which Augustus’ body was cremated in 14 AD. This interpretation has now been overturned. 

While this was not the site of Augustus’ cremation, its proximity to the Mausoleum made it a logical place to conduct the cremations of other Julio-Claudians who were interred in the family tomb. Notably, the three inscriptions that mention cremation all belong to children of Germanicus who died during the reign of Augustus. These include TI. CAESAR GERMANICI F. and an unnamed [CAES]AR, who died as infants, as well as C. CAESAR, GERMANICI F., the elder brother of the future emperor Gaius, whose death in childhood was mourned deeply by Augustus and Livia. 

Thus, although the archaeological remains from this site belong to a post-Augustan monument, we can at least be confident that cremations of persons in the imperial household did take place alongside the Via Flaminia in the vicinity of the Mausoleum.

properties.name: Muri Aureliani (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Aurelian Walls, Rome.

The Aurelian Walls are a line of city walls built between 271-275 AD in Rome during the reign of Emperors Aurelian and Probus. They superseded the earlier Servian Wall built during the 4th c. BC.

The walls enclosed all the seven hills of Rome plus the Campus Martius and, on the right bank of the Tiber, the Trastevere district. The river banks within the city limits appear to have been left unfortified, although they were fortified along the Campus Martius. The size of the entire enclosed area is 1,400 hectares (3,500 acres).

The actual effectiveness of the wall is disputable, given the relatively small size of the city's garrison. The entire combined strength of the Praetorian Guard, cohortes urbanae, and vigiles of Rome was only about 25,000 men – far too few to defend the circuit adequately. However, the military intention of the wall was not to withstand prolonged siege warfare; it was not common for the barbarian armies to besiege cities, as they were insufficiently equipped and provisioned for such a task. Instead, they carried out hit-and-run raids against ill-defended targets. The wall was a deterrent against such tactics.

Parts of the wall were doubled in height by Maxentius, who also improved the watch-towers. In 401, under Honorius, the walls and the gates were improved. At this time, the Tomb of Hadrian across the Tiber was incorporated as a fortress in the city defenses.

properties.name: Muri Servii Tullii (Roma, Italia)
properties.description:
Servian Walls, Rome.

The Servian Walls were a defensive barrier constructed around the city of Rome in the early 4th c. BC. 

The wall was built of volcanic tuff and was up to 10 m (33 ft) in height in places, 3.6 m (12 ft) wide at its base, 11 km (6.8 mi) long, and is believed to have had 16 main gates, and it enclosed a total area of 608 acres. 

In the 3rd c. AD it was superseded by the construction of the larger Aurelian Walls as the city of Rome grew beyond the boundary of the Servian Walls

The wall is named after the sixth Roman King, Servius Tullius.
